Python Fundamentals

Parse a .env file into typed settings★☆☆ · ex01_env_config

fundamentals.none, fundamentals.loops, fundamentals.loop_control, fundamentals.conditionals, fundamentals.variables

Problem

LLM apps are configured through env vars / .env files (model name, temperature, max tokens, feature flags...). Everything arrives as a string - converting it is your job.

  1. coerce(raw: str) -> bool | int | float | str | None

    • strip surrounding whitespace first
    • value wrapped in matching quotes ('...' or "...") -> the inner string, NOT converted ('"42"' -> "42", "'true'" -> "true")
    • "true" / "yes" / "on" -> True; "false" / "no" / "off" -> False (case-insensitive)
    • "" / "none" / "null" -> None (case-insensitive)
    • anything int() accepts -> int ("42", "-3", "+7", "1_000")
    • else anything float() accepts -> float ("0.7", "1e-4")
    • otherwise -> the stripped string unchanged ("gpt-4o-mini")

  2. parse_env(text: str) -> dict

    • one KEY=VALUE per line; split on the FIRST "=" only (values may contain "=", e.g. "DSN=postgres://h/db?sslmode=require")
    • skip blank lines and lines whose first non-space character is "#"
    • an optional leading "export " is ignored
    • key is stripped and must satisfy str.isidentifier(); value goes through coerce()
    • for an UNQUOTED value, " #" starts an inline comment: "MODEL=small # cheap" -> "small"
    • a non-blank, non-comment line without "=" or with an invalid key -> ValueError whose message contains "line <n>" (1-based line number)
    • later duplicates override earlier ones

  3. first_set(*values, default=None)

    • return the first value that is not None, else default
    • 0, 0.0, False and "" are legitimate settings and must be returned (precedence chain: CLI flag -> env var -> config file -> default)

Interviewers look for

  • bool("False") is True - bool() of a non-empty string is always True; parse explicitly.
  • int("3.0") raises ValueError; float("3") works - order of attempts matters.
  • cli or env or default is a bug: it skips 0 / False / "" (truthiness != "is set"). Use is not None.
  • str.partition / split("=", 1) instead of split("=") for values containing "=".
  • continue to skip lines keeps the happy path un-nested.

Work in exercises/py/01_fundamentals/ex01_env_config.py (or copy the starter code into any scratch file).

from typing import Any
Scalar = bool | int | float | str | None

def coerce(raw: str) -> Scalar:
    raise NotImplementedError

def parse_env(text: str) -> dict[str, Scalar]:
    raise NotImplementedError

def first_set(*values: Any, default: Any=None) -> Any:
    raise NotImplementedError

from typing import Any

Scalar = bool | int | float | str | None


def coerce(raw: str) -> Scalar:
    value = raw.strip()
    if len(value) >= 2 and value[0] == value[-1] and value[0] in "'\"":
        return value[1:-1]
    lowered = value.lower()
    if lowered in ("true", "yes", "on"):
        return True
    if lowered in ("false", "no", "off"):
        return False
    if lowered in ("", "none", "null"):
        return None
    try:
        return int(value)
    except ValueError:
        pass
    try:
        return float(value)
    except ValueError:
        return value


def parse_env(text: str) -> dict[str, Scalar]:
    env: dict[str, Scalar] = {}
    for lineno, line in enumerate(text.splitlines(), start=1):
        stripped = line.strip()
        if not stripped or stripped.startswith("#"):
            continue
        if stripped.startswith("export "):
            stripped = stripped.removeprefix("export ").lstrip()
        key, sep, value = stripped.partition("=")
        key = key.strip()
        if not sep:
            raise ValueError(f"line {lineno}: expected KEY=VALUE, got {line!r}")
        if not key.isidentifier():
            raise ValueError(f"line {lineno}: invalid key {key!r}")
        value = value.strip()
        if not value.startswith(("'", '"')):
            value = value.split(" #", 1)[0]
        env[key] = coerce(value)
    return env


def first_set(*values: Any, default: Any = None) -> Any:
    for value in values:
        if value is not None:
            return value
    return default

Text normalisation for an LLM pipeline★☆☆ · ex02_text_normalize

fundamentals.set_comprehensions, fundamentals.slicing

Problem

Prefer comprehensions where they stay readable; a plain loop is fine where it is clearer.

  1. normalize(text: str) -> str

    • casefold, split on any whitespace, strip punctuation (string.punctuation) from the edges of each token, drop tokens that become empty, join with a single space
    • " Hello, WORLD!! -- it's " -> "hello world it's" (inner apostrophe kept)

  2. vocabulary(docs: list[str], min_len: int = 1) -> set[str]

    • the set of distinct normalized tokens across all docs with len(token) >= min_len

  3. first_positions(tokens: list[str]) -> dict[str, int]

    • token -> index of its FIRST occurrence; keys in first-occurrence order
    • ["a", "b", "a", "c"] -> {"a": 0, "b": 1, "c": 3}
    • careful: the obvious {t: i for i, t in enumerate(tokens)} gives the LAST occurrence

  4. ngrams(tokens: list[str], n: int) -> list[tuple[str, ...]]

    • all contiguous n-grams in order; fewer than n tokens -> []
    • n <= 0 -> ValueError

  5. strip_code_fence(text: str) -> str

    • LLMs often wrap JSON in a markdown fence: a "json" line, the payload, a "" line
    • if the stripped text starts with : drop the first line ( or json ...), drop the last line if it is exactly, return the remainder stripped
    • otherwise return text.strip()

Interviewers look for

  • Duplicate keys in a dict comprehension: the last write wins (iterate reversed, or use dict.setdefault in a loop, to keep the first).
  • Strings are immutable: every strip/lower/replace returns a new string; build with " ".join(...), never += in a loop (quadratic in the worst case).
  • casefold() vs lower() (German "ß" -> "ss") for case-insensitive matching.
  • Slicing never raises IndexError: tokens[i:i+n] near the end just returns fewer items - which is why the range bound for ngrams matters.

Work in exercises/py/01_fundamentals/ex02_text_normalize.py (or copy the starter code into any scratch file).

import string

def normalize(text: str) -> str:
    raise NotImplementedError

def vocabulary(docs: list[str], min_len: int=1) -> set[str]:
    raise NotImplementedError

def first_positions(tokens: list[str]) -> dict[str, int]:
    raise NotImplementedError

def ngrams(tokens: list[str], n: int) -> list[tuple[str, ...]]:
    raise NotImplementedError

def strip_code_fence(text: str) -> str:
    raise NotImplementedError

import string


def normalize(text: str) -> str:
    tokens = (tok.strip(string.punctuation) for tok in text.casefold().split())
    return " ".join(tok for tok in tokens if tok)


def vocabulary(docs: list[str], min_len: int = 1) -> set[str]:
    return {tok for doc in docs for tok in normalize(doc).split() if len(tok) >= min_len}


def first_positions(tokens: list[str]) -> dict[str, int]:
    # a comprehension {tok: i ...} would keep the LAST index (later writes win);
    # setdefault only writes the first time a key is seen
    positions: dict[str, int] = {}
    for i, tok in enumerate(tokens):
        positions.setdefault(tok, i)
    return positions


def ngrams(tokens: list[str], n: int) -> list[tuple[str, ...]]:
    if n <= 0:
        raise ValueError("n must be >= 1")
    return [tuple(tokens[i : i + n]) for i in range(len(tokens) - n + 1)]


def strip_code_fence(text: str) -> str:
    stripped = text.strip()
    if not stripped.startswith("```"):
        return stripped
    lines = stripped.splitlines()[1:]
    if lines and lines[-1].strip() == "```":
        lines = lines[:-1]
    return "\n".join(lines).strip()

Fix the aliasing / identity bugs★★☆ · ex03_aliasing_bugs

fundamentals.operators, fundamentals.nested_structures

Problem

An eval harness has four helpers that "work on my machine". Each has a bug rooted in how Python names, objects and mutability work. Write the FIXED versions (same names/behaviour as described, minus the bug).

def init_scores(n_models, n_tasks):
    return [[0.0] * n_tasks] * n_models                 # (1)

def with_overrides(base, **overrides):                  # with_overrides(cfg, llm__temperature=0.2)
    cfg = base.copy()                                   # (2)
    for dotted, value in overrides.items():
        section, key = dotted.split("__")
        cfg[section][key] = value
    return cfg

def find_doc(docs, doc_id):
    for doc in docs:
        if doc["id"] is doc_id:                         # (3)
            return doc
    return None

def add_tag(tags, tag):
    if tag not in tags:
        tags += [tag]                                   # (4)
    return tags

def is_missing(value):
    return value == None                                # (5)

Required behaviour 1. init_scores(n_models, n_tasks) -> n_models x n_tasks grid of 0.0 whose rows are independent lists (writing grid[0][1] must not change any other row). 2. with_overrides(base, **overrides) -> new config dict; base (including its nested dicts) must be left completely unchanged. A missing section is created. 3. find_doc(docs, doc_id) -> the first doc whose "id" equals doc_id, else None - also when the id string was built at runtime (read from a file, concatenated, json-decoded...). 4. add_tag(tags, tag) -> a NEW list with tag appended if not already present; the caller's list is never mutated. 5. is_missing(value) -> True only for None, even for objects whose eq claims to equal everything (mocks, NumPy arrays, ORM columns).

Interviewers look for

  • [row] * n repeats a reference to one list; use a comprehension to build n lists.
  • dict.copy() / list.copy() / slicing are SHALLOW: nested containers are shared. copy.deepcopy, or rebuild the nested level you change.
  • is compares identity; equal strings are not guaranteed to be the same object (interning of literals is a CPython implementation detail). Use == for values, is only for singletons (None, True/False, sentinels).
  • a += b on a list mutates in place (list.iadd == extend) - every alias sees it; a = a + b rebinds to a new list. On a tuple, += always creates a new object.
  • x == None dispatches to x.eq which can return anything; x is None can't be fooled.

Work in exercises/py/01_fundamentals/ex03_aliasing_bugs.py (or copy the starter code into any scratch file).

import copy
from typing import Any

def init_scores(n_models: int, n_tasks: int) -> list[list[float]]:
    raise NotImplementedError

def with_overrides(base: dict[str, Any], **overrides: Any) -> dict[str, Any]:
    raise NotImplementedError

def find_doc(docs: list[dict[str, Any]], doc_id: str) -> dict[str, Any] | None:
    raise NotImplementedError

def add_tag(tags: list[str], tag: str) -> list[str]:
    raise NotImplementedError

    raise NotImplementedError

import copy
from typing import Any


def init_scores(n_models: int, n_tasks: int) -> list[list[float]]:
    return [[0.0] * n_tasks for _ in range(n_models)]


def with_overrides(base: dict[str, Any], **overrides: Any) -> dict[str, Any]:
    cfg = copy.deepcopy(base)
    for dotted, value in overrides.items():
        section, key = dotted.split("__", 1)
        cfg.setdefault(section, {})[key] = value
    return cfg


def find_doc(docs: list[dict[str, Any]], doc_id: str) -> dict[str, Any] | None:
    for doc in docs:
        if doc["id"] == doc_id:
            return doc
    return None


def add_tag(tags: list[str], tag: str) -> list[str]:
    return list(tags) if tag in tags else [*tags, tag]


def is_missing(value: object) -> bool:
    return value is None

Context-window slicing and usage formatting★★☆ · ex04_slice_and_format

fundamentals.conditionals

Problem

  1. last_turns(history: list, n: int) -> list

    • the last n items (a new list); n == 0 -> []; n larger than len -> all items
    • n < 0 -> ValueError
    • this is how a chat app keeps "the last n turns" inside the context window

  2. truncate_middle(text: str, max_len: int, marker: str = "...") -> str

    • len(text) <= max_len -> text unchanged
    • otherwise keep the head and the tail with marker in between so that the result is EXACTLY max_len characters; when the kept characters can't split evenly the head gets the extra one truncate_middle("abcdefghij", 7) -> "ab...ij"; truncate_middle("abcdefghij", 6) -> "ab...j"
    • max_len < len(marker) -> ValueError (used for logging huge prompts/tool outputs: the start AND the end are informative)

  3. format_usage(prompt_tokens: int, completion_tokens: int, cost_usd: float) -> str

    • "prompt=1,234 completion=56 total=1,290 cost=$0.0123"
    • thousands separators on all token counts, cost with exactly 4 decimals

  4. progress_bar(done: int, total: int, width: int = 20) -> str

    • f"[{'#' * filled}{'.' * (width - filled)}] {percent} ({done}/{total})"
    • filled = done * width // total (floor), percent is done/total as a whole-number percentage right-aligned in 4 chars: " 0%", " 25%", "100%" progress_bar(5, 20, 10) -> "[##........] 25% (5/20)"
    • total <= 0, width <= 0, or done outside 0..total -> ValueError

Interviewers look for

  • xs[-n:] with n == 0 is xs[0:] - the WHOLE list. A classic off-by-zero bug.
  • Slices clamp to bounds and never raise; they always return a new object (shallow copy).
  • Floor division and modulo: a // b, a % b, ceil via -(-a // b); / always gives float.
  • Format spec mini-language: {n:,}, {x:.4f}, {p:>4.0%}, {s:<10}, nested {x:{w}}, and {x=} for debugging.

Work in exercises/py/01_fundamentals/ex04_slice_and_format.py (or copy the starter code into any scratch file).

def last_turns[T](history: list[T], n: int) -> list[T]:
    raise NotImplementedError

def truncate_middle(text: str, max_len: int, marker: str='...') -> str:
    raise NotImplementedError

def format_usage(prompt_tokens: int, completion_tokens: int, cost_usd: float) -> str:
    raise NotImplementedError

def progress_bar(done: int, total: int, width: int=20) -> str:
    raise NotImplementedError

def last_turns[T](history: list[T], n: int) -> list[T]:
    if n < 0:
        raise ValueError("n must be >= 0")
    # history[-0:] would return everything
    return history[len(history) - n :] if n else []


def truncate_middle(text: str, max_len: int, marker: str = "...") -> str:
    if max_len < len(marker):
        raise ValueError("max_len shorter than marker")
    if len(text) <= max_len:
        return text
    keep = max_len - len(marker)
    tail = keep // 2
    head = keep - tail
    # text[-0:] is the whole string, so slice the tail with an explicit start index
    return text[:head] + marker + text[len(text) - tail :]


def format_usage(prompt_tokens: int, completion_tokens: int, cost_usd: float) -> str:
    total = prompt_tokens + completion_tokens
    return (
        f"prompt={prompt_tokens:,} completion={completion_tokens:,} "
        f"total={total:,} cost=${cost_usd:.4f}"
    )


def progress_bar(done: int, total: int, width: int = 20) -> str:
    if total <= 0 or width <= 0:
        raise ValueError("total and width must be positive")
    if not 0 <= done <= total:
        raise ValueError("done must be within 0..total")
    filled = done * width // total
    return f"[{'#' * filled}{'.' * (width - filled)}] {done / total:>4.0%} ({done}/{total})"

Safe access into nested LLM API responses★★☆ · ex05_nested_response

fundamentals.type_conversion, fundamentals.loops

Problem

LLM APIs return deeply nested JSON (choices -> message -> tool_calls -> function ...), and fields go missing (content filters, truncation, provider differences).

  1. get_path(obj, path, default=None)

    • path is either a dotted string "choices.0.message.content" or a list of segments (["choices", 0, "message", "content"])
    • at a dict: look the segment up as a key
    • at a list/tuple: the segment must be an int, or a str that int() accepts ("0", "-1"); negative indexes work like Python's
    • any miss (missing key, index out of range, non-numeric index into a list, descending into a scalar or None) -> default
    • a key that exists with value None returns None, NOT default
    • empty path ("" or []) -> obj itself
    • never raises for a missing/malformed path

  2. flatten(obj: dict, sep: str = ".") -> dict[str, Any]

    • {"a": {"b": 1, "c": [10, {"d": 2}]}} -> {"a.b": 1, "a.c.0": 10, "a.c.1.d": 2}
    • list elements are addressed by index; empty dicts/lists are kept as leaf values ({"meta": {}} -> {"meta": {}})
    • flatten({}) -> {}; obj that is not a dict -> TypeError
    • the order of keys follows a depth-first walk of the input

  3. extract_tool_calls(response: dict) -> list[tuple[str, dict | None]]

    • OpenAI-style: response["choices"][0]["message"]["tool_calls"] is a list of {"function": {"name": str, "arguments": "<JSON string>"}}
    • return [(name, parsed_arguments), ...]; arguments that are not valid JSON or don't decode to a dict -> None (the model produced broken JSON - caller can retry)
    • no choices / no message / tool_calls missing or None -> []
    • entries without a function name are skipped

Interviewers look for

  • "missing" vs "present but None" are different states - a sentinel object (not None) is how you tell them apart.
  • d.get(k, {}) chains break the moment a value is a list or None; write one helper.
  • isinstance checks on the container type decide how a segment is interpreted.
  • Never trust model output: json.loads in try/except json.JSONDecodeError, then validate the type you got.

Work in exercises/py/01_fundamentals/ex05_nested_response.py (or copy the starter code into any scratch file).

import json
from collections.abc import Sequence
from typing import Any

def get_path(obj: Any, path: str | Sequence[str | int], default: Any=None) -> Any:
    raise NotImplementedError

def flatten(obj: dict[str, Any], sep: str='.') -> dict[str, Any]:
    raise NotImplementedError

def extract_tool_calls(response: dict[str, Any]) -> list[tuple[str, dict[str, Any] | None]]:
    raise NotImplementedError

import json
from collections.abc import Sequence
from typing import Any

_MISSING = object()


def get_path(obj: Any, path: str | Sequence[str | int], default: Any = None) -> Any:
    if isinstance(path, str):
        segments: Sequence[str | int] = path.split(".") if path else []
    else:
        segments = path
    current = obj
    for seg in segments:
        if isinstance(current, dict):
            current = current.get(seg, _MISSING)
        elif isinstance(current, (list, tuple)):
            try:
                current = current[int(seg)]
            except (ValueError, TypeError, IndexError):
                return default
        else:
            return default
        if current is _MISSING:
            return default
    return current


def flatten(obj: dict[str, Any], sep: str = ".") -> dict[str, Any]:
    if not isinstance(obj, dict):
        raise TypeError(f"expected dict, got {type(obj).__name__}")
    flat: dict[str, Any] = {}
    if obj:
        _walk(obj, "", sep, flat)
    return flat


def _walk(node: Any, prefix: str, sep: str, out: dict[str, Any]) -> None:
    if isinstance(node, dict) and node:
        items: Any = node.items()
    elif isinstance(node, list) and node:
        items = enumerate(node)
    else:
        out[prefix] = node
        return
    for key, value in items:
        _walk(value, f"{prefix}{sep}{key}" if prefix else str(key), sep, out)


def extract_tool_calls(response: dict[str, Any]) -> list[tuple[str, dict[str, Any] | None]]:
    calls = get_path(response, "choices.0.message.tool_calls") or []
    out: list[tuple[str, dict[str, Any] | None]] = []
    for call in calls:
        name = get_path(call, "function.name")
        if not name:
            continue
        raw = get_path(call, "function.arguments")
        try:
            args = json.loads(raw)
        except (TypeError, json.JSONDecodeError):
            args = None
        out.append((name, args if isinstance(args, dict) else None))
    return out

Layered config: deep merge and diff★★★ · ex06_deep_merge

fundamentals.none, fundamentals.identity_equality

Problem

An LLM service loads config in layers: defaults.yaml <- env/prod.yaml <- CLI overrides.

  1. deep_merge(base: dict, override: dict) -> dict

    • returns a NEW dict; neither input is mutated
    • keys only in one side are kept; when both sides hold a dict -> merge recursively
    • any other value in override replaces the base value (lists are REPLACED, not concatenated; a dict replaces a scalar and vice versa)
    • an override value of None DELETES the key from the result (Helm-style "unset")
    • the result must share no mutable objects with the inputs: mutating anything inside the result (nested dicts, lists) must not affect base or override

  2. merge_all(*configs: dict) -> dict

    • deep_merge left-to-right (later layers win); no configs -> {}

  3. config_diff(old: dict, new: dict) -> dict[str, tuple[Any, Any]]

    • dotted path -> (old_value, new_value) for every leaf that differs
    • recurse only where BOTH sides hold a dict; everything else is compared with ==
    • a key only in new -> (MISSING, value); only in old -> (value, MISSING)
    • MISSING is the sentinel defined below (compare with is)
    • paths sorted alphabetically in the returned dict
    • config_diff(cfg, cfg) == {}

Interviewers look for

  • Shallow {**a, **b} / a | b only merges the top level: nested sections get REPLACED.
  • Mutating inputs during a merge is the classic bug (a "defaults" dict shared by the whole process silently changes after the first request).
  • Recursion on nested dicts; base case = "not both dicts".
  • A dedicated sentinel distinguishes "absent" from "present with value None".

Work in exercises/py/01_fundamentals/ex06_deep_merge.py (or copy the starter code into any scratch file).

import copy
from enum import Enum
from typing import Any

class _Sentinel(Enum):
    MISSING = 'MISSING'
MISSING = _Sentinel.MISSING

def deep_merge(base: dict[str, Any], override: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any]:
    raise NotImplementedError

def merge_all(*configs: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any]:
    raise NotImplementedError

def config_diff(old: dict[str, Any], new: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, tuple[Any, Any]]:
    raise NotImplementedError

import copy
from enum import Enum
from typing import Any


class _Sentinel(Enum):
    MISSING = "MISSING"


MISSING = _Sentinel.MISSING


def deep_merge(base: dict[str, Any], override: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any]:
    # deepcopy up front: the result must not alias anything inside `base`
    result = copy.deepcopy(base)
    for key, value in override.items():
        if value is None:
            result.pop(key, None)  # explicit "unset"
        elif isinstance(result.get(key), dict) and isinstance(value, dict):
            result[key] = deep_merge(result[key], value)
        else:
            result[key] = copy.deepcopy(value)
    return result


def merge_all(*configs: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any]:
    merged: dict[str, Any] = {}
    for cfg in configs:
        merged = deep_merge(merged, cfg)
    return merged


def config_diff(old: dict[str, Any], new: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, tuple[Any, Any]]:
    changes: dict[str, tuple[Any, Any]] = {}
    _diff(old, new, "", changes)
    return {path: changes[path] for path in sorted(changes)}


def _diff(old: dict[str, Any], new: dict[str, Any], prefix: str, out: dict[str, Any]) -> None:
    for key in old.keys() | new.keys():
        path = f"{prefix}.{key}" if prefix else str(key)
        a, b = old.get(key, MISSING), new.get(key, MISSING)
        if isinstance(a, dict) and isinstance(b, dict):
            _diff(a, b, path, out)
        elif a is MISSING or b is MISSING or a != b:
            out[path] = (a, b)

Token statistics and deduplication★☆☆ · ex01_token_stats

data_structures.set_operations, data_structures.lists

Problem

Tokenisation in this exercise is simply text.lower().split().

  1. top_k_tokens(docs, k, stopwords=()) -> list[tuple[str, int]]

    • the k most frequent tokens across all docs, excluding stopwords (compare lowercased)
    • sorted by count descending, ties broken alphabetically (deterministic!)
    • k <= 0 -> []; fewer than k distinct tokens -> all of them

  2. jaccard(a, b) -> float

    • Jaccard similarity of the token SETS of two texts: |A & B| / |A | B|
    • both texts without tokens -> 1.0 (two empty sets are identical)

  3. dedup(items) -> list

    • remove duplicates, keep the FIRST occurrence, preserve order; items are hashable; works on any iterable (including a generator), O(n)

  4. dedup_by(items, key) -> list

    • like dedup but two items are duplicates when key(item) is equal; keep the first
    • e.g. drop retrieved chunks whose whitespace-normalised text was already seen (results arrive sorted by score, so "first" == best)

Interviewers look for

  • Counter.most_common(k) breaks ties by insertion order - fine for a demo, not for a deterministic API/test. Sort by (-count, token) yourself.
  • list(set(xs)) deduplicates but LOSES order; dict.fromkeys(xs) or a seen set keeps it.
  • x in some_list inside a loop makes dedup O(n^2); a set makes membership O(1) average.
  • Sets need hashable elements: dedup a list of dicts by a key, not by the dict.

from collections import Counter
from collections.abc import Callable, Hashable, Iterable


def top_k_tokens(
    docs: Iterable[str], k: int, stopwords: Iterable[str] = ()
) -> list[tuple[str, int]]:
    if k <= 0:
        return []
    stop = {w.lower() for w in stopwords}
    counts = Counter(tok for doc in docs for tok in doc.lower().split() if tok not in stop)
    return sorted(counts.items(), key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0]))[:k]


def jaccard(a: str, b: str) -> float:
    sa, sb = set(a.lower().split()), set(b.lower().split())
    union = sa | sb
    if not union:
        return 1.0
    return len(sa & sb) / len(union)


def dedup[T: Hashable](items: Iterable[T]) -> list[T]:
    return list(dict.fromkeys(items))


def dedup_by[T](items: Iterable[T], key: Callable[[T], Hashable]) -> list[T]:
    seen: set[Hashable] = set()
    out: list[T] = []
    for item in items:
        k = key(item)
        if k not in seen:
            seen.add(k)
            out.append(item)
    return out

Inverted index for keyword (BM25-style) retrieval★★☆ · ex02_inverted_index

data_structures.dict_lookup, data_structures.list_vs_dict, data_structures.set_operations

Problem

Hybrid RAG systems pair vector search with a keyword index. Build a tiny one. Tokenisation: text.lower().split().

Hit is given: a namedtuple("Hit", ["doc_id", "score"]).

  1. build_index(docs: Mapping[str, str]) -> dict[str, dict[str, int]]

    • docs maps doc_id -> text; result maps term -> {doc_id: term_frequency}
    • return PLAIN dicts (outer and inner), not defaultdicts - see "Interviewers look for"

  2. search(index, query, mode="and") -> list[Hit]

    • query terms = distinct tokens of the query
    • mode "and": docs containing ALL terms; mode "or": docs containing ANY term
    • score = sum of the doc's term frequencies over the query terms
    • sorted by score descending, then doc_id ascending
    • empty query -> []; unknown mode -> ValueError
    • must NOT modify the index (searching for an unknown term must not add it)

  3. group_by(records: Iterable[dict], key: str) -> dict[Any, list[dict]]

    • group records by record[key] (records without the key go under None), keeping input order inside each group; returns a plain dict

Interviewers look for

  • defaultdict is great while BUILDING; returning it leaks a trap: index["typo"] silently inserts an empty entry (a read that writes). Convert to dict at the boundary, and use .get() / in for lookups.
  • Term lookup is O(1) average in a dict vs O(n) scanning a list of (term, postings) pairs - the whole point of an inverted index.
  • AND = set intersection of posting key-sets, OR = union; dict keys views support & and |. Intersect starting from the smallest posting list.
  • namedtuples are tuples: immutable, unpackable, comparable, light-weight, readable fields.

Work in exercises/py/02_data_structures/ex02_inverted_index.py (or copy the starter code into any scratch file).

from collections import Counter, defaultdict, namedtuple
from collections.abc import Iterable, Mapping
from typing import Any

Hit = namedtuple("Hit", ["doc_id", "score"])


def build_index(docs: Mapping[str, str]) -> dict[str, dict[str, int]]:
    index: defaultdict[str, dict[str, int]] = defaultdict(dict)
    for doc_id, text in docs.items():
        for term, tf in Counter(text.lower().split()).items():
            index[term][doc_id] = tf
    return dict(index)


def search(index: Mapping[str, Mapping[str, int]], query: str, mode: str = "and") -> list[Hit]:
    if mode not in ("and", "or"):
        raise ValueError(f"unknown mode {mode!r}")
    terms = set(query.lower().split())
    if not terms:
        return []
    postings = [index.get(t, {}) for t in terms]
    if mode == "and":
        postings.sort(key=len)  # intersect from the rarest term
        candidates = set(postings[0])
        for p in postings[1:]:
            candidates &= p.keys()
    else:
        candidates = set().union(*postings)
    hits = [Hit(d, sum(p.get(d, 0) for p in postings)) for d in candidates]
    return sorted(hits, key=lambda h: (-h.score, h.doc_id))


def group_by(records: Iterable[dict[str, Any]], key: str) -> dict[Any, list[dict[str, Any]]]:
    groups: defaultdict[Any, list[dict[str, Any]]] = defaultdict(list)
    for rec in records:
        groups[rec.get(key)].append(rec)
    return dict(groups)

Sliding-window rate limiter and streaming stats★★☆ · ex03_sliding_window

Problem

LLM providers enforce "N requests per T seconds". Protect yourself client-side.

  1. class RateLimiter(limit: int, window: float)

    • limit <= 0 or window <= 0 -> ValueError (at construction)
    • allow(now: float) -> bool
      • sliding-window log: a request at now is allowed if fewer than limit ALLOWED requests happened in the half-open window (now - window, now]
      • allowed requests are recorded; rejected ones are not
      • now must be non-decreasing across calls, else ValueError
    • remaining(now: float) -> int : how many more requests would be allowed at now (does not record anything)
    • each call must be amortised O(1): evict expired timestamps from the left end

  2. moving_average(values: Iterable[float], n: int) -> list[float]

    • for each input, the mean of the last min(i + 1, n) values (warm-up uses fewer)
    • O(1) per item: keep a running sum, don't re-sum the window
    • n <= 0 -> ValueError

  3. tail(lines: Iterable[str], n: int) -> list[str]

    • the last n items of a possibly huge stream (like tail -n), O(n) memory
    • n == 0 -> []; n < 0 -> ValueError

Interviewers look for

  • deque: O(1) append/pop at BOTH ends. list.pop(0) / insert(0, x) are O(n) - using a list as a FIFO queue is the classic performance bug.
  • deque(maxlen=n) silently discards from the opposite end - a bounded buffer for free.
  • Sliding log vs fixed window (bursty at boundaries) vs token bucket (O(1) memory).
  • Amortised analysis: each timestamp is appended once and popped at most once.

Work in exercises/py/02_data_structures/ex03_sliding_window.py (or copy the starter code into any scratch file).

from collections import deque
from collections.abc import Iterable

class RateLimiter:

    def __init__(self, limit: int, window: float) -> None:
        raise NotImplementedError

    def allow(self, now: float) -> bool:
        raise NotImplementedError

    def remaining(self, now: float) -> int:
        raise NotImplementedError

def moving_average(values: Iterable[float], n: int) -> list[float]:
    raise NotImplementedError

def tail(lines: Iterable[str], n: int) -> list[str]:
    raise NotImplementedError

from collections import deque
from collections.abc import Iterable


class RateLimiter:
    def __init__(self, limit: int, window: float) -> None:
        if limit <= 0 or window <= 0:
            raise ValueError("limit and window must be positive")
        self.limit = limit
        self.window = window
        self._log: deque[float] = deque()
        self._last = float("-inf")

    def allow(self, now: float) -> bool:
        _expire(self, now)
        if len(self._log) < self.limit:
            self._log.append(now)
            return True
        return False

    def remaining(self, now: float) -> int:
        _expire(self, now)
        return self.limit - len(self._log)


def _expire(limiter: RateLimiter, now: float) -> None:
    if now < limiter._last:
        raise ValueError("time went backwards")
    limiter._last = now
    cutoff = now - limiter.window
    log = limiter._log
    while log and log[0] <= cutoff:  # each timestamp is popped at most once
        log.popleft()


def moving_average(values: Iterable[float], n: int) -> list[float]:
    if n <= 0:
        raise ValueError("n must be positive")
    window: deque[float] = deque()
    total = 0.0
    out: list[float] = []
    for v in values:
        window.append(v)
        total += v
        if len(window) > n:
            total -= window.popleft()
        out.append(total / len(window))
    return out


def tail(lines: Iterable[str], n: int) -> list[str]:
    if n < 0:
        raise ValueError("n must be >= 0")
    return list(deque(lines, maxlen=n))

LRU cache for embeddings★★☆ · ex04_lru_cache

data_structures.namedtuple

Problem

Embedding calls cost money and latency; the same chunks/queries repeat. Cache them.

class LRUCache(capacity: int) * capacity <= 0 -> ValueError * get(key, default=None) - hit: return the value and mark the key MOST recently used; counts a hit - miss: return default; counts a miss - a stored value of None is a legitimate hit (don't confuse it with a miss) * put(key, value) -> tuple[key, value] | None - insert or update; the key becomes most recently used - if the cache is over capacity, evict the LEAST recently used entry and return it as (key, value); otherwise return None * key in cache -> bool : does NOT change recency or stats * len(cache) -> int * keys() -> list : keys from least to most recently used * stats() -> CacheStats : CacheStats(hits, misses, size) (namedtuple given below) * every operation is O(1)

Interviewers look for

  • OrderedDict.move_to_end(key) and popitem(last=False) are both O(1) - it is a dict plus a doubly linked list. (A plain dict keeps insertion order but can't cheaply move a key to the end without delete + reinsert, and has no "pop oldest".)
  • The from-scratch version (dict + doubly linked list) is a classic interview follow-up.
  • Sentinel for "missing" so cached None values aren't treated as misses.
  • functools.lru_cache exists - but only for hashable function args, per-process, no TTL, no visibility into individual entries.

        raise NotImplementedError

    def get(self, key: Hashable, default: Any=None) -> Any:
        raise NotImplementedError

    def put(self, key: Hashable, value: Any) -> tuple[Hashable, Any] | None:
        raise NotImplementedError

        raise NotImplementedError

from collections import OrderedDict, namedtuple
from collections.abc import Hashable
from typing import Any

CacheStats = namedtuple("CacheStats", ["hits", "misses", "size"])

_MISSING = object()


class LRUCache:
    def __init__(self, capacity: int) -> None:
        if capacity <= 0:
            raise ValueError("capacity must be positive")
        self.capacity = capacity
        self._data: OrderedDict[Hashable, Any] = OrderedDict()
        self._hits = 0
        self._misses = 0

    def get(self, key: Hashable, default: Any = None) -> Any:
        value = self._data.get(key, _MISSING)
        if value is _MISSING:
            self._misses += 1
            return default
        self._data.move_to_end(key)
        self._hits += 1
        return value

    def put(self, key: Hashable, value: Any) -> tuple[Hashable, Any] | None:
        self._data[key] = value
        self._data.move_to_end(key)
        if len(self._data) > self.capacity:
            return self._data.popitem(last=False)
        return None

    def __contains__(self, key: object) -> bool:
        return key in self._data

    def __len__(self) -> int:
        return len(self._data)

    def keys(self) -> list[Hashable]:
        return list(self._data)

    def stats(self) -> CacheStats:
        return CacheStats(self._hits, self._misses, len(self._data))

Binary search variants★★★ · ex05_binary_search

data_structures.linear_search

Problem

Implement 1-3 WITHOUT the bisect module (that's what the interviewer will ask for).

  1. lower_bound(xs, x) -> int

    • xs is sorted ascending; return the first index i with xs[i] >= x (== len(xs) if there is none). Same contract as bisect.bisect_left.

  2. upper_bound(xs, x) -> int

    • first index i with xs[i] > x. Same contract as bisect.bisect_right.
    • upper_bound(xs, x) - lower_bound(xs, x) == number of occurrences of x

  3. first_true(lo, hi, pred) -> int

    • pred is monotone on [lo, hi): False ... False True ... True
    • return the smallest i in [lo, hi) with pred(i) True, or hi if there is none
    • at most ceil(log2(hi - lo)) + 1 calls to pred; lo >= hi -> return hi without calling pred
    • e.g. "the smallest chunk size whose prompt overflows the context window" or "the first checkpoint where the eval regressed" (git bisect)

  4. events_between(timestamps, start, end) -> list

    • timestamps sorted ascending (may contain duplicates); return those in the half-open interval [start, end) in O(log n + k). Here you MAY use bisect.
    • start >= end -> []

Interviewers look for

  • Half-open [lo, hi) invariants: loop while lo < hi, mid = (lo + hi) // 2, then either hi = mid or lo = mid + 1. Off-by-one and infinite loops come from mixing conventions.
  • Binary search works on any MONOTONE predicate, not just arrays ("binary search the answer").
  • O(log n) requires random access AND sorted data. Sorting first costs O(n log n) - for a single lookup a linear scan O(n) is cheaper; for many lookups sort once (or use a dict/set for exact-match lookups, O(1)).
  • In Python, mid overflow isn't an issue (big ints) but it is in Java/C - worth mentioning.

from typing import Any

    raise NotImplementedError

def upper_bound(xs: Sequence[Any], x: Any) -> int:
    raise NotImplementedError

def first_true(lo: int, hi: int, pred: Callable[[int], bool]) -> int:

import bisect
from collections.abc import Callable, Sequence
from typing import Any


def lower_bound(xs: Sequence[Any], x: Any) -> int:
    lo, hi = 0, len(xs)
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if xs[mid] < x:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid
    return lo


def upper_bound(xs: Sequence[Any], x: Any) -> int:
    lo, hi = 0, len(xs)
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if xs[mid] <= x:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid
    return lo


def first_true(lo: int, hi: int, pred: Callable[[int], bool]) -> int:
    if lo >= hi:
        return hi
    # invariant: pred is False everywhere left of lo, True at hi (or hi is the original end)
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if pred(mid):
            hi = mid
        else:
            lo = mid + 1
    return lo


def events_between(timestamps: Sequence[float], start: float, end: float) -> list[float]:
    if start >= end:
        return []
    i = bisect.bisect_left(timestamps, start)
    j = bisect.bisect_left(timestamps, end)
    return list(timestamps[i:j])

Streaming JSON repair, BFS and pipeline ordering★★★ · ex06_graphs_and_stacks

data_structures.dicts, data_structures.complexity

Problem

  1. closing_suffix(partial: str) -> str (a STACK)

    • an LLM streams JSON token by token; to render/parse a partial object you need the brackets that would close it: '{"a": [1, {"b": 2' -> '}]}'
    • track { and [ ; a } or ] must match the most recent opener, else ValueError
    • brackets INSIDE string literals don't count; inside a string a backslash escapes the next character (an escaped quote does not end the string)
    • if the text ends inside a string, the suffix starts with '"' to close it
    • balanced input -> ""

  2. shortest_path(graph, start, goal) -> list | None (a QUEUE / BFS)

    • graph: Mapping[node, Iterable[node]] adjacency (directed); nodes that only appear as neighbours have no outgoing edges
    • return the path with the fewest edges as [start, ..., goal]; start == goal -> [start]
    • unreachable -> None
    • explore neighbours in the order given (so ties resolve deterministically)
    • use collections.deque; must handle cycles

  3. run_order(deps) -> list (Kahn's algorithm)

    • deps: Mapping[step, Iterable[step]] - the steps each step depends on {"embed": ["chunk"], "chunk": ["load"], "index": ["embed"], "load": []}
    • return every step (keys and anything mentioned as a dependency) such that each step comes after all its dependencies; among steps that are ready at the same time, pick the alphabetically smallest first (deterministic)
    • a cycle -> ValueError naming the steps involved

Interviewers look for

  • Stack (LIFO, list.append/pop) for nesting/matching; queue (FIFO, deque.popleft) for BFS. DFS with a stack does NOT give shortest paths in unweighted graphs; BFS does.
  • Mark nodes visited when ENQUEUED, not when dequeued - otherwise a node can be queued many times (still correct, but wasteful on dense graphs).
  • O(V + E) for BFS and Kahn's; a visited set gives O(1) membership.
  • Topological ordering = how agent/tool DAGs and data pipelines (Airflow, Prefect) schedule work; leftover nodes with in-degree > 0 mean a cycle.

Work in exercises/py/02_data_structures/ex06_graphs_and_stacks.py (or copy the starter code into any scratch file).

import heapq
from collections import deque
from collections.abc import Hashable, Iterable, Mapping

def closing_suffix(partial: str) -> str:
    raise NotImplementedError

def shortest_path[N: Hashable](graph: Mapping[N, Iterable[N]], start: N, goal: N) -> list[N] | None:
    raise NotImplementedError

def run_order(deps: Mapping[str, Iterable[str]]) -> list[str]:
    raise NotImplementedError

import heapq
from collections import deque
from collections.abc import Hashable, Iterable, Mapping

_PAIRS = {"}": "{", "]": "["}
_CLOSE = {"{": "}", "[": "]"}


def closing_suffix(partial: str) -> str:
    stack: list[str] = []
    in_string = escaped = False
    for ch in partial:
        if in_string:
            if escaped:
                escaped = False
            elif ch == "\\":
                escaped = True
            elif ch == '"':
                in_string = False
        elif ch == '"':
            in_string = True
        elif ch in _CLOSE:
            stack.append(ch)
        elif ch in _PAIRS:
            if not stack or stack[-1] != _PAIRS[ch]:
                raise ValueError(f"unexpected {ch!r}")
            stack.pop()
    suffix = '"' if in_string else ""
    return suffix + "".join(_CLOSE[op] for op in reversed(stack))


def shortest_path[N: Hashable](
    graph: Mapping[N, Iterable[N]], start: N, goal: N
) -> list[N] | None:
    parent: dict[N, N | None] = {start: None}
    queue = deque([start])
    while queue:
        node = queue.popleft()
        if node == goal:
            path = []
            cur: N | None = node
            while cur is not None:
                path.append(cur)
                cur = parent[cur]
            return path[::-1]
        for nxt in graph.get(node, ()):
            if nxt not in parent:  # visited-on-enqueue
                parent[nxt] = node
                queue.append(nxt)
    return None


def run_order(deps: Mapping[str, Iterable[str]]) -> list[str]:
    steps = set(deps)
    for ds in deps.values():
        steps.update(ds)
    indegree = dict.fromkeys(steps, 0)
    dependents: dict[str, list[str]] = {s: [] for s in steps}
    for step, ds in deps.items():
        for d in set(ds):
            indegree[step] += 1
            dependents[d].append(step)
    ready = [s for s, n in indegree.items() if n == 0]
    heapq.heapify(ready)
    order: list[str] = []
    while ready:
        step = heapq.heappop(ready)
        order.append(step)
        for nxt in dependents[step]:
            indegree[nxt] -= 1
            if indegree[nxt] == 0:
                heapq.heappush(ready, nxt)
    if len(order) != len(steps):
        stuck = sorted(s for s, n in indegree.items() if n > 0)
        raise ValueError(f"dependency cycle among: {', '.join(stuck)}")
    return order

Python Functions

Fix the default-argument and return-value bugs★☆☆ · ex01_default_args

functions.keyword_args

Problem

A chat backend has three helpers. They pass a quick manual test and break in production.

def new_conversation(system_prompt, messages=[]):
    messages.insert(0, {"role": "system", "content": system_prompt})
    return messages

def make_event(name, payload={}, created_at=time.time()):
    payload["name"] = name
    return {"payload": payload, "created_at": created_at}

def parse_model_id(model_id):
    provider, rest = model_id.split("/")
    name, version = rest.split(":")
    print(provider, name, version)

Write the fixed versions:

  1. new_conversation(system_prompt, messages=None) -> list[dict]

    • returns a NEW list: the system message followed by the given messages (if any)
    • never mutates the caller's list; independent calls never share state

  2. make_event(name, payload=None, *, clock=time.time) -> dict

    • returns {"name": name, "payload": <copy of payload or {}>, "created_at": clock()}
    • created_at is taken at CALL time, every call
    • the caller's payload dict is not mutated, and two events never share a payload dict
    • clock is keyword-only (inject a fake clock in tests)

  3. parse_model_id(model_id) -> tuple[str, str, str | None]

    • "anthropic/claude-x:2024-10" -> ("anthropic", "claude-x", "2024-10")
    • "openai/gpt-4o" -> ("openai", "gpt-4o", None)
    • split on the FIRST "/" and the FIRST ":" after it - the remainder may contain more ("local/llama:8b:q4" -> ("local", "llama", "8b:q4"), "hf/org/model" -> ("hf", "org/model", None))
    • missing "/" or empty provider/name -> ValueError
    • RETURN the values (a function that prints returns None)

Interviewers look for

  • Default values are evaluated ONCE, when def runs, and stored on the function (fn.defaults). A mutable default is shared by every call; time.time() is frozen at import time.
  • The idiom: param=None, then if param is None: param = []. (param or [] also works here only because we copy anyway - if you meant to mutate the caller's empty list, or would silently swap it for a new one.)
  • Mutating an argument the caller owns is a side effect - copy or build new.
  • Return a tuple (or a NamedTuple/dataclass) for multiple values; the caller unpacks it.

import time
from collections.abc import Callable
from typing import Any


def new_conversation(
    system_prompt: str, messages: list[dict[str, str]] | None = None
) -> list[dict[str, str]]:
    return [{"role": "system", "content": system_prompt}, *(messages or [])]


def make_event(
    name: str,
    payload: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
    *,
    clock: Callable[[], float] = time.time,
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    return {"name": name, "payload": dict(payload or {}), "created_at": clock()}


def parse_model_id(model_id: str) -> tuple[str, str, str | None]:
    provider, sep, rest = model_id.partition("/")
    name, colon, version = rest.partition(":")
    if not sep or not provider or not name:
        raise ValueError(f"expected 'provider/name[:version]', got {model_id!r}")
    return provider, name, version if colon else None

Designing call signatures for an LLM client★★☆ · ex02_call_signatures

functions.positional_args, functions.keyword_args

Problem

  1. build_request(model, messages, /, *, temperature=0.0, max_tokens=None, **extra) -> dict

    • model and messages are positional-only; everything else keyword-only
    • returns {"model": model, "messages": list(messages), "temperature": temperature} plus "max_tokens" only if it is not None, plus every extra item whose value is not None (provider-specific options: top_p, stop, seed, response_format...)
    • because model/messages are positional-only, a caller CAN pass model=... or messages=... and it lands in **extra - that would silently override the real value: raise TypeError for those keys

  2. call_with_retry(fn, /, *args, retries=2, retry_on=(TimeoutError, ConnectionError), **kwargs)

    • calls fn(*args, **kwargs) and returns its result
    • if it raises an exception that is an instance of a retry_on type, call again - at most retries extra attempts; if every attempt fails, re-raise the LAST exception
    • any other exception propagates immediately (no retry)
    • retries < 0 -> ValueError (before calling fn)
    • fn is positional-only so that the wrapped function may itself have a parameter called fn (call_with_retry(apply, fn=str.upper) must forward fn=... to apply)

  3. bind(fn, /, *args, **kwargs) -> callable (a mini functools.partial)

    • bind(f, 1, x=2)(3, y=4) == f(1, 3, x=2, y=4)
    • keyword arguments given at call time override bound ones
    • the bound args are captured at bind time (later mutation of the caller's kwargs dict must not leak in)

Interviewers look for

  • / (3.8+) makes parameter names private to the implementation - you can rename them later, and **kwargs can accept those names. * forces keyword use for readability (temperature=0.2, not a mystery positional 0.2) and safe future reordering.
  • *args collects extra positionals into a tuple, **kwargs extra keywords into a dict; f(*xs, **d) unpacks at the call site.
  • Only retry what is retryable (timeouts, 429, 5xx) - never validation errors.

Work in exercises/py/03_functions/ex02_call_signatures.py (or copy the starter code into any scratch file).

from collections.abc import Callable, Iterable
from typing import Any

def build_request(model: str, messages: Iterable[dict[str, Any]], /, *, temperature: float=0.0, max_tokens: int | None=None, **extra: Any) -> dict[str, Any]:
    raise NotImplementedError

def call_with_retry(fn: Callable[..., Any], /, *args: Any, retries: int=2, retry_on: tuple[type[BaseException], ...]=(TimeoutError, ConnectionError), **kwargs: Any) -> Any:
    raise NotImplementedError

def bind(fn: Callable[..., Any], /, *args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> Callable[..., Any]:
    raise NotImplementedError

from collections.abc import Callable, Iterable
from typing import Any


def build_request(
    model: str,
    messages: Iterable[dict[str, Any]],
    /,
    *,
    temperature: float = 0.0,
    max_tokens: int | None = None,
    **extra: Any,
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    clash = {"model", "messages"} & extra.keys()
    if clash:
        raise TypeError(f"{sorted(clash)} must be passed positionally")
    payload: dict[str, Any] = {"model": model, "messages": list(messages), "temperature": temperature}
    if max_tokens is not None:
        payload["max_tokens"] = max_tokens
    payload.update({k: v for k, v in extra.items() if v is not None})
    return payload


def call_with_retry(
    fn: Callable[..., Any],
    /,
    *args: Any,
    retries: int = 2,
    retry_on: tuple[type[BaseException], ...] = (TimeoutError, ConnectionError),
    **kwargs: Any,
) -> Any:
    if retries < 0:
        raise ValueError("retries must be >= 0")
    for attempt in range(retries + 1):
        try:
            return fn(*args, **kwargs)
        except retry_on:
            if attempt == retries:
                raise
    raise AssertionError("unreachable")


def bind(fn: Callable[..., Any], /, *args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> Callable[..., Any]:
    bound_args, bound_kwargs = args, dict(kwargs)

    def call(*more_args: Any, **more_kwargs: Any) -> Any:
        return fn(*bound_args, *more_args, **{**bound_kwargs, **more_kwargs})

    return call

Scope bugs: LEGB, UnboundLocalError, late binding★★☆ · ex03_scope_legb

Problem

Each snippet below is broken. Explain (to yourself) WHY, then write the fixed function.

total_tokens = 0
def record(n):
    total_tokens += n              # (A) UnboundLocalError
    return total_tokens

def make_counter():
    count = 0
    def inc():
        count += 1                 # (B) UnboundLocalError
        return count
    return inc

def make_formatters(templates):
    return [lambda x: t.format(x) for t in templates]   # (C) every lambda uses the LAST t
  1. make_meter() -> tuple[record, total]
    • replaces the global counter in (A) with state that is private to each meter
    • record(n) adds n tokens and returns the new running total; total() returns it
    • two meters are fully independent; no module-level state
  2. make_counter(start=0) -> inc fixed version of (B); inc() returns start+1, start+2, ...
  3. make_formatters(templates) -> list fixed version of (C); the i-th function formats with templates[i]
  4. resolve(name, local_ns, enclosing, global_ns) -> tuple[str, object]
    • simulate how Python looks up a name: Local -> Enclosing -> Global -> Builtins
    • local_ns and global_ns are dicts; enclosing is a list of dicts, INNERMOST first
    • return (scope, value) where scope is "local", "enclosing", "global" or "builtin"
    • not found anywhere -> NameError (mention the name in the message)
    • e.g. resolve("len", {}, [], {}) -> ("builtin", len)

Interviewers look for

  • Assignment ANYWHERE in a function body makes the name local for the WHOLE body - decided at compile time. So x += 1 reads a local that doesn't exist yet -> UnboundLocalError.
  • global (module scope) / nonlocal (nearest enclosing function scope) change that; prefer closures or objects over global for state.
  • Closures capture VARIABLES, not values: the lambdas share one t cell, looked up when called. Fix with a default arg (lambda x, t=t: ...) or a factory function.
  • Shadowing builtins (list = [...], max = 3) breaks later code in that scope.

Work in exercises/py/03_functions/ex03_scope_legb.py (or copy the starter code into any scratch file).

import builtins
from collections.abc import Callable, Mapping, Sequence

def make_meter() -> tuple[Callable[[int], int], Callable[[], int]]:
    raise NotImplementedError

def make_counter(start: int=0) -> Callable[[], int]:
    raise NotImplementedError

def make_formatters(templates: Sequence[str]) -> list[Callable[[object], str]]:
    raise NotImplementedError

def resolve(name: str, local_ns: Mapping[str, object], enclosing: Sequence[Mapping[str, object]], global_ns: Mapping[str, object]) -> tuple[str, object]:
    raise NotImplementedError

import builtins
from collections.abc import Callable, Mapping, Sequence


def make_meter() -> tuple[Callable[[int], int], Callable[[], int]]:
    total_tokens = 0

    def record(n: int) -> int:
        nonlocal total_tokens
        total_tokens += n
        return total_tokens

    def total() -> int:
        return total_tokens

    return record, total


def make_counter(start: int = 0) -> Callable[[], int]:
    count = start

    def inc() -> int:
        nonlocal count
        count += 1
        return count

    return inc


def make_formatters(templates: Sequence[str]) -> list[Callable[[object], str]]:
    # bind the CURRENT t as a default value, evaluated once per lambda creation
    return [lambda x, t=t: t.format(x) for t in templates]


def resolve(
    name: str,
    local_ns: Mapping[str, object],
    enclosing: Sequence[Mapping[str, object]],
    global_ns: Mapping[str, object],
) -> tuple[str, object]:
    if name in local_ns:
        return "local", local_ns[name]
    for ns in enclosing:
        if name in ns:
            return "enclosing", ns[name]
    if name in global_ns:
        return "global", global_ns[name]
    if hasattr(builtins, name):
        return "builtin", getattr(builtins, name)
    raise NameError(f"name {name!r} is not defined")

Agent tool registry and dispatcher★★★ · ex04_tool_dispatch

functions.kwargs, functions.unpacking, functions.definition, functions.pos_kw_only

Problem

An agent loop gets tool calls from the model as JSON: {"name": "search", "arguments": {...}}. Functions are objects - store them, inspect them, call them later.

  1. tools_from(*fns) -> dict[str, Callable]

    • maps fn.name -> fn
    • an argument that is not callable -> TypeError (the classic bug: registering search() - the RESULT of a call - instead of search)
    • two functions with the same name -> ValueError

  2. tool_schema(fn) -> dict

    • {"name": fn.name, "description": <first line of the docstring, stripped, or "">, "required": [names of params without defaults, in order], "optional": {name: default, ...}}
    • use inspect.signature
    • the model passes arguments BY NAME, so a tool may not have *args, **kwargs or positional-only parameters -> TypeError

  3. run_tool(tools, call) -> dict

    • call["arguments"] may be a dict or a JSON string (models emit strings); missing -> {}
    • unknown tool -> {"ok": False, "error": "unknown tool: <name>"}
    • invalid JSON / not a dict -> {"ok": False, "error": "bad arguments: ..."}
    • arguments that don't fit the signature (missing / unexpected) -> {"ok": False, "error": "bad arguments: ..."} WITHOUT calling the tool
    • exception raised INSIDE the tool -> {"ok": False, "error": "tool error: <ExceptionType>: <message>"} (a TypeError from inside the tool is a tool error, not "bad arguments"!)
    • success -> {"ok": True, "result": <return value>}
    • the error dict is fed back to the model so it can correct itself - never crash the loop

Interviewers look for

  • f is a reference, f() is a call. handlers = {"a": run_a()} calls at build time and stores the result.
  • Higher-order design: a registry is just a dict of callables; dispatch is tools[name](**args).
  • Validate the call with inspect.signature(fn).bind(**args) BEFORE invoking, instead of catching TypeError afterwards (which can't tell a bad call from a bug inside the tool).
  • Treat model output as untrusted input: parse, validate, return structured errors.

Work in exercises/py/03_functions/ex04_tool_dispatch.py (or copy the starter code into any scratch file).

import inspect
import json
from collections.abc import Callable, Mapping
from typing import Any

def tools_from(*fns: Callable[..., Any]) -> dict[str, Callable[..., Any]]:
    raise NotImplementedError

def tool_schema(fn: Callable[..., Any]) -> dict[str, Any]:
    raise NotImplementedError

def run_tool(tools: Mapping[str, Callable[..., Any]], call: Mapping[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any]:
    raise NotImplementedError

import inspect
import json
from collections.abc import Callable, Mapping
from typing import Any

_BY_NAME_OK = (inspect.Parameter.POSITIONAL_OR_KEYWORD, inspect.Parameter.KEYWORD_ONLY)


def tools_from(*fns: Callable[..., Any]) -> dict[str, Callable[..., Any]]:
    tools: dict[str, Callable[..., Any]] = {}
    for fn in fns:
        if not callable(fn):
            raise TypeError(f"{fn!r} is not callable - did you call the function instead of passing it?")
        name = fn.__name__
        if name in tools:
            raise ValueError(f"duplicate tool name {name!r}")
        tools[name] = fn
    return tools


def tool_schema(fn: Callable[..., Any]) -> dict[str, Any]:
    required: list[str] = []
    optional: dict[str, Any] = {}
    for p in inspect.signature(fn).parameters.values():
        if p.kind not in _BY_NAME_OK:
            raise TypeError(f"parameter {p.name!r} of {fn.__name__} can't be passed by name")
        if p.default is inspect.Parameter.empty:
            required.append(p.name)
        else:
            optional[p.name] = p.default
    doc = inspect.getdoc(fn) or ""
    return {
        "name": fn.__name__,
        "description": doc.splitlines()[0].strip() if doc else "",
        "required": required,
        "optional": optional,
    }


def run_tool(tools: Mapping[str, Callable[..., Any]], call: Mapping[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any]:
    name = call.get("name")
    fn = tools.get(name) if isinstance(name, str) else None
    if fn is None:
        return {"ok": False, "error": f"unknown tool: {name}"}
    args = call.get("arguments") or {}
    if isinstance(args, str):
        try:
            args = json.loads(args)
        except json.JSONDecodeError as e:
            return {"ok": False, "error": f"bad arguments: invalid JSON ({e})"}
    if not isinstance(args, dict):
        return {"ok": False, "error": "bad arguments: expected a JSON object"}
    try:
        inspect.signature(fn).bind(**args)
    except TypeError as e:
        return {"ok": False, "error": f"bad arguments: {e}"}
    try:
        result = fn(**args)
    except Exception as e:  # the agent loop must survive any tool failure
        return {"ok": False, "error": f"tool error: {type(e).__name__}: {e}"}
    return {"ok": True, "result": result}

Recursion over nested documents★★★ · ex05_recursion

Problem

Parsed documents are trees: JSON payloads, or heading outlines {"title": "Guide", "children": [{"title": "Install", "children": []}, ...]}

  1. depth(obj) -> int (recursive)

    • nesting depth of dicts/lists: a scalar -> 0, [] or {} -> 1, [1, [2]] -> 2, {"a": {"b": [1]}} -> 3 (for dicts, look at the values)

  2. depth_iterative(obj) -> int (NO recursion)

    • same result as depth(), using an explicit stack, so it works on inputs nested far deeper than sys.getrecursionlimit() (e.g. 100_000 levels from a hostile payload)

  3. outline(node) -> str

    • render the heading tree as lines "<2 spaces per level>- <title>", root at level 0, children in order, lines joined with newlines (no trailing newline)
    • a node without "children" is a leaf

  4. find_path(node, title) -> list[str] | None

    • titles from the root down to the FIRST node (pre-order: node, then children left to right) whose title == title; not found -> None
    • this is the "breadcrumb" (Guide > Install > Linux) you attach to RAG chunks

Interviewers look for

  • Every recursive function needs a base case and progress toward it; the return value of the recursive call must be USED (a forgotten return -> None bubbling up).
  • CPython has no tail-call optimisation; default recursion limit ~1000 -> RecursionError on deep inputs. Raising the limit risks a hard C-stack crash - convert to an explicit stack.
  • Recursion is natural for trees; an explicit stack/queue gives control (depth limits, BFS vs DFS order, early exit).
  • Untrusted JSON can be adversarially deep - cap the depth at the boundary.

Work in exercises/py/03_functions/ex05_recursion.py (or copy the starter code into any scratch file).

from typing import Any

def depth(obj: Any) -> int:
    raise NotImplementedError

def depth_iterative(obj: Any) -> int:
    raise NotImplementedError

def outline(node: dict[str, Any]) -> str:
    raise NotImplementedError

def find_path(node: dict[str, Any], title: str) -> list[str] | None:
    raise NotImplementedError

from typing import Any


def depth(obj: Any) -> int:
    if isinstance(obj, dict):
        children = list(obj.values())
    elif isinstance(obj, list):
        children = obj
    else:
        return 0
    return 1 + max((depth(c) for c in children), default=0)


def depth_iterative(obj: Any) -> int:
    best = 0
    stack: list[tuple[Any, int]] = [(obj, 0)]
    while stack:
        node, level = stack.pop()
        if isinstance(node, dict):
            children: Any = node.values()
        elif isinstance(node, list):
            children = node
        else:
            continue
        best = max(best, level + 1)
        stack.extend((c, level + 1) for c in children)
    return best


def outline(node: dict[str, Any]) -> str:
    return "\n".join(_outline_lines(node, 0))


def _outline_lines(node: dict[str, Any], level: int) -> list[str]:
    lines = [f"{'  ' * level}- {node['title']}"]
    for child in node.get("children", []):
        lines.extend(_outline_lines(child, level + 1))
    return lines


def find_path(node: dict[str, Any], title: str) -> list[str] | None:
    if node["title"] == title:
        return [node["title"]]
    for child in node.get("children", []):
        sub = find_path(child, title)
        if sub is not None:
            return [node["title"], *sub]
    return None

Functional Programming

Ranking retrieval results with lambda/map/filter★☆☆ · ex01_rank_results

Problem

A retriever returns results like {"doc_id": "d1", "score": 0.82, "source": "wiki"}.

  1. sort_results(results) -> list[dict]

    • a NEW list sorted by score descending, ties broken by doc_id ascending
    • use sorted() with a lambda key (one sort, tuple key)

  2. top_ids(results, min_score) -> list[str]

    • doc_ids of results with score >= min_score, in ranked order (as sort_results)
    • build it with filter() and map()

  3. score_at_least(threshold) -> Callable[[dict], bool]

    • returns a predicate (a lambda) usable with filter(): r["score"] >= threshold

  4. apply_boosts(results, boosts) -> list[dict]

    • boosts maps source -> multiplier (missing source -> 1.0); return NEW dicts with the boosted score (all other keys copied); the input dicts must not be modified
    • use map()

Interviewers look for

  • key=lambda r: (-r["score"], r["doc_id"]) - a tuple key sorts by several fields in one pass; negating a number reverses just that field.
  • Lambdas are single-expression anonymous functions - fine as short keys/predicates, but name anything non-trivial with def (better tracebacks, testable).
  • map/filter return lazy ITERATORS in Python 3 - wrap in list() when you need a list.
  • {**r, "score": ...} builds a new dict instead of mutating shared data.

Work in exercises/py/04_functional/ex01_rank_results.py (or copy the starter code into any scratch file).

from collections.abc import Callable, Iterable, Mapping
from typing import Any
Result = Mapping[str, Any]

def sort_results(results: Iterable[Result]) -> list[Result]:
    raise NotImplementedError

def top_ids(results: Iterable[Result], min_score: float) -> list[str]:
    raise NotImplementedError

def score_at_least(threshold: float) -> Callable[[Result], bool]:
    raise NotImplementedError

def apply_boosts(results: Iterable[Result], boosts: Mapping[str, float]) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
    raise NotImplementedError

from collections.abc import Callable, Iterable, Mapping
from typing import Any

Result = Mapping[str, Any]


def sort_results(results: Iterable[Result]) -> list[Result]:
    return sorted(results, key=lambda r: (-r["score"], r["doc_id"]))


def top_ids(results: Iterable[Result], min_score: float) -> list[str]:
    kept = filter(score_at_least(min_score), sort_results(results))
    return list(map(lambda r: r["doc_id"], kept))


def score_at_least(threshold: float) -> Callable[[Result], bool]:
    return lambda r: r["score"] >= threshold


def apply_boosts(results: Iterable[Result], boosts: Mapping[str, float]) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
    return list(map(lambda r: {**r, "score": r["score"] * boosts.get(r.get("source"), 1.0)}, results))

compose, pipe and reduce-based aggregation★★☆ · ex02_reduce_compose

Problem

Implement each of these with functools.reduce (no explicit loops).

  1. compose(*fns) -> callable

    • RIGHT-to-left: compose(f, g, h)(x) == f(g(h(x)))
    • compose() is the identity function
    • e.g. clean = compose(str.strip, str.lower, remove_markup) (remove_markup runs first)

  2. pipe(value, *fns) -> Any

    • LEFT-to-right application: pipe(x, f, g) == g(f(x)); no fns -> value

  3. merge_usage(usages) -> dict[str, int]

    • usages: iterable of token-usage dicts from many LLM calls, e.g. {"prompt_tokens": 120, "completion_tokens": 30}; keys may differ between dicts (missing key counts as 0)
    • returns a NEW dict with the per-key sums; no input dict is modified
    • empty input -> {} (think about reduce's initializer!)

  4. max_by(items, key) -> item

    • the item with the largest key(item); on ties the FIRST one wins
    • empty -> ValueError; key() is called exactly once per item (it may be expensive)
    • e.g. pick the best answer from n samples by a judge score

Interviewers look for

  • reduce(f, xs) without an initializer raises TypeError on empty input and uses xs[0] as the start value - give an initializer whenever the input can be empty.
  • reduce folds left: f(f(f(init, x1), x2), x3). Function composition IS a fold over functions.
  • The reducer should be pure: return a new accumulator instead of mutating the one you got (mutating acc in place works but makes the initializer a shared mutable object).
  • Readability: sum/min/max/any/all/"".join beat reduce for the common cases - Guido moved reduce to functools for a reason. Use it when no builtin fits.

Work in exercises/py/04_functional/ex02_reduce_compose.py (or copy the starter code into any scratch file).

from collections.abc import Callable, Iterable, Mapping
from functools import reduce
from typing import Any

def compose(*fns: Callable[[Any], Any]) -> Callable[[Any], Any]:
    raise NotImplementedError

def pipe(value: Any, *fns: Callable[[Any], Any]) -> Any:
    raise NotImplementedError

def merge_usage(usages: Iterable[Mapping[str, int]]) -> dict[str, int]:
    raise NotImplementedError

def max_by[T](items: Iterable[T], key: Callable[[T], Any]) -> T:
    raise NotImplementedError

from collections.abc import Callable, Iterable, Mapping
from functools import reduce
from typing import Any


def compose(*fns: Callable[[Any], Any]) -> Callable[[Any], Any]:
    return reduce(lambda f, g: lambda x: f(g(x)), fns, lambda x: x)


def pipe(value: Any, *fns: Callable[[Any], Any]) -> Any:
    return reduce(lambda acc, fn: fn(acc), fns, value)


def merge_usage(usages: Iterable[Mapping[str, int]]) -> dict[str, int]:
    def add(acc: dict[str, int], usage: Mapping[str, int]) -> dict[str, int]:
        return {k: acc.get(k, 0) + usage.get(k, 0) for k in acc.keys() | usage.keys()}

    return reduce(add, usages, {})


def max_by[T](items: Iterable[T], key: Callable[[T], Any]) -> T:
    empty: Any = object()
    # decorate once so key() runs exactly once per item
    pairs = ((key(x), x) for x in items)
    best = reduce(lambda a, b: b if a is empty or b[0] > a[0] else a, pairs, empty)
    if best is empty:
        raise ValueError("max_by() of an empty iterable")
    return best[1]

Lazy map/filter pitfalls★★☆ · ex03_lazy_pitfalls

functional.filter, functional.side_effects

Problem

Three helpers from an ingestion job are subtly broken because map/filter are LAZY, ONE-SHOT iterators:

def embed_valid(docs, embed):
    valid = filter(lambda d: d.strip(), docs)
    print(f"embedding {len(list(valid))} docs")
    return list(map(embed, valid))          # always [] - `valid` was already consumed

def warm_cache(keys, load):
    map(load, keys)                          # loads nothing at all

def min_max(scores):                         # scores is often a generator
    return min(scores), max(scores)          # ValueError: max() arg is an empty sequence

Write correct versions, plus one helper:

  1. embed_valid(docs, embed) -> tuple[int, list]

    • (number of docs that are not blank, [embed(doc) for each such doc] in order)
    • docs may be a one-shot iterator; embed must be called EXACTLY once per valid doc

  2. warm_cache(keys, load) -> int

    • call load(key) for every key, eagerly, in order; return how many were loaded

  3. min_max(scores) -> tuple[float, float]

    • ONE pass over any iterable (generators included); empty -> ValueError

  4. peek(iterable) -> tuple[first, iterator]

    • look at the first item of a stream without losing it: returns (first, it) where it yields ALL items including the first, lazily
    • pulls exactly ONE item from the source when called
    • empty iterable -> ValueError
    • use case: sniff the first JSONL record to detect the schema, then process everything

Interviewers look for

  • map/filter/zip/generator expressions compute nothing until iterated, and can be iterated only once; a second pass silently yields nothing - no error.
  • Using map() for side effects is a smell: it's lazy (does nothing) and allocates results you don't want. Side effects belong in a plain for loop.
  • len(list(it)) consumes it. Materialise once (list(...)) if you need both a count and the items, or count while you go.
  • itertools.chain([first], it) "un-reads" an item; itertools.tee buffers for multiple consumers (memory!).

Work in exercises/py/04_functional/ex03_lazy_pitfalls.py (or copy the starter code into any scratch file).

import itertools
from collections.abc import Callable, Iterable, Iterator
from typing import Any

def embed_valid[V](docs: Iterable[str], embed: Callable[[str], V]) -> tuple[int, list[V]]:
    raise NotImplementedError

def warm_cache(keys: Iterable[Any], load: Callable[[Any], Any]) -> int:
    raise NotImplementedError

def min_max(scores: Iterable[float]) -> tuple[float, float]:
    raise NotImplementedError

def peek[T](iterable: Iterable[T]) -> tuple[T, Iterator[T]]:
    raise NotImplementedError

import itertools
from collections.abc import Callable, Iterable, Iterator
from typing import Any


def embed_valid[V](docs: Iterable[str], embed: Callable[[str], V]) -> tuple[int, list[V]]:
    valid = [d for d in docs if d.strip()]  # materialise once
    return len(valid), [embed(d) for d in valid]


def warm_cache(keys: Iterable[Any], load: Callable[[Any], Any]) -> int:
    count = 0
    for key in keys:  # side effects -> a plain loop, not map()
        load(key)
        count += 1
    return count


def min_max(scores: Iterable[float]) -> tuple[float, float]:
    it = iter(scores)
    try:
        lo = hi = next(it)
    except StopIteration:
        raise ValueError("min_max() of an empty iterable") from None
    for s in it:
        if s < lo:
            lo = s
        elif s > hi:
            hi = s
    return lo, hi


def peek[T](iterable: Iterable[T]) -> tuple[T, Iterator[T]]:
    it = iter(iterable)
    try:
        first = next(it)
    except StopIteration:
        raise ValueError("peek() of an empty iterable") from None
    return first, itertools.chain([first], it)

Pure functions and immutable conversation state★★★ · ex04_pure_state

functional.reduce, functional.concepts

Problem

Part A - refactor this impure function into a pure one:

SEEN = set()

def normalize_scores(results):
    top = max(r["score"] for r in results)
    for r in results:
        r["score"] = r["score"] / top        # mutates the caller's dicts
        SEEN.add(r["id"])                     # hidden global side effect
    return results
  1. normalize_scores(results) -> tuple[dict, ...]
    • min-max normalise "score" to [0, 1]: (s - lo) / (hi - lo); if all scores are equal every score becomes 1.0; empty input -> ()
    • returns NEW dicts (other keys copied) in input order; never touches the inputs; no global state; same input -> same output

Part B - conversation state as immutable values + a pure reducer (Redux/event-sourcing style). Message and ChatState are given below (both immutable).

  1. apply(state, event) -> ChatState (pure, never mutates)

    • {"type": "user" | "assistant", "content": str, "tokens": int} -> append Message(role, content, tokens); tokens_used += tokens
    • {"type": "truncate", "keep": n} -> keep only the last n messages (n == 0 -> none); tokens_used = sum of the kept messages' tokens
    • {"type": "reset"} -> ChatState()
    • anything else -> ValueError

  2. replay(events, initial=EMPTY) -> ChatState

    • fold all events over the initial state with functools.reduce
    • (EMPTY is one shared ChatState() used as a default - why is that safe here when a shared [] default would not be?)

  3. history(events, initial=EMPTY) -> list[ChatState]

    • every intermediate state, starting with initial (len == len(events) + 1); because states are immutable, older states are never affected by newer ones
    • hint: itertools.accumulate

Interviewers look for

  • Pure = output depends only on inputs + no observable side effects (no mutation of args, globals, I/O). Pure code is trivially testable, cacheable, parallelisable, replayable.
  • "Functional core, imperative shell": keep I/O (LLM calls, DB writes, logging) at the edges and the decision logic pure.
  • frozen dataclass + tuples: mutation raises FrozenInstanceError; "updates" are dataclasses.replace(...) returning new objects that share unchanged parts.
  • Immutable defaults are safe; immutable state makes undo/time-travel debugging, caching and concurrent reads easy. Cost: allocation/copying - fine at chat scale.

Work in exercises/py/04_functional/ex04_pure_state.py (or copy the starter code into any scratch file).

from collections.abc import Iterable, Mapping, Sequence

from typing import Any, NamedTuple

class Message(NamedTuple):
    role: str
    content: str
    tokens: int

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ChatState:
    messages: tuple[Message, ...] = ()
    tokens_used: int = 0
EMPTY = ChatState()

def normalize_scores(results: Sequence[Mapping[str, Any]]) -> tuple[dict[str, Any], ...]:
    raise NotImplementedError

def apply(state: ChatState, event: Mapping[str, Any]) -> ChatState:
    raise NotImplementedError

def replay(events: Iterable[Mapping[str, Any]], initial: ChatState=EMPTY) -> ChatState:

import itertools
from collections.abc import Iterable, Mapping, Sequence
from dataclasses import dataclass, replace
from functools import reduce
from typing import Any, NamedTuple


class Message(NamedTuple):
    role: str
    content: str
    tokens: int


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ChatState:
    messages: tuple[Message, ...] = ()
    tokens_used: int = 0


EMPTY = ChatState()  # one shared instance is fine: it can never change


def normalize_scores(results: Sequence[Mapping[str, Any]]) -> tuple[dict[str, Any], ...]:
    if not results:
        return ()
    scores = [r["score"] for r in results]
    lo, hi = min(scores), max(scores)
    span = hi - lo
    return tuple({**r, "score": (r["score"] - lo) / span if span else 1.0} for r in results)


def apply(state: ChatState, event: Mapping[str, Any]) -> ChatState:
    match event.get("type"):
        case "user" | "assistant" as role:
            msg = Message(role, event["content"], event["tokens"])
            return replace(state, messages=(*state.messages, msg), tokens_used=state.tokens_used + msg.tokens)
        case "truncate":
            n = event["keep"]
            kept = state.messages[len(state.messages) - n :] if n > 0 else ()
            return ChatState(kept, sum(m.tokens for m in kept))
        case "reset":
            return ChatState()
        case other:
            raise ValueError(f"unknown event type {other!r}")


def replay(events: Iterable[Mapping[str, Any]], initial: ChatState = EMPTY) -> ChatState:
    return reduce(apply, events, initial)


def history(events: Iterable[Mapping[str, Any]], initial: ChatState = EMPTY) -> list[ChatState]:
    return list(itertools.accumulate(events, apply, initial=initial))
