An immutable Embedding vector with dunder methods★★☆ · ex03_embedding

Problem

Write Embedding, an immutable, hashable vector type that behaves like a built-in:

  • init(values, *, model="") - store the values as a tuple of floats; empty -> ValueError. Use slots = ("_values", "_model") (millions of these may live in memory), and expose read-only properties values (the tuple) and model. Assigning to e.values / e.model or to any new attribute must raise AttributeError.
  • repr: dim <= 4: "Embedding([0.1, 0.2], model='m')" dim > 4: "Embedding([0.1, 0.2, ..., 0.9], dim=10, model='m')" (first two, last one)
  • len (dimension), iter (over the floats), getitem: an int index -> float; a slice -> a new Embedding with the same model.
  • eq: equal if same values AND same model. Comparing with a non-Embedding returns NotImplemented (so e == [0.1, 0.2] is simply False). hash consistent with eq.
  • add / sub: element-wise. Different dimension or different model -> ValueError. Non-Embedding operand -> NotImplemented (Python then raises TypeError).
  • mul / rmul by a number (int/float, not bool): 2 * e and e * 2. Otherwise NotImplemented.
  • matmul: e1 @ e2 -> dot product (float); dims must match (ValueError).
  • abs -> L2 norm; bool -> False only for the all-zeros vector.
  • cosine(other) -> float in [-1, 1]; a zero vector on either side -> ValueError.

Interviewers look for

  • Returning NotImplemented (not raising) lets Python try the reflected operation (rmul etc.) and produce the standard TypeError.
  • eq without hash makes the class unhashable; equal objects MUST hash equal; hashable objects should be immutable.
  • slots: no per-instance dict -> less memory, faster attribute access, no stray attributes - at the price of flexibility (no dynamic attrs, care with inheritance).
  • Real systems use NumPy for the math - this is about the data-model protocol.

import math
from collections.abc import Iterable, Iterator
from typing import Any


class Embedding:
    __slots__ = ("_values", "_model")

    def __init__(self, values: Iterable[float], *, model: str = "") -> None:
        vals = tuple(float(v) for v in values)
        if not vals:
            raise ValueError("an embedding needs at least one value")
        self._values = vals
        self._model = model

    @property
    def values(self) -> tuple[float, ...]:
        return self._values

    @property
    def model(self) -> str:
        return self._model

    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        v = self._values
        if len(v) <= 4:
            return f"Embedding({list(v)!r}, model={self._model!r})"
        return f"Embedding([{v[0]!r}, {v[1]!r}, ..., {v[-1]!r}], dim={len(v)}, model={self._model!r})"

    def __len__(self) -> int:
        return len(self._values)

    def __iter__(self) -> Iterator[float]:
        return iter(self._values)

    def __getitem__(self, index: int | slice) -> Any:
        if isinstance(index, slice):
            return Embedding(self._values[index], model=self._model)
        return self._values[index]

    def __eq__(self, other: object) -> bool:
        if not isinstance(other, Embedding):
            return NotImplemented
        return self._values == other._values and self._model == other._model

    def __hash__(self) -> int:
        return hash((self._values, self._model))

    def _check_compatible(self, other: "Embedding") -> None:
        if len(self) != len(other):
            raise ValueError(f"dimension mismatch: {len(self)} vs {len(other)}")
        if self._model != other._model:
            raise ValueError(f"model mismatch: {self._model!r} vs {other._model!r}")

    def __add__(self, other: object) -> "Embedding":
        if not isinstance(other, Embedding):
            return NotImplemented
        self._check_compatible(other)
        return Embedding((a + b for a, b in zip(self, other, strict=True)), model=self._model)

    def __sub__(self, other: object) -> "Embedding":
        if not isinstance(other, Embedding):
            return NotImplemented
        self._check_compatible(other)
        return Embedding((a - b for a, b in zip(self, other, strict=True)), model=self._model)

    def __mul__(self, scalar: object) -> "Embedding":
        if isinstance(scalar, bool) or not isinstance(scalar, (int, float)):
            return NotImplemented
        return Embedding((v * scalar for v in self._values), model=self._model)

    __rmul__ = __mul__

    def __matmul__(self, other: object) -> float:
        if not isinstance(other, Embedding):
            return NotImplemented
        if len(self) != len(other):
            raise ValueError("dimension mismatch")
        return math.fsum(a * b for a, b in zip(self, other, strict=True))

    def __abs__(self) -> float:
        return math.sqrt(self @ self)

    def __bool__(self) -> bool:
        return any(self._values)

    def cosine(self, other: "Embedding") -> float:
        denom = abs(self) * abs(other)
        if denom == 0:
            raise ValueError("cosine similarity is undefined for a zero vector")
        return (self @ other) / denom

dataclasses for model configs and eval results★★☆ · ex04_dataclasses

Problem

The field declarations below are part of the spec - implement the methods.

  1. ModelConfig - @dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True): name, temperature=0.7, max_tokens=1024, stop=() (a tuple of stop sequences). * post_init validates: empty name -> ValueError; temperature outside [0, 2] -> ValueError; max_tokens < 1 -> ValueError. It also NORMALISES stop: a list (or any iterable of str) is converted to a tuple, so configs stay hashable. The instance is frozen - find the sanctioned way to set a field inside post_init. * from_dict(data) - classmethod. Unknown keys -> TypeError listing them sorted (don't let a typo like "temprature" be silently ignored). Use dataclasses.fields(). * from_env(environ, prefix="LLM_") - classmethod, reads e.g. LLM_NAME="gpt-x" LLM_TEMPERATURE="0.2" LLM_MAX_TOKENS="256" LLM_STOP="###,END" converting types (float / int / comma-separated tuple; empty LLM_STOP -> ()). Missing variables use the defaults; missing NAME -> KeyError. environ is any mapping (pass os.environ in real code; tests pass a dict). * with_overrides(**changes) -> a NEW validated ModelConfig (dataclasses.replace).

  2. EvalResult - @dataclass(order=True, frozen=True): name, score, latency_ms=0.0, plus a sort_key field that is not an init parameter, not in the repr and is the ONLY field used for comparisons. post_init sets sort_key = (-score, latency_ms, name), so sorted(results) puts the best first: highest score, then the fastest, then by name.

  3. EvalRun - a regular @dataclass: config: ModelConfig, results: list[EvalResult] and tags: dict[str, str], both defaulting to a fresh empty container per run. * add(result) appends; leaderboard(n=None) -> the n best results (all if None); * mean_score property -> average score; no results -> ValueError.

Interviewers look for

  • Why results: list = [] is rejected by dataclasses and field(default_factory=list) is the fix (shared mutable default).
  • frozen=True -> immutability + generated hash (with eq=True): safe dict keys/cache keys. object.setattr inside post_init is the escape hatch.
  • slots=True: memory + typo protection; order=True compares fields as tuples in definition order - control it with field(compare=False) or a sort key.
  • classmethod alternative constructors (from_dict / from_env) keep init simple.
  • dataclass vs NamedTuple vs pydantic (runtime validation/parsing at boundaries).

import dataclasses
from collections.abc import Mapping
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Any


@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class ModelConfig:
    name: str
    temperature: float = 0.7
    max_tokens: int = 1024
    stop: tuple[str, ...] = ()

    def __post_init__(self) -> None:
        if not self.name:
            raise ValueError("name must be non-empty")
        if not 0.0 <= self.temperature <= 2.0:
            raise ValueError("temperature must be in [0, 2]")
        if self.max_tokens < 1:
            raise ValueError("max_tokens must be >= 1")
        # frozen: normal assignment raises FrozenInstanceError
        object.__setattr__(self, "stop", tuple(self.stop))

    @classmethod
    def from_dict(cls, data: Mapping[str, Any]) -> "ModelConfig":
        known = {f.name for f in dataclasses.fields(cls)}
        unknown = sorted(set(data) - known)
        if unknown:
            raise TypeError(f"unknown config keys: {', '.join(unknown)}")
        return cls(**data)

    @classmethod
    def from_env(cls, environ: Mapping[str, str], prefix: str = "LLM_") -> "ModelConfig":
        kwargs: dict[str, Any] = {"name": environ[f"{prefix}NAME"]}
        if (t := environ.get(f"{prefix}TEMPERATURE")) is not None:
            kwargs["temperature"] = float(t)
        if (m := environ.get(f"{prefix}MAX_TOKENS")) is not None:
            kwargs["max_tokens"] = int(m)
        if (s := environ.get(f"{prefix}STOP")) is not None:
            kwargs["stop"] = tuple(part for part in s.split(",") if part)
        return cls(**kwargs)

    def with_overrides(self, **changes: Any) -> "ModelConfig":
        return dataclasses.replace(self, **changes)  # runs __init__ + __post_init__ again


@dataclass(order=True, frozen=True)
class EvalResult:
    sort_key: tuple = field(init=False, repr=False)
    name: str = field(compare=False)
    score: float = field(compare=False)
    latency_ms: float = field(default=0.0, compare=False)

    def __post_init__(self) -> None:
        object.__setattr__(self, "sort_key", (-self.score, self.latency_ms, self.name))


@dataclass
class EvalRun:
    config: ModelConfig
    results: list[EvalResult] = field(default_factory=list)
    tags: dict[str, str] = field(default_factory=dict)

    def add(self, result: EvalResult) -> None:
        self.results.append(result)

    def leaderboard(self, n: int | None = None) -> list[EvalResult]:
        return sorted(self.results)[:n]

    @property
    def mean_score(self) -> float:
        if not self.results:
            raise ValueError("no results")
        return sum(r.score for r in self.results) / len(self.results)

Cooperative mixins, MRO and super() in a diamond★★★ · ex05_cooperative_mixins

Problem

An LLM client is assembled from mixins that all inherit from Component (a diamond):

RedactMixin, LoggingMixin, CacheMixin  -- each one subclasses Component
SafeClient(RedactMixin, LoggingMixin, CacheMixin)                      <- given

Each layer's process(text) does its bit and hands over with super().process(...). Every layer appends a marker to self.trace so the order is observable.

  • Component
  • init(**kwargs): if any keyword arguments are left over -> TypeError whose message contains the sorted leftover names (e.g. "unexpected config: colour"); sets self.trace = [].
  • process(text): appends "core", returns f"<{text}>" (stands in for the model call).
  • RedactMixin(Component)
  • init(*, redact=(), **kwargs): stores tuple(redact) as self.redact
  • process(text): appends "redact", replaces every term in self.redact with "[REDACTED]", passes the result on.
  • LoggingMixin(Component)
  • init(*, log_prefix="llm", **kwargs): stores self.log_prefix, self.logs = []
  • process(text): appends "log", passes text on unchanged, then appends f"{log_prefix}: {text} -> {result}" to self.logs (text as THIS layer received it).
  • CacheMixin(Component)
  • init(**kwargs): self.cache = {}
  • process(text): on a hit append "cache-hit" and return the cached result WITHOUT calling further down; on a miss append "cache-miss", call on, store, return.

Rules: each init takes the keyword arguments it understands and passes the REST on via super().init(**kwargs) - set your attributes AFTER that call (Component.init resets trace). Never call a specific parent class directly (no Component.__init__(self)): mixins must keep working when someone inserts another class into the MRO.

Interviewers look for

  • super() means "next class in the MRO of type(self)", not "my parent". That is what makes the diamond call Component.init exactly once.
  • C3 linearization: SafeClient, RedactMixin, LoggingMixin, CacheMixin, Component, object.
  • Cooperative signatures: keyword-only args + **kwargs, and a root that rejects leftovers.
  • Base order is behaviour: with Logging before Redact, raw PII reaches the logs.
  • When composition (a list of middleware objects) would be simpler than mixins.

Work in exercises/py/09_oop/ex05_cooperative_mixins.py (or copy the starter code into any scratch file).

from typing import Any

class Component:

    def __init__(self, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
        raise NotImplementedError

    def process(self, text: str) -> str:
        raise NotImplementedError

class RedactMixin(Component):

    def __init__(self, *, redact: tuple[str, ...]=(), **kwargs: Any) -> None:
        raise NotImplementedError

    def process(self, text: str) -> str:
        raise NotImplementedError

class LoggingMixin(Component):

    def __init__(self, *, log_prefix: str='llm', **kwargs: Any) -> None:
        raise NotImplementedError

    def process(self, text: str) -> str:
        raise NotImplementedError

class CacheMixin(Component):

    def __init__(self, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
        raise NotImplementedError

    def process(self, text: str) -> str:
        raise NotImplementedError

class SafeClient(RedactMixin, LoggingMixin, CacheMixin):
    """Redact first so that neither the logs nor the cache ever see raw PII."""

from typing import Any


class Component:
    def __init__(self, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
        if kwargs:
            raise TypeError(f"unexpected config: {', '.join(sorted(kwargs))}")
        self.trace: list[str] = []

    def process(self, text: str) -> str:
        self.trace.append("core")
        return f"<{text}>"


class RedactMixin(Component):
    def __init__(self, *, redact: tuple[str, ...] = (), **kwargs: Any) -> None:
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self.redact = tuple(redact)

    def process(self, text: str) -> str:
        self.trace.append("redact")
        for term in self.redact:
            text = text.replace(term, "[REDACTED]")
        return super().process(text)


class LoggingMixin(Component):
    def __init__(self, *, log_prefix: str = "llm", **kwargs: Any) -> None:
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self.log_prefix = log_prefix
        self.logs: list[str] = []

    def process(self, text: str) -> str:
        self.trace.append("log")
        result = super().process(text)
        self.logs.append(f"{self.log_prefix}: {text} -> {result}")
        return result


class CacheMixin(Component):
    def __init__(self, **kwargs: Any) -> None:
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self.cache: dict[str, str] = {}

    def process(self, text: str) -> str:
        if text in self.cache:
            self.trace.append("cache-hit")
            return self.cache[text]
        self.trace.append("cache-miss")
        result = super().process(text)
        self.cache[text] = result
        return result


class SafeClient(RedactMixin, LoggingMixin, CacheMixin):
    """Redact first so that neither the logs nor the cache ever see raw PII."""

Composition over inheritance + shallow vs deep copy★★★ · ex06_conversation_copy

Problem

The first version of the chat history was class Conversation(FakeLLMClient) - every conversation WAS a client (its own connection pool), and "branching" a conversation with copy.deepcopy crashed with TypeError: cannot pickle '_thread.lock' object. Rewrite it with composition: a Conversation HAS a client (any object with complete(messages) -> str).

Conversation(client, system_prompt) * self.client = client (shared, never copied); self.messages = a list of message dicts, starting with {"role": "system", "content": system_prompt, "metadata": {}} * add(role, content, **metadata) - role must be one of ROLES (ValueError otherwise); appends {"role": role, "content": content, "metadata": dict(metadata)} * ask(text) -> str - add the user message, call self.client.complete(self.messages), add the reply as an "assistant" message, return the reply (delegation). * len -> number of messages __co -> copyopy(conv): a new Conversation with the SAME client, a NEW messages list that holds the SAME message dicts (appending to one conversation doesn't affect the other, but editing a shared message dict does - that's what "shallow" means). __decopy(me) -> copy.deepcopy(conv): a new Conversation with the SAME client and a fully independent deep copy of the messages (nested metadata included). Pass memo on when deep-copying the messages. * fork() -> a deep copy (a "what if" branch of the conversation). * Build copies WITHOUT re-running init (that would add a second system message): e.g. new = type(self).new(type(self)), then set its attributes.

FakeLLMClient (given) holds a threading.Lock, like real SDK clients hold connection pools.

Interviewers look for

  • Composition: Conversation delegates to a client instead of being one -> share one client across thousands of conversations, swap providers/mocks freely (duck typing).
  • b = a (alias) vs copy.copy (new outer container, shared inner objects) vs copy.deepcopy (recursively copied) - and which bug each one causes.
  • Customising copying with copy / deepcopy (and why some objects - locks, sockets, clients - must be shared, not copied).

Work in exercises/py/09_oop/ex06_conversation_copy.py (or copy the starter code into any scratch file).

import copy
import threading
from typing import Any
ROLES = frozenset({'system', 'user', 'assistant', 'tool'})

class FakeLLMClient:
    """Expensive, shared resource. Holds a lock, so it can't be deep-copied or pickled."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._lock = threading.Lock()
        self.requests = 0

    def complete(self, messages: list[dict[str, Any]]) -> str:
        with self._lock:
            self.requests += 1
        return f"echo: {messages[-1]['content']}"

class Conversation:

    def __init__(self, client: Any, system_prompt: str) -> None:
        raise NotImplementedError

    def add(self, role: str, content: str, **metadata: Any) -> None:
        raise NotImplementedError

    def ask(self, text: str) -> str:
        raise NotImplementedError

    def __len__(self) -> int:
        raise NotImplementedError

    def __copy__(self) -> 'Conversation':
        raise NotImplementedError

    def __deepcopy__(self, memo: dict[int, Any]) -> 'Conversation':
        raise NotImplementedError

    def fork(self) -> 'Conversation':
        raise NotImplementedError

import copy
import threading
from typing import Any

__stub_keep__ = ["FakeLLMClient"]

ROLES = frozenset({"system", "user", "assistant", "tool"})


class FakeLLMClient:
    """Expensive, shared resource. Holds a lock, so it can't be deep-copied or pickled."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._lock = threading.Lock()
        self.requests = 0

    def complete(self, messages: list[dict[str, Any]]) -> str:
        with self._lock:
            self.requests += 1
        return f"echo: {messages[-1]['content']}"


class Conversation:
    def __init__(self, client: Any, system_prompt: str) -> None:
        self.client = client
        self.messages: list[dict[str, Any]] = []
        self.add("system", system_prompt)

    def add(self, role: str, content: str, **metadata: Any) -> None:
        if role not in ROLES:
            raise ValueError(f"unknown role {role!r}")
        self.messages.append({"role": role, "content": content, "metadata": dict(metadata)})

    def ask(self, text: str) -> str:
        self.add("user", text)
        reply = self.client.complete(self.messages)
        self.add("assistant", reply)
        return reply

    def __len__(self) -> int:
        return len(self.messages)

    def __copy__(self) -> "Conversation":
        new = type(self).__new__(type(self))
        new.client = self.client
        new.messages = list(self.messages)  # new list, same dicts
        return new

    def __deepcopy__(self, memo: dict[int, Any]) -> "Conversation":
        new = type(self).__new__(type(self))
        memo[id(self)] = new
        new.client = self.client  # shared on purpose: never copy the client
        new.messages = copy.deepcopy(self.messages, memo)
        return new

    def fork(self) -> "Conversation":
        return copy.deepcopy(self)

Parsing LLM tool calls safely★☆☆ · ex01_tool_call_parsing

exceptions.chaining, exceptions.syntax_vs_runtime

Problem

An LLM returns a tool call as JSON text: {"name": "search", "arguments": {"q": "..."}} ("arguments" may also be a JSON-encoded string, which is how the OpenAI API sends it).

  1. class ToolCallError(ValueError) init(self, message: str, raw: str) -> stores .raw (the offending text); str(err) == message

  2. parse_tool_call(raw: str) -> ToolCall (ToolCall dataclass is given)

    • "arguments" missing -> {} ; if it is a str, json-decode it too
    • every data problem raises ToolCallError - callers must never see a bare json.JSONDecodeError / KeyError / TypeError coming out of this function:
      • invalid JSON (outer text, or the inner arguments string) -> ToolCallError chained with raise ... from e, so err.cause is the json.JSONDecodeError
      • top level is not an object, or "name" is missing -> ToolCallError (hint: data["name"] raises KeyError for a dict without it and TypeError for a list/str/int - one except (KeyError, TypeError) handles both; chain it)
      • "name" not a non-empty str, arguments not an object -> ToolCallError
    • raw that is not a str at all (None, bytes...) is a programming bug, not bad data: let the TypeError from json.loads propagate - don't wrap it.

  3. parse_many(raws: Iterable[str]) -> tuple[list[ToolCall], list[tuple[int, ToolCallError]]]

    • parse every item; failures are collected as (index, error) and don't stop the loop
    • catch ToolCallError ONLY (a None item must still blow up with TypeError)

  4. syntax_error_at(source: str) -> tuple[int, str] | None

    • LLM-generated Python: return (lineno, msg) of its SyntaxError WITHOUT executing it (compile() / ast.parse), else None
    • code that would only fail at runtime (1/0, undefined names) is syntactically valid -> None, and it must not run (no side effects)
    • source containing NUL bytes counts as a syntax error too (lineno 0 if unknown)

Interviewers look for

  • Small try blocks: only the line that can raise the expected error goes in try; the rest goes in else (so you don't accidentally catch your own bugs).
  • Translating low-level errors into a domain error at an API boundary, with from e so the original traceback is kept ("The above exception was the direct cause...").
  • Catching exactly what you expect - a broad except Exception here would also hide the TypeError for None input, a real bug.
  • SyntaxError is raised when code is compiled, before any of it runs; runtime errors only when the offending line executes.

Work in exercises/py/10_exceptions/ex01_tool_call_parsing.py (or copy the starter code into any scratch file).

import json
from collections.abc import Iterable
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Any

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ToolCall:
    name: str
    arguments: dict[str, Any] = field(default_factory=dict)

class ToolCallError(ValueError):

    def __init__(self, message: str, raw: str) -> None:
        raise NotImplementedError

def parse_tool_call(raw: str) -> ToolCall:
    raise NotImplementedError

def parse_many(raws: Iterable[str]) -> tuple[list[ToolCall], list[tuple[int, ToolCallError]]]:
    raise NotImplementedError

def syntax_error_at(source: str) -> tuple[int, str] | None:
    raise NotImplementedError

import json
from collections.abc import Iterable
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Any


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ToolCall:
    name: str
    arguments: dict[str, Any] = field(default_factory=dict)


class ToolCallError(ValueError):
    def __init__(self, message: str, raw: str) -> None:
        super().__init__(message)
        self.raw = raw


def parse_tool_call(raw: str) -> ToolCall:
    try:
        data = json.loads(raw)
    except json.JSONDecodeError as e:
        raise ToolCallError(f"tool call is not valid JSON: {e.msg}", raw) from e

    try:
        name = data["name"]
    except (KeyError, TypeError) as e:
        raise ToolCallError("tool call must be an object with a 'name'", raw) from e
    if not isinstance(name, str) or not name:
        raise ToolCallError("'name' must be a non-empty string", raw)

    args = data.get("arguments", {})
    if isinstance(args, str):
        try:
            args = json.loads(args)
        except json.JSONDecodeError as e:
            raise ToolCallError(f"arguments are not valid JSON: {e.msg}", raw) from e
    if not isinstance(args, dict):
        raise ToolCallError("'arguments' must be a JSON object", raw)
    return ToolCall(name, args)


def parse_many(
    raws: Iterable[str],
) -> tuple[list[ToolCall], list[tuple[int, ToolCallError]]]:
    ok: list[ToolCall] = []
    failed: list[tuple[int, ToolCallError]] = []
    for i, raw in enumerate(raws):
        try:
            call = parse_tool_call(raw)
        except ToolCallError as e:
            failed.append((i, e))
        else:
            ok.append(call)
    return ok, failed


def syntax_error_at(source: str) -> tuple[int, str] | None:
    try:
        compile(source, "<llm-generated>", "exec")  # compiles only; nothing is executed
    except SyntaxError as e:
        return (e.lineno or 0, e.msg)
    return None

Exception hierarchy for an LLM client★★☆ · ex02_llm_error_hierarchy

exceptions.best_practices

Problem

Build the error types an LLM SDK exposes, and map HTTP responses onto them.

LLMError(Exception)                      retryable = False
├── AuthError                            401, 403
├── BadRequestError                      400, 404, 409, 422
│   └── ContextLengthError               400 with error code "context_length_exceeded"
├── RateLimitError                       429                     retryable = True
├── ServerError                          >= 500                  retryable = True
└── APITimeoutError(LLMError, TimeoutError)   408               retryable = True

  1. LLMError.init(self, message: str, *, status: int | None = None, provider: str | None = None)

    • attributes .message .status .provider ; class attribute retryable
    • str(err): "[openai 429] slow down" / without status: "[openai] slow down"; provider defaults to "llm" in the text: "[llm 500] boom" RateLimitError.init(message, *, retry_after: float | None = None, **kw) -> .retry_after ContextLengthError.init(message, *, max_tokens: int | None = None, requested_tokens: int | None = None, **kw) (the classes with nothing extra to store need no init at all)

  2. Errors must survive pickle / copy (they cross process boundaries in multiprocessing, concurrent.futures, Celery...). BaseException pickles as cls(*self.args) + __dict__: think about what self.args contains for your classes, and make pickle.loads(pickle.dumps(err)) give back an equal-looking error of the same class with every attribute intact (hint: one __reduce__ on LLMError is enough).

  3. error_from_response(status: int, body: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None, headers: Mapping[str, str] | None = None, provider: str | None = None) -> LLMError

    • RETURNS the error (the caller decides to raise it)
    • body shape: {"error": {"message": str, "code": str, "max_tokens": int, "requested_tokens": int}} - any part may be missing; a missing message becomes f"HTTP {status}"
    • 429: retry_after from the "Retry-After" header (header names are case-insensitive; seconds as a number; unparsable -> None)
    • unknown 4xx (e.g. 418) -> plain LLMError; status is always stored

Interviewers look for

  • One base class so callers can except LLMError, specific subclasses so they can react differently (re-auth vs back off vs truncate the prompt).
  • Retryability as data on the class, not a status-code if-chain repeated in every caller.
  • Multiple inheritance from a builtin (TimeoutError) so generic code that catches the builtin still works.
  • Custom exceptions with extra required init args break pickling - a production bug that only shows up when errors cross a process boundary.

Work in exercises/py/10_exceptions/ex02_llm_error_hierarchy.py (or copy the starter code into any scratch file).

from collections.abc import Mapping
from typing import Any

class LLMError(Exception):
    retryable: bool = False

    def __init__(self, message: str, *, status: int | None=None, provider: str | None=None) -> None:
        raise NotImplementedError

    def __str__(self) -> str:
        raise NotImplementedError

    def __reduce__(self) -> tuple[Any, ...]:
        raise NotImplementedError

class AuthError(LLMError):
    pass

class BadRequestError(LLMError):
    pass

class ContextLengthError(BadRequestError):

    def __init__(self, message: str, *, max_tokens: int | None=None, requested_tokens: int | None=None, **kw: Any) -> None:
        raise NotImplementedError

class RateLimitError(LLMError):
    retryable = True

    def __init__(self, message: str, *, retry_after: float | None=None, **kw: Any) -> None:
        raise NotImplementedError

class ServerError(LLMError):
    retryable = True

class APITimeoutError(LLMError, TimeoutError):
    retryable = True

def error_from_response(status: int, body: Mapping[str, Any] | None=None, headers: Mapping[str, str] | None=None, provider: str | None=None) -> LLMError:
    raise NotImplementedError

from collections.abc import Mapping
from typing import Any


class LLMError(Exception):
    retryable: bool = False

    def __init__(self, message: str, *, status: int | None = None, provider: str | None = None) -> None:
        super().__init__(message)
        self.message = message
        self.status = status
        self.provider = provider

    def __str__(self) -> str:
        where = self.provider or "llm"
        if self.status is not None:
            where = f"{where} {self.status}"
        return f"[{where}] {self.message}"

    def __reduce__(self) -> tuple[Any, ...]:
        # args holds only the message; every other attribute lives in __dict__ and is
        # restored by BaseException.__setstate__ - so subclasses need no extra code.
        return (type(self), (self.message,), self.__dict__)


class AuthError(LLMError):
    pass


class BadRequestError(LLMError):
    pass


class ContextLengthError(BadRequestError):
    def __init__(
        self,
        message: str,
        *,
        max_tokens: int | None = None,
        requested_tokens: int | None = None,
        **kw: Any,
    ) -> None:
        super().__init__(message, **kw)
        self.max_tokens = max_tokens
        self.requested_tokens = requested_tokens


class RateLimitError(LLMError):
    retryable = True

    def __init__(self, message: str, *, retry_after: float | None = None, **kw: Any) -> None:
        super().__init__(message, **kw)
        self.retry_after = retry_after


class ServerError(LLMError):
    retryable = True


class APITimeoutError(LLMError, TimeoutError):
    retryable = True


def _retry_after(headers: Mapping[str, str] | None) -> float | None:
    if not headers:
        return None
    lowered = {k.lower(): v for k, v in headers.items()}
    try:
        return float(lowered["retry-after"])
    except (KeyError, ValueError):
        return None


def error_from_response(
    status: int,
    body: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None,
    headers: Mapping[str, str] | None = None,
    provider: str | None = None,
) -> LLMError:
    err = (body or {}).get("error") or {}
    message = err.get("message") or f"HTTP {status}"
    kw: dict[str, Any] = {"status": status, "provider": provider}
    if status in (401, 403):
        return AuthError(message, **kw)
    if status == 429:
        return RateLimitError(message, retry_after=_retry_after(headers), **kw)
    if status == 408:
        return APITimeoutError(message, **kw)
    if status == 400 and err.get("code") == "context_length_exceeded":
        return ContextLengthError(
            message,
            max_tokens=err.get("max_tokens"),
            requested_tokens=err.get("requested_tokens"),
            **kw,
        )
    if status in (400, 404, 409, 422):
        return BadRequestError(message, **kw)
    if status >= 500:
        return ServerError(message, **kw)
    return LLMError(message, **kw)

Retrying transient LLM errors★★☆ · ex03_retry_with_backoff

exceptions.raising, exceptions.try_except

Problem

TransientError / PermanentError are given (think RateLimitError / AuthError).

  1. class RetryError(Exception) init(self, attempts: int, last: BaseException) .attempts, .last ; str(err) == f"gave up after {attempts} attempts: {last!r}"

  2. call_with_retry(fn, *, attempts=3, base_delay=0.5, max_delay=8.0, sleep=time.sleep, logger=None) -> T

    • calls fn() (no args) until it returns; returns its value
    • attempts < 1 -> ValueError, before fn is ever called
    • ONLY TransientError is retried. Anything else (PermanentError, a ValueError bug, KeyboardInterrupt...) propagates immediately: the same exception object, unwrapped, after a single call, with no sleep
    • delay before retry k (k = 0 for the first retry): err.retry_after if it is not None, else base_delay * 2**k ; always capped at max_delay. sleep(delay) is called between attempts - never after the last one.
    • every failed attempt that will be retried is logged at WARNING on logger (default: logging.getLogger(name)), mentioning the attempt number and delay
    • when all attempts fail: log at ERROR, then raise RetryError(attempts, last_error) from last_error

Interviewers look for

  • Retry only what's retryable - retrying a 401 or a bug just burns quota and hides it.
  • Never catch BaseException in a retry loop: Ctrl-C / task cancellation must stop it.
  • raise ... from last keeps the real root cause in the traceback of the summary error.
  • Injecting sleep (and a logger) makes timing logic testable without real waiting.
  • Bounded exponential backoff + server-provided Retry-After; add jitter in production.

Work in exercises/py/10_exceptions/ex03_retry_with_backoff.py (or copy the starter code into any scratch file).

import logging
import time
from collections.abc import Callable
from typing import TypeVar
T = TypeVar('T')

class TransientError(Exception):
    """Retryable failure, e.g. HTTP 429/503. retry_after is in seconds (server hint)."""

    def __init__(self, message: str, retry_after: float | None=None) -> None:
        super().__init__(message)
        self.retry_after = retry_after

class PermanentError(Exception):
    """Non-retryable failure, e.g. HTTP 401."""

class RetryError(Exception):

    def __init__(self, attempts: int, last: BaseException) -> None:
        raise NotImplementedError

def call_with_retry(fn: Callable[[], T], *, attempts: int=3, base_delay: float=0.5, max_delay: float=8.0, sleep: Callable[[float], object]=time.sleep, logger: logging.Logger | None=None) -> T:
    raise NotImplementedError

import logging
import time
from collections.abc import Callable
from typing import TypeVar

T = TypeVar("T")

__stub_keep__ = ["TransientError", "PermanentError"]


class TransientError(Exception):
    """Retryable failure, e.g. HTTP 429/503. retry_after is in seconds (server hint)."""

    def __init__(self, message: str, retry_after: float | None = None) -> None:
        super().__init__(message)
        self.retry_after = retry_after


class PermanentError(Exception):
    """Non-retryable failure, e.g. HTTP 401."""


class RetryError(Exception):
    def __init__(self, attempts: int, last: BaseException) -> None:
        super().__init__(f"gave up after {attempts} attempts: {last!r}")
        self.attempts = attempts
        self.last = last


def call_with_retry(
    fn: Callable[[], T],
    *,
    attempts: int = 3,
    base_delay: float = 0.5,
    max_delay: float = 8.0,
    sleep: Callable[[float], object] = time.sleep,
    logger: logging.Logger | None = None,
) -> T:
    if attempts < 1:
        raise ValueError("attempts must be >= 1")
    log = logger or logging.getLogger(__name__)
    for attempt in range(1, attempts + 1):
        try:
            return fn()
        except TransientError as e:  # everything else propagates untouched
            if attempt == attempts:
                log.error("attempt %d/%d failed: %s; giving up", attempt, attempts, e)
                raise RetryError(attempts, e) from e
            hint = e.retry_after
            delay = min(hint if hint is not None else base_delay * 2 ** (attempt - 1), max_delay)
            log.warning("attempt %d/%d failed: %s; retrying in %.2fs", attempt, attempts, e, delay)
            sleep(delay)
    raise AssertionError("unreachable")  # pragma: no cover

Enriching and reporting errors in an ingest job★★☆ · ex04_error_context

exceptions.chaining

Problem

A document-ingest job must tell you which document broke, without losing the original exception or its traceback.

  1. error_context(**context) - a context manager

    • any Exception leaving the block gets ONE note (BaseException.add_note, 3.11+): "context: doc_id=a1, stage=embed" (keys in the order given) and is re-raised: same object, same type, traceback intact
    • BaseExceptions that are not Exceptions (KeyboardInterrupt, SystemExit) pass through untouched; nothing happens on success

  2. ingest(docs, process, *, logger, strict=False) -> IngestReport

    • docs: iterable of dicts with an "id"; calls process(doc) for each
    • success -> id appended to report.ok
    • an Exception in process():
      • strict=False: logger.exception("failed to ingest %s", doc_id, extra={"doc_id": doc_id}) (logs at ERROR with the traceback), record report.failed[doc_id] = f"{type(e).name}: {e}", continue with the next doc
      • strict=True: add the note f"doc_id={doc_id}" and re-raise the same exception with a bare raise (don't log it AND raise it - pick one)
    • KeyboardInterrupt etc. are never caught

  3. root_cause(exc) -> BaseException follow cause, or context when suppress_context is False, to the end.

  4. error_chain(exc) -> str "TypeName: message" for exc and each exception below it (same walk as root_cause), joined with " <- ", e.g. "IngestError: doc a1 failed <- KeyError: 'text'"

Interviewers look for

  • Adding context without changing the exception type (add_note) vs wrapping it in a new type (raise X from e) - both valid, different contracts for callers.
  • logger.exception (= error + exc_info) inside an except block, structured extra fields for log search; never "log and re-raise" at every layer (duplicate logs).
  • Partial-failure reporting for batch jobs instead of crashing hour 3 of a run.
  • Knowing how cause / context / suppress_context form the chain.

Work in exercises/py/10_exceptions/ex04_error_context.py (or copy the starter code into any scratch file).

@dataclass
class IngestReport:
    ok: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    failed: dict[str, str] = field(default_factory=dict)

@contextmanager
def error_context(**context: Any) -> Iterator[None]:
    raise NotImplementedError

def ingest(docs: Iterable[dict[str, Any]], process: Callable[[dict[str, Any]], object], *, logger: logging.Logger, strict: bool=False) -> IngestReport:
    raise NotImplementedError

def root_cause(exc: BaseException) -> BaseException:
    raise NotImplementedError

def error_chain(exc: BaseException) -> str:
    raise NotImplementedError

import logging
from collections.abc import Callable, Iterable, Iterator
from contextlib import contextmanager
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Any


@dataclass
class IngestReport:
    ok: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    failed: dict[str, str] = field(default_factory=dict)


@contextmanager
def error_context(**context: Any) -> Iterator[None]:
    try:
        yield
    except Exception as e:
        e.add_note("context: " + ", ".join(f"{k}={v}" for k, v in context.items()))
        raise


def ingest(
    docs: Iterable[dict[str, Any]],
    process: Callable[[dict[str, Any]], object],
    *,
    logger: logging.Logger,
    strict: bool = False,
) -> IngestReport:
    report = IngestReport()
    for doc in docs:
        doc_id = doc["id"]
        try:
            process(doc)
        except Exception as e:
            if strict:
                e.add_note(f"doc_id={doc_id}")
                raise
            logger.exception("failed to ingest %s", doc_id, extra={"doc_id": doc_id})
            report.failed[doc_id] = f"{type(e).__name__}: {e}"
        else:
            report.ok.append(doc_id)
    return report


def _next_in_chain(exc: BaseException) -> BaseException | None:
    if exc.__cause__ is not None:
        return exc.__cause__
    if not exc.__suppress_context__:
        return exc.__context__
    return None


def root_cause(exc: BaseException) -> BaseException:
    seen = {id(exc)}
    while (nxt := _next_in_chain(exc)) is not None and id(nxt) not in seen:
        seen.add(id(nxt))
        exc = nxt
    return exc


def error_chain(exc: BaseException) -> str:
    parts = [f"{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}"]
    seen = {id(exc)}
    cur: BaseException | None = _next_in_chain(exc)
    while cur is not None and id(cur) not in seen:
        seen.add(id(cur))
        parts.append(f"{type(cur).__name__}: {cur}")
        cur = _next_in_chain(cur)
    return " <- ".join(parts)

Batch failures with ExceptionGroup / except*★★★ · ex05_exception_groups

exceptions.best_practices

Problem

Embedding 10 document batches concurrently can fail in several different ways at once. Python 3.11+ models that with ExceptionGroup and except*. TransientError is given.

  1. run_all(tasks: Mapping[str, Callable[[], T]]) -> dict[str, T]

    • run EVERY task (in order) even after some fail; return {name: result} if all succeed
    • if any failed: raise ExceptionGroup(f"{n_failed} of {n_total} tasks failed", errors) with errors in task order; before grouping, add the note f"task={name}" to each
    • only Exception failures are grouped - a BaseException (KeyboardInterrupt) stops immediately and propagates as-is (ExceptionGroup can't even hold one)

  2. task_name(exc: BaseException) -> str | None the name from a "task=<name>" note, or None

  3. flatten(exc: BaseException) -> list[BaseException] leaf exceptions of (possibly nested) groups, depth-first, in order; a non-group exception -> [exc]

  4. triage(fn: Callable[[], object]) -> Triage (Triage dataclass given)

    • call fn(); use except* to sort what it raised: TransientError -> task names into Triage.retry ValueError -> task names into Triage.invalid (task names via task_name(); in order of appearance)
    • anything else must propagate - and Python does that for you: the unmatched remainder is re-raised as an ExceptionGroup
    • a naked TransientError / ValueError (not in a group) is handled the same way
    • no error -> empty Triage
    • note: return is not allowed inside an except* block - why?

Interviewers look for

  • except* runs EVERY matching clause (unlike except, which picks one), each with a sub-group of the matching leaves; unmatched leaves are re-raised automatically.
  • asyncio.TaskGroup raises ExceptionGroup; code catching except ValueError around it silently stops working - you need except*.
  • Attaching context (notes) so a group of 7 failures is debuggable.

Work in exercises/py/10_exceptions/ex05_exception_groups.py (or copy the starter code into any scratch file).

from collections.abc import Callable, Mapping
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import TypeVar
T = TypeVar('T')

class TransientError(Exception):
    """Retryable failure (rate limit / 503)."""

@dataclass
class Triage:
    retry: list[str | None] = field(default_factory=list)
    invalid: list[str | None] = field(default_factory=list)

def run_all(tasks: Mapping[str, Callable[[], T]]) -> dict[str, T]:
    raise NotImplementedError

def task_name(exc: BaseException) -> str | None:
    raise NotImplementedError

def flatten(exc: BaseException) -> list[BaseException]:
    raise NotImplementedError

def triage(fn: Callable[[], object]) -> Triage:
    raise NotImplementedError

from collections.abc import Callable, Mapping
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import TypeVar

T = TypeVar("T")

__stub_keep__ = ["TransientError"]


class TransientError(Exception):
    """Retryable failure (rate limit / 503)."""


@dataclass
class Triage:
    retry: list[str | None] = field(default_factory=list)
    invalid: list[str | None] = field(default_factory=list)


def run_all(tasks: Mapping[str, Callable[[], T]]) -> dict[str, T]:
    results: dict[str, T] = {}
    errors: list[Exception] = []
    for name, task in tasks.items():
        try:
            results[name] = task()
        except Exception as e:
            e.add_note(f"task={name}")
            errors.append(e)
    if errors:
        raise ExceptionGroup(f"{len(errors)} of {len(tasks)} tasks failed", errors)
    return results


def task_name(exc: BaseException) -> str | None:
    notes: list[str] = getattr(exc, "__notes__", [])
    for note in notes:
        if note.startswith("task="):
            return note.removeprefix("task=")
    return None


def flatten(exc: BaseException) -> list[BaseException]:
    if isinstance(exc, BaseExceptionGroup):
        return [leaf for sub in exc.exceptions for leaf in flatten(sub)]
    return [exc]


def triage(fn: Callable[[], object]) -> Triage:
    result = Triage()
    try:
        fn()
    except* TransientError as eg:
        result.retry.extend(task_name(e) for e in flatten(eg))
    except* ValueError as eg:
        result.invalid.extend(task_name(e) for e in flatten(eg))
    return result

JSONL datasets: write, append, stream★☆☆ · ex01_jsonl_io

files.open_close, files.encoding

Problem

JSONL (one JSON object per line) is the format of fine-tuning sets, eval results and batch-API requests. Implement:

  1. write_jsonl(path, records: Iterable[Mapping[str, Any]]) -> int

    • (over)writes the file; one compact JSON object per line, each ending in "\n"
    • UTF-8, non-ASCII kept as-is (ensure_ascii=False: "café", not "caf\u00e9")
    • returns the number of records written

  2. append_jsonl(path, record) -> None

    • adds one line at the end; creates the file if it doesn't exist

  3. iter_jsonl(path, *, skip_invalid=False, errors=None) -> Iterator[dict[str, Any]]

    • LAZY: yields one dict per line, never reads the whole file into memory
    • blank / whitespace-only lines are ignored
    • a line that isn't valid JSON, or is valid JSON but not an object (e.g. [1, 2]):
      • skip_invalid=False -> ValueError(f"{path}:{lineno}: ...") chained from the original error where there is one (lineno is 1-based)
      • skip_invalid=True -> skipped; if errors (a list) is given, append (lineno, stripped_line) to it
    • a missing file raises FileNotFoundError when iter_jsonl() is CALLED, not on the first next()
    • the file must be closed once the iterator is exhausted (or closed early)

Interviewers look for

  • Always pass encoding= explicitly - the default is platform/locale dependent.
  • with guarantees close() even on exceptions; why leaked handles matter at scale ("Too many open files").
  • Mode semantics: "w" truncates, "a" appends (and creates), "x" fails if it exists.
  • Iterating a file object is line-by-line and lazy; f.read()/readlines() is not.

from collections.abc import Iterable, Iterator, Mapping
from pathlib import Path
from typing import IO, Any

    raise NotImplementedError

def append_jsonl(path: str | Path, record: Mapping[str, Any]) -> None:
    raise NotImplementedError

def iter_jsonl(path: str | Path, *, skip_invalid: bool=False, errors: list[tuple[int, str]] | None=None) -> Iterator[dict[str, Any]]:
    raise NotImplementedError

import json
from collections.abc import Iterable, Iterator, Mapping
from pathlib import Path
from typing import IO, Any


def write_jsonl(path: str | Path, records: Iterable[Mapping[str, Any]]) -> int:
    n = 0
    with open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8", newline="\n") as f:
        for rec in records:
            f.write(json.dumps(rec, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n")
            n += 1
    return n


def append_jsonl(path: str | Path, record: Mapping[str, Any]) -> None:
    with open(path, "a", encoding="utf-8", newline="\n") as f:
        f.write(json.dumps(record, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n")


def iter_jsonl(
    path: str | Path,
    *,
    skip_invalid: bool = False,
    errors: list[tuple[int, str]] | None = None,
) -> Iterator[dict[str, Any]]:
    f = open(path, encoding="utf-8")  # noqa: SIM115 - opened eagerly, closed by _lines
    return _records(f, str(path), skip_invalid, errors)


def _records(
    f: IO[str], name: str, skip_invalid: bool, errors: list[tuple[int, str]] | None
) -> Iterator[dict[str, Any]]:
    with f:
        for lineno, line in enumerate(f, start=1):
            line = line.strip()
            if not line:
                continue
            try:
                obj = json.loads(line)
            except json.JSONDecodeError as e:
                if not skip_invalid:
                    raise ValueError(f"{name}:{lineno}: invalid JSON ({e.msg})") from e
                obj = None
            if not isinstance(obj, dict):
                if not skip_invalid:
                    raise ValueError(f"{name}:{lineno}: expected a JSON object")
                if errors is not None:
                    errors.append((lineno, line))
                continue
            yield obj

Problem

An eval harness exports one row per test case. CSV has no types - everything is a string.

id,model,score,passed,latency_ms,tags
q1,gpt-4o,0.92,true,812,rag;faq
q2,claude,0.40,no,,

  1. read_eval_csv(path) -> list[EvalRow] (EvalRow dataclass is given)

    • header required columns: id, model, score, passed -> otherwise ValueError naming the missing column(s). latency_ms and tags are optional columns (absent column -> None / []). Extra columns are ignored.
    • coercion: score -> float; passed -> bool from "true/false/1/0/yes/no" (case-insensitive, surrounding whitespace ignored); latency_ms "" -> None else int; tags "a; b" -> ["a", "b"], "" -> []
    • a value that can't be coerced -> ValueError mentioning f"line {n}" where n is the file line number the row ends on (csv.reader's line_num), chained from the original error if there is one
    • quoted fields may contain commas, quotes and newlines (including "\r\n" inside model output) - they must come back exactly

  2. write_eval_csv(path, rows: Iterable[EvalRow]) -> int

    • header id,model,score,passed,latency_ms,tags ; passed written as "true"/"false", None as "", tags joined with ";" ; returns the number of rows
    • read_eval_csv(write_eval_csv(rows)) must give back equal rows

Interviewers look for

  • open(..., newline="") for csv in BOTH directions: the csv module does its own newline handling; without it embedded "\r\n" gets mangled (and on Windows you get blank rows).
  • csv.DictReader/DictWriter instead of split(",") (quoting!).
  • Validating at the boundary with a helpful line number instead of a KeyError later.

import csv
from collections.abc import Iterable
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from pathlib import Path

REQUIRED = ("id", "model", "score", "passed")
COLUMNS = ("id", "model", "score", "passed", "latency_ms", "tags")
_TRUE = {"true", "1", "yes"}
_FALSE = {"false", "0", "no"}


@dataclass
class EvalRow:
    id: str
    model: str
    score: float
    passed: bool
    latency_ms: int | None = None
    tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)


def _to_bool(value: str) -> bool:
    v = value.strip().lower()
    if v in _TRUE:
        return True
    if v in _FALSE:
        return False
    raise ValueError(f"not a boolean: {value!r}")


def _row(rec: dict[str, str]) -> EvalRow:
    latency = (rec.get("latency_ms") or "").strip()
    tags = rec.get("tags") or ""
    return EvalRow(
        id=rec["id"],
        model=rec["model"],
        score=float(rec["score"]),
        passed=_to_bool(rec["passed"]),
        latency_ms=int(latency) if latency else None,
        tags=[t.strip() for t in tags.split(";") if t.strip()],
    )


def read_eval_csv(path: str | Path) -> list[EvalRow]:
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8", newline="") as f:
        reader = csv.DictReader(f)
        missing = [c for c in REQUIRED if c not in (reader.fieldnames or [])]
        if missing:
            raise ValueError(f"missing required column(s): {', '.join(missing)}")
        rows: list[EvalRow] = []
        for rec in reader:
            try:
                rows.append(_row(rec))
            except ValueError as e:
                raise ValueError(f"line {reader.line_num}: {e}") from e
        return rows


def write_eval_csv(path: str | Path, rows: Iterable[EvalRow]) -> int:
    n = 0
    with open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8", newline="") as f:
        writer = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=COLUMNS)
        writer.writeheader()
        for r in rows:
            writer.writerow(
                {
                    "id": r.id,
                    "model": r.model,
                    "score": repr(r.score),
                    "passed": "true" if r.passed else "false",
                    "latency_ms": "" if r.latency_ms is None else r.latency_ms,
                    "tags": ";".join(r.tags),
                }
            )
            n += 1
    return n

Ingesting text files of unknown encoding★★☆ · ex03_encoding_detection

Problem

A RAG corpus scraped from a shared drive has UTF-8, UTF-8-with-BOM (Excel/Notepad), UTF-16 and legacy Windows-1252 files - plus some binaries named .txt.

  1. detect_encoding(data: bytes) -> str (check in this order)

    • starts with the UTF-8 BOM b"\xef\xbb\xbf" -> "utf-8-sig"
    • starts with a UTF-16 BOM (b"\xff\xfe" / b"\xfe\xff") -> "utf-16"
    • decodes as strict UTF-8 -> "utf-8"
    • decodes as strict cp1252 -> "cp1252"
    • otherwise -> "latin-1" (latin-1 maps every byte to a char, so it never fails - which is also why it can't detect anything; it must be the last resort)

  2. is_binary(path, sample_size=8192) -> bool

    • read at most sample_size bytes (never the whole file)
    • a file with a UTF-16 BOM is text; otherwise a NUL byte in the sample -> binary
    • empty file -> False

  3. read_text_any(path) -> tuple[str, str]

    • returns (text, encoding) using detect_encoding on the raw bytes
    • the BOM is not part of the text; "\r\n" and lone "\r" become "\n"

  4. convert_to_utf8(src, dst) -> str

    • write dst as UTF-8 without BOM and with "\n" line endings (also on Windows); return the detected source encoding

Interviewers look for

  • Text vs bytes: a file is bytes on disk; decoding is an explicit step with a codec. Text mode = bytes + decoding + newline translation.
  • Why "utf-8-sig" exists (a stray \ufeff at the start of chunk 0 breaks exact-match, JSON parsing and tokenization).
  • errors="strict" for detection; know errors="replace"/"surrogateescape" and when silent replacement corrupts data.
  • Detect binaries before feeding them to an embedding model.

from pathlib import Path

def detect_encoding(data: bytes) -> str:
    raise NotImplementedError

def is_binary(path: str | Path, sample_size: int=8192) -> bool:
    raise NotImplementedError

def read_text_any(path: str | Path) -> tuple[str, str]:
    raise NotImplementedError

def convert_to_utf8(src: str | Path, dst: str | Path) -> str:
    raise NotImplementedError

import codecs
from pathlib import Path

_UTF16_BOMS = (codecs.BOM_UTF16_LE, codecs.BOM_UTF16_BE)


def detect_encoding(data: bytes) -> str:
    if data.startswith(codecs.BOM_UTF8):
        return "utf-8-sig"
    if data.startswith(_UTF16_BOMS):
        return "utf-16"
    for enc in ("utf-8", "cp1252"):
        try:
            data.decode(enc)
        except UnicodeDecodeError:
            continue
        return enc
    return "latin-1"


def is_binary(path: str | Path, sample_size: int = 8192) -> bool:
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        sample = f.read(sample_size)
    if sample.startswith(_UTF16_BOMS):
        return False
    return b"\x00" in sample


def read_text_any(path: str | Path) -> tuple[str, str]:
    data = Path(path).read_bytes()
    enc = detect_encoding(data)
    text = data.decode(enc)  # "utf-8-sig" / "utf-16" codecs drop the BOM
    return text.replace("\r\n", "\n").replace("\r", "\n"), enc


def convert_to_utf8(src: str | Path, dst: str | Path) -> str:
    text, enc = read_text_any(src)
    with open(dst, "w", encoding="utf-8", newline="\n") as f:
        f.write(text)
    return enc

Walking a document corpus with pathlib★★☆ · ex04_corpus_walker

Problem

Collect the documents of a repo/knowledge base for indexing.

  1. find_documents(root, suffixes=(".md", ".txt"), ignore=DEFAULT_IGNORE) -> list[Path]

    • recursive; returns paths RELATIVE to root, sorted by their POSIX string
    • files only - a directory called "notes.md" is not a document
    • suffix match is case-insensitive ("README.MD" counts); suffixes are given with dot
    • ignore: fnmatch-style patterns matched against EVERY path component (directory names and the file name), e.g. "." drops hidden files and dirs, ".draft.md" drops drafts, "node_modules" drops the whole subtree. Don't descend into ignored directories at all (prune the walk - big node_modules / .venv trees are why indexing jobs are slow)
    • root that is not a directory -> NotADirectoryError (missing -> FileNotFoundError)

  2. corpus_stats(root, suffixes=..., ignore=...) -> dict[str, tuple[int, int]] lower-cased suffix -> (file count, total size in bytes), over find_documents()

  3. export_tree(src_root, dst_root, files, transform, new_suffix=".txt") -> list[Path]

    • for each relative path in files: read src_root/rel as UTF-8, write transform(text) to dst_root/rel with its suffix replaced by new_suffix, creating missing parent directories; returns the written paths in order
    • SECURITY: a relative path that would end up outside dst_root (e.g. "../../etc/passwd", or an absolute path) -> ValueError, nothing written for that entry

Interviewers look for

  • pathlib over string concatenation: /, .suffix/.stem/.with_suffix, .relative_to, .is_relative_to, .mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True), .stat().st_size.
  • Pruning os.walk / Path.walk (3.12+) by editing the dirnames list in place vs rglob, which can't skip a subtree.
  • Path traversal: never join untrusted relative paths without resolving and checking containment.
  • Deterministic output order (sorted) - os.listdir/scandir order is filesystem-dependent.

def corpus_stats(root: str | Path, suffixes: Sequence[str]=('.md', '.txt'), ignore: Sequence[str]=DEFAULT_IGNORE) -> dict[str, tuple[int, int]]:

import fnmatch
import os
from collections.abc import Callable, Iterable, Sequence
from pathlib import Path

DEFAULT_IGNORE = (".*", "node_modules", "__pycache__", "*.draft.md")


def _ignored(name: str, ignore: Sequence[str]) -> bool:
    return any(fnmatch.fnmatch(name, pat) for pat in ignore)


def find_documents(
    root: str | Path,
    suffixes: Sequence[str] = (".md", ".txt"),
    ignore: Sequence[str] = DEFAULT_IGNORE,
) -> list[Path]:
    root = Path(root)
    if not root.exists():
        raise FileNotFoundError(root)
    if not root.is_dir():
        raise NotADirectoryError(root)
    wanted = {s.lower() for s in suffixes}
    found: list[Path] = []
    for dirpath, dirnames, filenames in os.walk(root):
        dirnames[:] = [d for d in dirnames if not _ignored(d, ignore)]  # prune in place
        for name in filenames:
            if _ignored(name, ignore) or Path(name).suffix.lower() not in wanted:
                continue
            found.append(Path(dirpath, name).relative_to(root))
    return sorted(found, key=lambda p: p.as_posix())


def corpus_stats(
    root: str | Path,
    suffixes: Sequence[str] = (".md", ".txt"),
    ignore: Sequence[str] = DEFAULT_IGNORE,
) -> dict[str, tuple[int, int]]:
    root = Path(root)
    stats: dict[str, tuple[int, int]] = {}
    for rel in find_documents(root, suffixes, ignore):
        suffix = rel.suffix.lower()
        count, size = stats.get(suffix, (0, 0))
        stats[suffix] = (count + 1, size + (root / rel).stat().st_size)
    return stats


def export_tree(
    src_root: str | Path,
    dst_root: str | Path,
    files: Iterable[str | Path],
    transform: Callable[[str], str],
    new_suffix: str = ".txt",
) -> list[Path]:
    src_root, dst_root = Path(src_root), Path(dst_root).resolve()
    written: list[Path] = []
    for rel in files:
        target = (dst_root / rel).with_suffix(new_suffix).resolve()
        if not target.is_relative_to(dst_root):
            raise ValueError(f"refusing to write outside {dst_root}: {rel}")
        text = (src_root / rel).read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        target.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        target.write_text(transform(text), encoding="utf-8")
        written.append(target)
    return written

Crash-safe checkpoints (atomic writes)★★☆ · ex05_atomic_write

Problem

A long embedding job saves its progress to state.json. If the process dies mid-write (OOM kill, Ctrl-C, full disk) a plain open(path, "w") leaves a truncated, unparsable file - and the job can't resume.

  1. atomic_write_text(path, text, *, encoding="utf-8") -> None

    • write to a NEW temporary file in the SAME directory as path (tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(dir=..., delete=False) or tempfile.mkstemp), flush + os.fsync it, close it, then os.replace(tmp, path)
    • readers only ever see the old content or the complete new content
    • if anything fails (writing, encoding, fsync, os.replace): delete the temp file and re-raise; the original file is untouched and no temp files are left behind

  2. atomic_write_json(path, obj) -> None same guarantees; a non-JSON-serializable obj -> TypeError, original intact

  3. class Checkpoint(path)

    • load() -> dict: {} if the file doesn't exist yet, else the parsed JSON
    • save(state: dict) -> None: atomic
    • update(**changes) -> dict: load, merge, save, return the merged state

Interviewers look for

  • os.replace is atomic on POSIX and Windows within one filesystem - that's why the temp file must live in the target's directory, not in /tmp (cross-device rename fails or degrades to copy).
  • flush() empties Python's buffer, fsync() asks the OS to persist to disk - different things. (Fully durable also fsyncs the directory; mention it.)
  • tempfile module: NamedTemporaryFile, mkstemp, TemporaryDirectory, SpooledTemporaryFile
  • unique names, no races, automatic cleanup.
  • try/except BaseException + re-raise is legitimate here: cleanup must also run on Ctrl-C.

import json
import os
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any


def atomic_write_text(path: str | Path, text: str, *, encoding: str = "utf-8") -> None:
    path = Path(path)
    tmp = tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(  # noqa: SIM115 - closed explicitly below
        "w",
        encoding=encoding,
        dir=path.parent,
        prefix=f".{path.name}.",
        suffix=".tmp",
        delete=False,
    )
    try:
        with tmp:
            tmp.write(text)
            tmp.flush()
            os.fsync(tmp.fileno())
        os.replace(tmp.name, path)
    except BaseException:
        Path(tmp.name).unlink(missing_ok=True)
        raise


def atomic_write_json(path: str | Path, obj: Any) -> None:
    # serialize first: a TypeError then never even creates a temp file
    atomic_write_text(path, json.dumps(obj, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2))


class Checkpoint:
    def __init__(self, path: str | Path) -> None:
        self.path = Path(path)

    def load(self) -> dict[str, Any]:
        try:
            with open(self.path, encoding="utf-8") as f:
                state: dict[str, Any] = json.load(f)
                return state
        except FileNotFoundError:
            return {}

    def save(self, state: dict[str, Any]) -> None:
        atomic_write_json(self.path, state)

    def update(self, **changes: Any) -> dict[str, Any]:
        state = self.load() | changes
        self.save(state)
        return state

Large logs: count, tail, resume★★★ · ex06_large_files

Problem

LLM request logs grow to many GB. Memory use must stay O(chunk), not O(file). All three functions work in BINARY mode.

  1. count_lines(path, chunk_size=1 << 20) -> int

    • number of lines = number of b"\n", plus 1 if the file is non-empty and does not end with b"\n"; read fixed-size chunks (no readlines(), no read() of everything)

  2. tail(path, n=10, chunk_size=8192) -> list[str]

    • the last n lines, decoded as UTF-8, without the "\n", oldest first
    • seek to the end and read chunks BACKWARDS until you have enough newlines; reading the whole file is not allowed (the test checks memory usage)
    • a trailing newline does not create an empty last line; n <= 0 -> []; fewer than n lines -> all of them
    • a multi-byte UTF-8 character may straddle a chunk boundary - collect bytes, decode once at the end

  3. read_new_lines(path, offset=0) -> tuple[list[str], int]

    • resumable ingestion of a file another process is still appending to: start at byte offset, return the COMPLETE lines found (decoded, without "\n") and the new offset = the byte position just after the last complete line
    • a final partial line (no "\n" yet) is NOT returned and not consumed - the next call (with the returned offset) picks it up once it is complete
    • offset beyond the end of the file -> ValueError (file was truncated/rotated)

Interviewers look for

  • Why binary mode: byte offsets from tell()/seek() are only meaningful for binary files (text-mode tell() returns an opaque cookie), and you avoid decoding cost.
  • Chunked reading with a bounded buffer; how for line in f is already buffered and lazy, and when it isn't enough (one 2 GB line).
  • Checkpointing a byte offset to resume after a crash - how log shippers work.

import os
from pathlib import Path


def count_lines(path: str | Path, chunk_size: int = 1 << 20) -> int:
    lines = 0
    last = b""
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        while chunk := f.read(chunk_size):
            lines += chunk.count(b"\n")
            last = chunk[-1:]
    if last and last != b"\n":
        lines += 1
    return lines


def tail(path: str | Path, n: int = 10, chunk_size: int = 8192) -> list[str]:
    if n <= 0:
        return []
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        end = f.seek(0, os.SEEK_END)
        pos = end
        buf = b""
        # n lines need n+1 newlines unless we reach the start of the file
        while pos > 0 and buf.count(b"\n") <= n:
            step = min(chunk_size, pos)
            pos -= step
            f.seek(pos)
            buf = f.read(step) + buf
    lines = buf.split(b"\n")
    if lines and lines[-1] == b"":
        lines.pop()  # trailing newline
    return [ln.decode("utf-8") for ln in lines[-n:]]


def read_new_lines(path: str | Path, offset: int = 0) -> tuple[list[str], int]:
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        size = f.seek(0, os.SEEK_END)
        if offset > size:
            raise ValueError(f"offset {offset} beyond end of file ({size} bytes)")
        f.seek(offset)
        lines: list[str] = []
        for raw in f:  # binary iteration still splits on b"\n", lazily
            if not raw.endswith(b"\n"):
                break  # partial line: leave it for the next call
            lines.append(raw[:-1].decode("utf-8"))
            offset += len(raw)
    return lines, offset

Context Managers

Class-based context managers: Timer & suppress★☆☆ · ex01_timer_and_suppress

context_managers.custom

Problem

  1. class Timer - time a block (an LLM call, a retrieval step) Timer(name="block", *, clock=time.perf_counter, on_exit=None)

    • with Timer("embed") as t: binds t to the Timer itself (enter returns self)
    • t.elapsed is None until the block finishes, then the float seconds (clock() at exit - clock() at enter)
    • on_exit(name, elapsed) is called after every block, also when it raised
    • a Timer NEVER swallows exceptions
    • reusable: entering it again starts a new measurement

  2. class suppress_errors - like contextlib.suppress, but remembers what it swallowed suppress_errors(*exc_types)

    • exceptions that are instances of exc_types are swallowed and stored in .error
    • anything else propagates (and .error stays None)
    • .error is None when the block succeeded; reset on each entry
    • as target is the suppress_errors object itself

Interviewers look for

  • The protocol: __enter__(self) -> value bound by as; __exit__(self, exc_type, exc, tb) -> truthy return value SWALLOWS the exception. Returning None (falsy) lets it propagate - which is what you want 99% of the time.
  • as binds enter's return value, not the CM object (open() returns self, but e.g. a lock's enter returns True).
  • Cleanup in exit runs on success AND failure.

Work in exercises/py/12_context_managers/ex01_timer_and_suppress.py (or copy the starter code into any scratch file).

import time
from collections.abc import Callable
from types import TracebackType

class Timer:

    def __init__(self, name: str='block', *, clock: Callable[[], float]=time.perf_counter, on_exit: Callable[[str, float], object] | None=None) -> None:
        raise NotImplementedError

    def __enter__(self) -> 'Timer':
        raise NotImplementedError

    def __exit__(self, exc_type: type[BaseException] | None, exc: BaseException | None, tb: TracebackType | None) -> None:
        raise NotImplementedError

class suppress_errors:

    def __init__(self, *exc_types: type[BaseException]) -> None:
        raise NotImplementedError

    def __enter__(self) -> 'suppress_errors':
        raise NotImplementedError

    def __exit__(self, exc_type: type[BaseException] | None, exc: BaseException | None, tb: TracebackType | None) -> bool:
        raise NotImplementedError

import time
from collections.abc import Callable
from types import TracebackType


class Timer:
    def __init__(
        self,
        name: str = "block",
        *,
        clock: Callable[[], float] = time.perf_counter,
        on_exit: Callable[[str, float], object] | None = None,
    ) -> None:
        self.name = name
        self._clock = clock
        self._on_exit = on_exit
        self._start = 0.0
        self.elapsed: float | None = None

    def __enter__(self) -> "Timer":
        self.elapsed = None
        self._start = self._clock()
        return self

    def __exit__(
        self,
        exc_type: type[BaseException] | None,
        exc: BaseException | None,
        tb: TracebackType | None,
    ) -> None:
        self.elapsed = self._clock() - self._start
        if self._on_exit is not None:
            self._on_exit(self.name, self.elapsed)
        # returning None == falsy -> any exception propagates


class suppress_errors:  # noqa: N801 - mirrors contextlib.suppress
    def __init__(self, *exc_types: type[BaseException]) -> None:
        self.exc_types = exc_types
        self.error: BaseException | None = None

    def __enter__(self) -> "suppress_errors":
        self.error = None
        return self

    def __exit__(
        self,
        exc_type: type[BaseException] | None,
        exc: BaseException | None,
        tb: TracebackType | None,
    ) -> bool:
        if exc is not None and isinstance(exc, self.exc_types):
            self.error = exc
            return True
        return False

@contextmanager: temporary env vars, cwd, attrs★★☆ · ex02_temp_env_and_cwd

context_managers.resources

Problem

Tests and scripts often need "change this global thing just for this block" - an API key env var, the working directory, a module attribute. Write them with contextlib.contextmanager (generator-based context managers).

  1. temp_env(**overrides: str | None)

    • on enter: for each key set os.environ[key] = value; value None means UNSET the var
    • on exit - also when the block raises - restore the exact previous state: vars that existed get their old value back, vars that didn't exist are removed again
    • any value that is not str/None -> TypeError on enter, BEFORE anything is changed
    • yields nothing (with temp_env(OPENAI_API_KEY="test"):)

  2. working_directory(path)

    • chdir into path, yield the new cwd as a resolved Path, always chdir back on exit

  3. patched(obj, name, value)

    • setattr(obj, name, value) for the block, then restore the old value; if the attribute didn't exist before, delete it on exit

All three must restore state when the block raises and must not swallow the exception. They must also nest correctly (with temp_env(A="1"), temp_env(A="2"):).

Interviewers look for

  • The classic @contextmanager bug: yield not wrapped in try/finally -> restore code is skipped when the block raises (the exception is thrown INTO the generator at the yield).
  • Code before yield == enter, code after == exit; the yielded value is the as target; swallowing would require catching the exception around the yield.
  • Distinguishing "was unset" from "was empty string" when restoring.
  • Validate everything before mutating global state (no half-applied changes).

Work in exercises/py/12_context_managers/ex02_temp_env_and_cwd.py (or copy the starter code into any scratch file).

import os
from collections.abc import Iterator
from contextlib import contextmanager
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any

@contextmanager
def temp_env(**overrides: str | None) -> Iterator[None]:
    raise NotImplementedError

@contextmanager
def working_directory(path: str | Path) -> Iterator[Path]:
    raise NotImplementedError

@contextmanager
def patched(obj: Any, name: str, value: Any) -> Iterator[None]:
    raise NotImplementedError

import os
from collections.abc import Iterator
from contextlib import contextmanager
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any

_MISSING = object()


@contextmanager
def temp_env(**overrides: str | None) -> Iterator[None]:
    for key, value in overrides.items():
        if value is not None and not isinstance(value, str):
            raise TypeError(f"env var {key} must be str or None, got {type(value).__name__}")
    saved = {key: os.environ.get(key) for key in overrides}
    try:
        for key, value in overrides.items():
            if value is None:
                os.environ.pop(key, None)
            else:
                os.environ[key] = value
        yield
    finally:
        for key, old in saved.items():
            if old is None:
                os.environ.pop(key, None)
            else:
                os.environ[key] = old


@contextmanager
def working_directory(path: str | Path) -> Iterator[Path]:
    old = Path.cwd()
    os.chdir(path)
    try:
        yield Path.cwd().resolve()
    finally:
        os.chdir(old)


@contextmanager
def patched(obj: Any, name: str, value: Any) -> Iterator[None]:
    old = getattr(obj, name, _MISSING)
    setattr(obj, name, value)
    try:
        yield
    finally:
        if old is _MISSING:
            delattr(obj, name)
        else:
            setattr(obj, name, old)

Transactions with rollback (sqlite3)★★☆ · ex03_sqlite_transaction

context_managers.contextmanager, context_managers.exit

Problem

A tiny document store for a RAG app. Adding a document means inserting the document row AND all of its chunk rows - all or nothing.

  1. connect(path) - context manager yielding a sqlite3.Connection opened with isolation_level=None (autocommit: we control transactions explicitly) and CLOSED on exit, even on error. (Note: with sqlite3.connect(...) as conn: does NOT close the connection - it only commits/rolls back. That surprises many people.)

  2. transaction(conn) - context manager

    • outermost use: "BEGIN" on enter; "COMMIT" on success; "ROLLBACK" if the block raises, then re-raise the same exception
    • nested use (conn.in_transaction is already True): use a SAVEPOINT instead ("SAVEPOINT name" / "RELEASE name" / "ROLLBACK TO name" then "RELEASE name"), so an inner failure that the caller catches only undoes the inner work. Savepoint names must be unique (e.g. sp_1, sp_2, ... from a counter).

  3. class DocumentStore(conn)

    • init creates (if missing) tables docs(id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT NOT NULL) chunks(doc_id TEXT NOT NULL, idx INTEGER NOT NULL, text TEXT NOT NULL)
    • add_document(doc_id, title, chunks: list[str]) - atomic (use transaction()); a duplicate id or a None chunk raises sqlite3.IntegrityError and leaves nothing of that document behind
    • counts() -> tuple[int, int] (number of docs, number of chunks)

Interviewers look for

  • "Release the resource no matter what" (close) vs "decide the outcome by success or failure" (commit/rollback) - exit gets the exception info to make that decision.
  • Re-raising after rollback: a transaction CM must not swallow errors.
  • Savepoints for nesting; knowing that sqlite3's implicit transaction handling (isolation_level != None) can surprise you.

Work in exercises/py/12_context_managers/ex03_sqlite_transaction.py (or copy the starter code into any scratch file).

    def __init__(self, conn: sqlite3.Connection) -> None:
        raise NotImplementedError

import itertools
import sqlite3
from collections.abc import Iterator
from contextlib import contextmanager
from pathlib import Path


@contextmanager
def connect(path: str | Path) -> Iterator[sqlite3.Connection]:
    conn = sqlite3.connect(path, isolation_level=None)
    try:
        yield conn
    finally:
        conn.close()


_savepoint_ids = itertools.count(1)


@contextmanager
def transaction(conn: sqlite3.Connection) -> Iterator[sqlite3.Connection]:
    if not conn.in_transaction:
        conn.execute("BEGIN")
        try:
            yield conn
        except BaseException:  # also roll back on Ctrl-C / cancellation, then re-raise
            conn.execute("ROLLBACK")
            raise
        conn.execute("COMMIT")
        return

    name = f"sp_{next(_savepoint_ids)}"
    conn.execute(f"SAVEPOINT {name}")
    try:
        yield conn
    except BaseException:
        conn.execute(f"ROLLBACK TO {name}")
        conn.execute(f"RELEASE {name}")
        raise
    conn.execute(f"RELEASE {name}")


class DocumentStore:
    def __init__(self, conn: sqlite3.Connection) -> None:
        self.conn = conn
        conn.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS docs (id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT NOT NULL)")
        conn.execute(
            "CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS chunks "
            "(doc_id TEXT NOT NULL, idx INTEGER NOT NULL, text TEXT NOT NULL)"
        )

    def add_document(self, doc_id: str, title: str, chunks: list[str]) -> None:
        with transaction(self.conn):
            self.conn.execute("INSERT INTO docs (id, title) VALUES (?, ?)", (doc_id, title))
            self.conn.executemany(
                "INSERT INTO chunks (doc_id, idx, text) VALUES (?, ?, ?)",
                [(doc_id, i, text) for i, text in enumerate(chunks)],
            )

    def counts(self) -> tuple[int, int]:
        (docs,) = self.conn.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM docs").fetchone()
        (chunks,) = self.conn.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM chunks").fetchone()
        return docs, chunks
