Client-side rate limiting (token bucket)★★☆ · ex04_rate_limiter

Problem

LLM providers limit requests/min (RPM) and tokens/min (TPM). Instead of hammering the API and eating 429s, throttle on the client with a token bucket.

TokenBucket(rate, capacity, , clock=time.monotonic, sleep=asyncio.sleep) * rate: tokens added per second (float > 0); capacity: max tokens (> 0). Invalid values -> ValueError. * starts FULL (capacity tokens): allows an initial burst of capacity. * refill is continuous: tokens = min(capacity, tokens + elapsed * rate), computed lazily from clock() whenever you look at the bucket - no background task. * clock/sleep are injected so tests can use a fake clock (never call time. or asyncio.sleep directly).

available() -> float current token count (after refill) try_acquire(cost=1) -> bool take cost tokens now if available, else False (no waiting) async acquire(cost=1) -> float * wait until cost tokens are available, take them, return the total seconds slept (0.0 if no wait was needed) * sleep for exactly the time needed for the deficit: (cost - tokens) / rate, then re-check (loop - never assume one sleep was enough) * cost > capacity can never succeed -> ValueError immediately; cost <= 0 -> ValueError * FIFO fairness: concurrent acquirers are served in arrival order - a big request that is waiting must not be starved by a stream of small ones (hint: hold an asyncio.Lock while waiting; asyncio.Lock wakes waiters in FIFO order)

async run_rate_limited(calls, bucket, *, cost=1) -> list * calls is a list of zero-arg async callables; run them all concurrently, each one first doing await bucket.acquire(cost); return results in input order

Interviewers look for

  • Token bucket (bursts up to capacity, average = rate) vs fixed window (allows 2x bursts at window edges) vs sliding window log (exact but O(n) memory) vs leaky bucket (smooth).
  • Rate limit (requests per time) is not a concurrency limit (requests in flight) - you often need both (Semaphore for the latter).
  • TPM limits: cost = estimated tokens of the request, not 1.
  • Client-side limiting is per process; multiple workers need a shared limiter (Redis) or a per-worker share of the quota - and you still must handle 429s.

Work in exercises/py/17_http/ex04_rate_limiter.py (or copy the starter code into any scratch file).

import asyncio
import time
from collections.abc import Awaitable, Callable
from typing import Any

class TokenBucket:

    def __init__(self, rate: float, capacity: float, *, clock: Callable[[], float]=time.monotonic, sleep: Callable[[float], Awaitable[Any]]=asyncio.sleep) -> None:
        raise NotImplementedError

    def available(self) -> float:
        raise NotImplementedError

    def try_acquire(self, cost: float=1) -> bool:
        raise NotImplementedError

    async def acquire(self, cost: float=1) -> float:
        raise NotImplementedError

async def run_rate_limited(calls: list[Callable[[], Awaitable[Any]]], bucket: TokenBucket, *, cost: float=1) -> list[Any]:
    raise NotImplementedError

import asyncio
import time
from collections.abc import Awaitable, Callable
from typing import Any


class TokenBucket:
    def __init__(
        self,
        rate: float,
        capacity: float,
        *,
        clock: Callable[[], float] = time.monotonic,
        sleep: Callable[[float], Awaitable[Any]] = asyncio.sleep,
    ) -> None:
        if rate <= 0 or capacity <= 0:
            raise ValueError("rate and capacity must be > 0")
        self.rate = rate
        self.capacity = capacity
        self._clock = clock
        self._sleep = sleep
        self._tokens = float(capacity)
        self._last = clock()
        self._lock = asyncio.Lock()

    def _refill(self) -> None:
        now = self._clock()
        self._tokens = min(self.capacity, self._tokens + (now - self._last) * self.rate)
        self._last = now

    def available(self) -> float:
        self._refill()
        return self._tokens

    def _check_cost(self, cost: float) -> None:
        if cost <= 0:
            raise ValueError("cost must be > 0")
        if cost > self.capacity:
            raise ValueError(f"cost {cost} exceeds bucket capacity {self.capacity}")

    def try_acquire(self, cost: float = 1) -> bool:
        self._check_cost(cost)
        self._refill()
        if self._tokens >= cost:
            self._tokens -= cost
            return True
        return False

    async def acquire(self, cost: float = 1) -> float:
        self._check_cost(cost)
        waited = 0.0
        async with self._lock:  # FIFO: the head of the queue waits; others queue behind it
            while True:
                self._refill()
                if self._tokens >= cost:
                    self._tokens -= cost
                    return waited
                delay = (cost - self._tokens) / self.rate
                await self._sleep(delay)
                waited += delay


async def run_rate_limited(
    calls: list[Callable[[], Awaitable[Any]]], bucket: TokenBucket, *, cost: float = 1
) -> list[Any]:
    async def one(call: Callable[[], Awaitable[Any]]) -> Any:
        await bucket.acquire(cost)
        return await call()

    return await asyncio.gather(*(one(c) for c in calls))

Retries: exponential backoff, full jitter, Retry-After, idempotency★★★ · ex05_retry_backoff

http.rate_limiting, http.error_handling

Problem

RetryPolicy and RetriesExhausted are given.

  1. backoff_delay(retry_number, policy, rng=random.random) -> float

    • "full jitter": rng() * min(policy.max_delay, policy.base_delay * 2 ** retry_number)
    • retry_number is 0 for the first retry, 1 for the second, ...
    • rng() returns a float in [0, 1)

  2. retry_after_seconds(response) -> float | None

    • the Retry-After header as delta-seconds (float); missing / unparseable / negative -> None (also accept the non-standard "retry-after-ms" header, in milliseconds, preferred when present - OpenAI sends it)

  3. is_idempotent(request) -> bool

    • GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, DELETE are idempotent; anything else only if the request carries an "Idempotency-Key" header

  4. async send_with_retries(client, request, policy=RetryPolicy(), *, sleep=asyncio.sleep, rng=random.random) -> httpx.Response Send request (an httpx.Request) with await client.send(request); at most policy.max_attempts attempts in total. Decide after each attempt:

    outcome retry?

    response, status NOT in policy.retry_statuses no - return it (even a 400/401/404: the caller maps errors) status 429 or 503 yes, always (server refused, did not process the request) other status in retry_statuses (500/502/504) only if is_idempotent(request) httpx.ConnectError / ConnectTimeout / yes, always (request never left) PoolTimeout any other httpx.TransportError (ReadTimeout, only if is_idempotent(request) RemoteProtocolError, WriteError, ...) any other exception no - propagate

    • "no" for a retryable-looking error = re-raise the exception / return the response
    • delay before retry k (k = 0, 1, ...): if the last response had a Retry-After -> min(that, policy.max_delay); otherwise backoff_delay(k, policy, rng)
    • await sleep(delay) - the injected function - never time.sleep
    • when attempts run out: raise RetriesExhausted(attempts, last_response) - chained from the last exception if the last attempt raised (last_response is then None)
    • policy.max_attempts < 1 -> ValueError
    • close (await response.aclose()) a response you're about to discard for a retry, so its connection returns to the pool

Interviewers look for

  • Retry only what can succeed next time: 408/429/5xx/connection errors - never 400/401/403/ 404/422 (they fail identically and burn quota).
  • Non-idempotent POSTs (e.g. "charge card", "create fine-tune job") may have been executed when a read timeout / 502 happens: retrying duplicates them. Idempotency keys fix that.
  • Exponential backoff spreads retries out; JITTER de-synchronises many clients that failed at the same moment (thundering herd). Full jitter = random in [0, cap].
  • Bounded attempts AND a max delay (and in real systems an overall deadline/retry budget), honouring the server's Retry-After.

Work in exercises/py/17_http/ex05_retry_backoff.py (or copy the starter code into any scratch file).

import asyncio
import random
from collections.abc import Awaitable, Callable
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Any
import httpx
IDEMPOTENT_METHODS = frozenset({'GET', 'HEAD', 'OPTIONS', 'PUT', 'DELETE'})
ALWAYS_SAFE_STATUSES = frozenset({429, 503})
NOT_SENT_ERRORS = (httpx.ConnectError, httpx.ConnectTimeout, httpx.PoolTimeout)

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class RetryPolicy:
    max_attempts: int = 4
    base_delay: float = 0.5
    max_delay: float = 8.0
    retry_statuses: frozenset[int] = field(default=frozenset({429, 500, 502, 503, 504}))

class RetriesExhausted(Exception):

    def __init__(self, attempts: int, last_response: httpx.Response | None) -> None:
        status = last_response.status_code if last_response is not None else None
        super().__init__(f'gave up after {attempts} attempt(s) (last status: {status})')
        self.attempts = attempts
        self.last_response = last_response

def backoff_delay(retry_number: int, policy: RetryPolicy, rng: Callable[[], float]=random.random) -> float:
    raise NotImplementedError

def retry_after_seconds(response: httpx.Response) -> float | None:
    raise NotImplementedError

def is_idempotent(request: httpx.Request) -> bool:
    raise NotImplementedError

async def send_with_retries(client: httpx.AsyncClient, request: httpx.Request, policy: RetryPolicy=RetryPolicy(), *, sleep: Callable[[float], Awaitable[Any]]=asyncio.sleep, rng: Callable[[], float]=random.random) -> httpx.Response:
    raise NotImplementedError

import asyncio
import random
from collections.abc import Awaitable, Callable
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Any

import httpx

__stub_keep__ = ["RetriesExhausted"]

IDEMPOTENT_METHODS = frozenset({"GET", "HEAD", "OPTIONS", "PUT", "DELETE"})
ALWAYS_SAFE_STATUSES = frozenset({429, 503})
NOT_SENT_ERRORS = (httpx.ConnectError, httpx.ConnectTimeout, httpx.PoolTimeout)


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class RetryPolicy:
    max_attempts: int = 4
    base_delay: float = 0.5
    max_delay: float = 8.0
    retry_statuses: frozenset[int] = field(default=frozenset({429, 500, 502, 503, 504}))


class RetriesExhausted(Exception):
    def __init__(self, attempts: int, last_response: httpx.Response | None) -> None:
        status = last_response.status_code if last_response is not None else None
        super().__init__(f"gave up after {attempts} attempt(s) (last status: {status})")
        self.attempts = attempts
        self.last_response = last_response


def backoff_delay(retry_number: int, policy: RetryPolicy, rng: Callable[[], float] = random.random) -> float:
    return rng() * min(policy.max_delay, policy.base_delay * 2**retry_number)


def retry_after_seconds(response: httpx.Response) -> float | None:
    for header, scale in (("retry-after-ms", 1000.0), ("retry-after", 1.0)):
        raw = response.headers.get(header)
        if raw is None:
            continue
        try:
            value = float(raw) / scale
        except ValueError:
            continue
        if value >= 0:
            return value
    return None


def is_idempotent(request: httpx.Request) -> bool:
    return request.method.upper() in IDEMPOTENT_METHODS or "idempotency-key" in request.headers


def _should_retry_status(status: int, request: httpx.Request, policy: RetryPolicy) -> bool:
    if status not in policy.retry_statuses:
        return False
    return status in ALWAYS_SAFE_STATUSES or is_idempotent(request)


async def send_with_retries(
    client: httpx.AsyncClient,
    request: httpx.Request,
    policy: RetryPolicy = RetryPolicy(),  # noqa: B008 - frozen dataclass, safe default
    *,
    sleep: Callable[[float], Awaitable[Any]] = asyncio.sleep,
    rng: Callable[[], float] = random.random,
) -> httpx.Response:
    if policy.max_attempts < 1:
        raise ValueError("max_attempts must be >= 1")
    last_exc: httpx.TransportError | None = None
    last_response: httpx.Response | None = None
    for attempt in range(policy.max_attempts):
        last_response = None
        try:
            response = await client.send(request)
        except NOT_SENT_ERRORS as exc:
            last_exc = exc
        except httpx.TransportError as exc:
            if not is_idempotent(request):
                raise
            last_exc = exc
        else:
            if not _should_retry_status(response.status_code, request, policy):
                return response
            last_exc, last_response = None, response

        if attempt == policy.max_attempts - 1:
            break
        retry_after = retry_after_seconds(last_response) if last_response is not None else None
        if retry_after is not None:
            delay = min(retry_after, policy.max_delay)
        else:
            delay = backoff_delay(attempt, policy, rng)
        if last_response is not None:
            await last_response.aclose()
        await sleep(delay)

    error = RetriesExhausted(policy.max_attempts, last_response)
    if last_exc is not None:
        raise error from last_exc
    raise error

Batched, concurrency-limited embedding with partial failures★★★ · ex06_embedding_batcher

http.response_validation, http.get_post

Problem

Embed 10,000 chunks for a RAG index: send them in batches, a few batches at a time, and don't let one bad batch throw away 99% of the work. Models/dataclasses are given.

async embed_all(client, texts, , model="text-embedding-3-small", batch_size=64, max_concurrency=4) -> EmbedResult * batch_size < 1 or max_concurrency < 1 -> ValueError (before any request) * no texts -> EmbedResult([], []) without any request * split texts into consecutive batches of batch_size (last one may be smaller); batch i covers input indices [ibatch_size, ...) * each batch: POST /embeddings {"model": model, "input": [...batch texts...]} * all batches run concurrently, but never more than max_concurrency requests in flight (asyncio.Semaphore - acquire it around the request only) * the response is EmbeddingResponse JSON; data[k].index is the position WITHIN the batch and items may come back in any order -> put every vector at its global input position * a batch FAILS (its texts get None vectors, and one BatchFailure is recorded) when: - any httpx.HTTPError while sending error = type(exc).name - status >= 400 error = f"HTTP {status}" - body isn't valid EmbeddingResponse JSON error = "invalid response" - indices aren't exactly 0..len(batch)-1 error = "invalid response" * other batches are unaffected; EmbedResult.vectors has exactly len(texts) entries (vector or None) in input order; failures are sorted by batch_index * BatchFailure(batch_index, input_indices=[global indices], error=...)

Interviewers look for

  • Batching amortises per-request overhead and is how embedding APIs are priced/limited (max inputs per request, max tokens per request).
  • gather/TaskGroup for concurrency, a Semaphore for the in-flight cap (a rate limiter would cap requests per SECOND - different thing).
  • Reassembly by index, never by completion order or response list order.
  • Partial failure as a first-class result: return successes + a failure report so the caller can retry just the failed batches. With a plain gather() the first exception propagates and the results of the batches that succeeded are lost (they keep running, unobserved) - handle errors per batch, or use return_exceptions=True / a TaskGroup with per-task try/except.

    error: str

@dataclass
class EmbedResult:

    failures: list[BatchFailure] = field(default_factory=list)

async def embed_all(client: httpx.AsyncClient, texts: list[str], *, model: str='text-embedding-3-small', batch_size: int=64, max_concurrency: int=4) -> EmbedResult:

import asyncio
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

import httpx
from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError


class EmbeddingItem(BaseModel):
    index: int
    embedding: list[float]


class EmbeddingResponse(BaseModel):
    data: list[EmbeddingItem]


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class BatchFailure:
    batch_index: int
    input_indices: list[int]
    error: str


@dataclass
class EmbedResult:
    vectors: list[list[float] | None]
    failures: list[BatchFailure] = field(default_factory=list)


async def _embed_batch(
    client: httpx.AsyncClient,
    sem: asyncio.Semaphore,
    model: str,
    batch: list[str],
) -> list[list[float]] | str:
    """Return vectors in batch order, or an error string."""
    try:
        async with sem:
            response = await client.post("/embeddings", json={"model": model, "input": batch})
    except httpx.HTTPError as exc:
        return type(exc).__name__
    if response.status_code >= 400:
        return f"HTTP {response.status_code}"
    try:
        parsed = EmbeddingResponse.model_validate_json(response.content)
    except ValidationError:
        return "invalid response"
    by_index = {item.index: item.embedding for item in parsed.data}
    if len(parsed.data) != len(batch) or set(by_index) != set(range(len(batch))):
        return "invalid response"
    return [by_index[i] for i in range(len(batch))]


async def embed_all(
    client: httpx.AsyncClient,
    texts: list[str],
    *,
    model: str = "text-embedding-3-small",
    batch_size: int = 64,
    max_concurrency: int = 4,
) -> EmbedResult:
    if batch_size < 1 or max_concurrency < 1:
        raise ValueError("batch_size and max_concurrency must be >= 1")
    if not texts:
        return EmbedResult([], [])
    sem = asyncio.Semaphore(max_concurrency)
    starts = range(0, len(texts), batch_size)
    outcomes = await asyncio.gather(
        *(_embed_batch(client, sem, model, texts[s : s + batch_size]) for s in starts)
    )
    result = EmbedResult(vectors=[None] * len(texts))
    for batch_index, (start, outcome) in enumerate(zip(starts, outcomes, strict=True)):
        indices = list(range(start, min(start + batch_size, len(texts))))
        if isinstance(outcome, str):
            result.failures.append(BatchFailure(batch_index, indices, outcome))
            continue
        for i, vector in zip(indices, outcome, strict=True):
            result.vectors[i] = vector
    return result

Python Memory Management

Aliasing bugs in nested configs★☆☆ · ex01_config_copies

Problem

Python variables are names bound to objects; assignment never copies. Three small functions about identity and copying:

  1. identity_groups(items) -> list[list[int]] Group the INDICES of items that refer to the very same object (is, not ==). Groups are ordered by first appearance; indices inside a group ascend. a = [1]; b = [1] identity_groups([a, b, a]) == [[0, 2], [1]] # a == b, but a is not b Must work for unhashable items (lists, dicts).

  2. make_run_configs(base, seeds) -> list[dict] A teammate wrote this to fan one experiment config out into one config per seed:

    def make_run_configs(base, seeds): configs = [] for seed in seeds: cfg = base.copy() cfg["training"]["seed"] = seed configs.append(cfg) return configs

Every config ends up with the LAST seed, and base gets mutated too. Write the fixed version: each returned config is fully independent (mutating any nested value in one never affects another, nor base), and base is left untouched. Assume base["training"] exists and is a dict.

  1. merge_config(base, override) -> dict Recursive merge for layered config (defaults <- env file <- CLI flags):
    • keys only in one side are kept
    • if BOTH values are dicts -> merge them recursively
    • otherwise the override value wins (lists are replaced, not concatenated)
    • neither input is mutated, and the result shares NO mutable containers with either input (mutating result["a"]["b"] must not change base or override)

Interviewers look for

  • dict.copy() / list(x) / copy.copy are SHALLOW: the outer container is new, the nested objects are shared. copy.deepcopy recursively copies (and handles cycles via its memo dict).
  • is compares identity (same object, same id() while both alive); == compares value.
  • Deep copies cost time and memory - copy at the boundary where ownership changes, not everywhere "just in case".

Work in exercises/py/18_memory/ex01_config_copies.py (or copy the starter code into any scratch file).

import copy
from typing import Any

def identity_groups(items: list[Any]) -> list[list[int]]:
    raise NotImplementedError

def make_run_configs(base: dict[str, Any], seeds: list[int]) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
    raise NotImplementedError

def merge_config(base: dict[str, Any], override: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any]:
    raise NotImplementedError

import copy
from typing import Any


def identity_groups(items: list[Any]) -> list[list[int]]:
    # key by id(): valid here because every item stays alive (referenced by `items`)
    # for the whole call, so ids cannot be reused.
    groups: dict[int, list[int]] = {}
    for i, item in enumerate(items):
        groups.setdefault(id(item), []).append(i)
    return list(groups.values())


def make_run_configs(base: dict[str, Any], seeds: list[int]) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
    configs = []
    for seed in seeds:
        cfg = copy.deepcopy(base)
        cfg["training"]["seed"] = seed
        configs.append(cfg)
    return configs


def merge_config(base: dict[str, Any], override: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any]:
    result = copy.deepcopy(base)
    for key, value in override.items():
        if isinstance(result.get(key), dict) and isinstance(value, dict):
            result[key] = merge_config(result[key], value)
        else:
            result[key] = copy.deepcopy(value)
    return result

__slots__ and the true size of an object★★☆ · ex02_slots_deep_sizeof

Problem

You hold millions of retrieval hits in memory and want to know what they really cost.

  1. EmbeddingRecord - a class with exactly the attributes doc_id, vector, score (score defaults to 0.0), declared with slots so instances have NO per-instance dict:

    • assigning an undeclared attribute (rec.foo = 1) raises AttributeError
    • repr -> "EmbeddingRecord(doc_id='d1', score=0.5)" (vector omitted: it's big) PlainRecord (given, kept in the stub) is the same thing without slots, for comparison.

  2. deep_sizeof(obj) -> int sys.getsizeof() is SHALLOW: a list of 1000 long strings reports only the list's own pointer array. Write the deep version:

    • sum sys.getsizeof() over obj and everything reachable from it through dict keys and values, list/tuple/set/frozenset elements, an instance's dict (count the dict itself too) and its slots attributes (only the ones that are set; walk slots of every class in type(obj).mro)
    • count every object ONCE, by identity - shared references are not double counted, and reference cycles must terminate
    • don't count or descend into classes, functions or modules
    • don't recurse: a 100_000-deep nested list must not hit RecursionError (use an explicit stack)

Interviewers look for

  • Everything in CPython is a heap-allocated PyObject with a header (refcount + type pointer); a list stores pointers, not values.
  • slots replaces the per-instance dict with fixed descriptors: less memory, faster attribute access, no ad-hoc attributes (and no weakrefs unless 'weakref' is listed). Since 3.11+ plain instances store attributes inline too, so the gap is smaller than old blog posts claim - but it's still real, measure it.
  • Identity-based visited set - the same trick copy.deepcopy uses with its memo.

import sys
import types
from typing import Any

__stub_keep__ = ["PlainRecord"]

_SKIP = (type, types.ModuleType, types.FunctionType, types.BuiltinFunctionType, types.MethodType)


class PlainRecord:
    def __init__(self, doc_id: str, vector: Any, score: float = 0.0) -> None:
        self.doc_id = doc_id
        self.vector = vector
        self.score = score


class EmbeddingRecord:
    __slots__ = ("doc_id", "vector", "score")

    def __init__(self, doc_id: str, vector: Any, score: float = 0.0) -> None:
        self.doc_id = doc_id
        self.vector = vector
        self.score = score

    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        return f"EmbeddingRecord(doc_id={self.doc_id!r}, score={self.score!r})"


def deep_sizeof(obj: Any) -> int:
    seen: set[int] = set()
    stack = [obj]
    total = 0
    while stack:
        o = stack.pop()
        if id(o) in seen or isinstance(o, _SKIP):
            continue
        seen.add(id(o))  # safe: everything reachable stays alive while we walk
        total += sys.getsizeof(o)
        if isinstance(o, dict):
            stack.extend(o.keys())
            stack.extend(o.values())
        elif isinstance(o, (list, tuple, set, frozenset)):
            stack.extend(o)
        else:
            if hasattr(o, "__dict__"):
                stack.append(vars(o))
            for cls in type(o).__mro__:
                slots = cls.__dict__.get("__slots__", ())
                for name in (slots,) if isinstance(slots, str) else slots:
                    if hasattr(o, name):
                        stack.append(getattr(o, name))
    return total

Measure it: tracemalloc, streaming vs loading★★☆ · ex03_tracemalloc_streaming

Problem

"Use a generator, it's more memory-efficient" - prove it with numbers.

  1. measure_peak(fn, *args, kwargs) -> tuple[result, peak_bytes] Run fn(rgs, **kwargs) under tracemalloc and return its result together with the PEAK traced memory during the call, measured relative to the traced memory at the start of the call (so it's ~0 for a function that allocates nothing).

    • if tracemalloc is NOT already tracing: start it, and always stop it afterwards (even if fn raises - the exception must propagate)
    • if it IS already tracing (someone else's profiling session): don't stop it - use tracemalloc.reset_peak() and leave tracing on

  2. iter_docs(path) -> iterator of dicts, one per line of a JSONL file (each line is {"id": ..., "text": ...}); blank lines are skipped. Lazy: hold at most one line in memory, and keep the file open only while iterating.

  3. corpus_stats(docs) -> {"docs": int, "tokens": int, "longest": int} tokens = whitespace-separated words in doc["text"] summed over all docs, longest = the max per-doc token count (0 for no docs). Consume docs in ONE pass without materialising it (it may be a generator over a 50 GB file). corpus_stats_eager(path) (given) is the "readlines + list" version for comparison.

  4. biggest_allocation_site(fn) -> (filename, lineno, size_bytes) Take a tracemalloc snapshot, call fn() and KEEP its result alive, take a second snapshot, compare them by "lineno" and return the source line whose allocations grew the most. Same start/stop rule as measure_peak.

Interviewers look for

  • tracemalloc traces Python-level allocations (pymalloc + PyMem): it shows WHERE memory was allocated (file:line), current vs peak. RSS-based tools (psutil, memray for native allocations) answer different questions.
  • Peak memory is what gets your container OOM-killed, not the final number.
  • A generator pipeline makes peak memory O(one record) instead of O(file).

import json
import tracemalloc
from collections.abc import Callable, Iterable, Iterator
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any

__stub_keep__ = ["corpus_stats_eager"]


def corpus_stats_eager(path: Path) -> dict[str, int]:
    """Reference "load everything" version - correct but O(file) memory."""
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:
        lines = f.readlines()
    docs = [json.loads(line) for line in lines if line.strip()]
    counts = [len(d["text"].split()) for d in docs]
    return {"docs": len(docs), "tokens": sum(counts), "longest": max(counts, default=0)}


def measure_peak(fn: Callable[..., Any], *args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> tuple[Any, int]:
    was_tracing = tracemalloc.is_tracing()
    if not was_tracing:
        tracemalloc.start()
    try:
        tracemalloc.reset_peak()
        baseline, _ = tracemalloc.get_traced_memory()
        result = fn(*args, **kwargs)
        _, peak = tracemalloc.get_traced_memory()
        return result, max(0, peak - baseline)
    finally:
        if not was_tracing:
            tracemalloc.stop()


def iter_docs(path: Path) -> Iterator[dict[str, Any]]:
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for line in f:  # file objects are lazy line iterators
            if line.strip():
                yield json.loads(line)


def corpus_stats(docs: Iterable[dict[str, Any]]) -> dict[str, int]:
    n = tokens = longest = 0
    for doc in docs:
        count = len(doc["text"].split())
        n += 1
        tokens += count
        longest = max(longest, count)
    return {"docs": n, "tokens": tokens, "longest": longest}


def biggest_allocation_site(fn: Callable[[], Any]) -> tuple[str, int, int]:
    was_tracing = tracemalloc.is_tracing()
    if not was_tracing:
        tracemalloc.start()
    try:
        before = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()
        result = fn()  # noqa: F841 - must stay alive until the second snapshot
        after = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()
    finally:
        if not was_tracing:
            tracemalloc.stop()
    ignore = [tracemalloc.Filter(False, tracemalloc.__file__)]
    stats = after.filter_traces(ignore).compare_to(before.filter_traces(ignore), "lineno")
    top = max(stats, key=lambda s: s.size_diff)
    frame = top.traceback[0]
    return frame.filename, frame.lineno, top.size_diff

Refcounting, the cycle collector and a leaky chat history★★☆ · ex04_lifetimes_cycles

Problem

CPython frees most objects the instant their reference count hits zero; only objects stuck in reference CYCLES need the cyclic garbage collector (module gc).

  1. added_references(obj, action) -> int Return how many references to obj were created (positive) or dropped (negative) by calling action() - the change in sys.getrefcount(obj) across the call. cache = [] added_references(obj, lambda: cache.extend([obj, obj])) -> 2 (Absolute getrefcount values vary between Python versions - only the DELTA is meaningful.)

  2. classify_lifetime(factory) -> "refcount" | "gc" | "leak" Call factory() to build an object, keep only a weakref.ref to it, drop the strong reference, and report how it dies:

    • "refcount" - already dead right after the last strong reference was dropped
    • "gc" - still alive, but dead after gc.collect() (it was in a cycle)
    • "leak" - still alive even after gc.collect() (something else holds it) The automatic collector must NOT run in the middle of your measurement (it could turn a "gc" into a "refcount"): disable it for the duration and restore the previous gc.isenabled() state afterwards, even on error. If the object doesn't support weak references, let the TypeError propagate.

  3. Conversation / Message - fix the cycle. A conversation holds its messages; each message needs to reach its conversation. The naive version (self.conversation = conversation) creates a cycle for every conversation, so dropped conversations pile up until the GC runs.

    • Conversation(title); .add(role, text) -> creates, stores and returns a Message; .messages -> list of Message in insertion order
    • Message(conversation, role, text); attributes role, text; property conversation returns the Conversation while it is alive, else None. Hold it via weakref.ref so a Conversation (with messages) is freed by refcounting alone: classify_lifetime(lambda: build_conversation_with_messages()) == "refcount"

Interviewers look for

  • Refcounting is deterministic and immediate; the generational cycle GC (thresholds: gc.get_threshold()) is periodic. del x deletes a NAME, not the object.
  • Cycles are not leaks in Python - they're freed later - but "later" can mean big memory spikes, delayed del/close, and GC pauses. Break parent<->child cycles with weakrefs (parent owns children strongly; child points back weakly).
  • Names live in frames (conceptually "the stack"); all objects live on the heap.

import gc
import sys
import weakref
from collections.abc import Callable
from typing import Any, Literal


def added_references(obj: Any, action: Callable[[], Any]) -> int:
    before = sys.getrefcount(obj)
    action()
    return sys.getrefcount(obj) - before


def classify_lifetime(factory: Callable[[], Any]) -> Literal["refcount", "gc", "leak"]:
    was_enabled = gc.isenabled()
    gc.disable()
    try:
        obj = factory()
        ref = weakref.ref(obj)
        del obj  # drop our only strong reference (the name, not the object)
        if ref() is None:
            return "refcount"
        gc.collect()
        return "gc" if ref() is None else "leak"
    finally:
        if was_enabled:
            gc.enable()


class Conversation:
    def __init__(self, title: str) -> None:
        self.title = title
        self.messages: list[Message] = []

    def add(self, role: str, text: str) -> "Message":
        msg = Message(self, role, text)
        self.messages.append(msg)
        return msg


class Message:
    def __init__(self, conversation: Conversation, role: str, text: str) -> None:
        self._conversation = weakref.ref(conversation)
        self.role = role
        self.text = text

    @property
    def conversation(self) -> Conversation | None:
        return self._conversation()

A weak-reference model cache★★★ · ex05_weak_model_cache

Problem

An inference service loads models (tokenizers, rerankers, embedding models) on demand. Loading is slow, so concurrent requests should share one instance - but a model nobody uses any more should be freed, not pinned in RAM forever by the cache.

Build ModelRegistry(loader), where loader(name) -> Model (Model is given):

  • get(name) -> Model
    • returns the cached instance while ANY strong reference to it exists elsewhere
    • otherwise calls loader(name), caches it WEAKLY, and returns it
    • thread-safe: N threads calling get("x") at the same time trigger exactly ONE loader call and all receive the same object
  • loads -> int (property): how many times loader was called
  • name in registry -> True only while that model is alive; len(registry) -> number of live models
  • evicted -> list[str]: names of models in the order they were freed - recorded by a weakref.finalize callback registered when the model is loaded
  • close() -> detach all pending finalizers (no more evicted entries after close) and empty the cache. Idempotent.

Use weakref.WeakValueDictionary for the cache.

Classic bug to avoid: self._cache[name] = self._loader(name) return self._cache[name] # KeyError! nothing else holds the model, so it # died the moment the assignment finished Keep a strong local reference until you return.

Interviewers look for

  • weakref.ref / WeakValueDictionary / WeakKeyDictionary / WeakSet: refer to an object without keeping it alive; entries vanish when the referent is freed.
  • weakref.finalize(obj, fn, *args) must not capture obj (a bound method of obj or obj in args would keep it alive forever). It's safer than del: runs at most once, can be detached, and runs at interpreter exit if still alive.
  • Not every object is weak-referenceable (int, str, tuple, list; slots classes need 'weakref').
  • When you DO want to keep models resident, a bounded LRU (strong refs) is the right tool - weak caching only dedups what's already in use.

Work in exercises/py/18_memory/ex05_weak_model_cache.py (or copy the starter code into any scratch file).

import threading
import weakref
from collections.abc import Callable

__stub_keep__ = ["Model"]


class Model:
    """Stand-in for a heavyweight loaded model."""

    def __init__(self, name: str, size_mb: int = 100) -> None:
        self.name = name
        self.size_mb = size_mb

    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        return f"Model({self.name!r})"


class ModelRegistry:
    def __init__(self, loader: Callable[[str], Model]) -> None:
        self._loader = loader
        self._cache: weakref.WeakValueDictionary[str, Model] = weakref.WeakValueDictionary()
        self._finalizers: list[weakref.finalize] = []
        self._lock = threading.Lock()
        self._loads = 0
        self.evicted: list[str] = []

    def get(self, name: str) -> Model:
        with self._lock:  # one lock: simple; per-name locks would let different models load in parallel
            model = self._cache.get(name)
            if model is None:
                model = self._loader(name)
                self._loads += 1
                self._cache[name] = model
                # callback args reference the list and the name - never the model itself
                self._finalizers = [f for f in self._finalizers if f.alive]
                self._finalizers.append(weakref.finalize(model, self.evicted.append, name))
            return model

    @property
    def loads(self) -> int:
        return self._loads

    def __contains__(self, name: object) -> bool:
        return name in self._cache

    def __len__(self) -> int:
        return len(self._cache)

    def close(self) -> None:
        with self._lock:
            for fin in self._finalizers:
                fin.detach()
            self._finalizers.clear()
            self._cache.clear()

Python Internals and Performance

Reading bytecode with dis★☆☆ · ex01_bytecode_dis

Problem

CPython compiles source to bytecode for a stack-based virtual machine; each function carries a code object (func.code). Write small introspection helpers - the kind of tool you'd use to answer "why is version A faster than version B?".

  1. opnames(func) -> set[str] The set of opcode names in func's bytecode (use dis.get_instructions or dis.Bytecode).

  2. global_names(func) -> set[str] Names func loads with LOAD_GLOBAL - globals AND builtins (len, print, ...). Locals and attributes are not included. Only func's own code object.

  3. code_info(func) -> dict with keys: "argcount" - number of positional parameters (co_argcount) "locals" - tuple of local variable names, parameters first (co_varnames) "is_generator" - True if func is a generator function (check co_flags) "is_coroutine" - True if func is an async def function (check co_flags)

  4. folded_constants(source) -> tuple Compile source (module-level code) and return the code object's co_consts. Lets you see compile-time constant folding: "X = 24 * 60 * 60" stores 86400 directly.

  5. disassembly(func) -> str The human-readable dis listing of func as a string (don't print it: dis.dis accepts a file= argument, or use dis.Bytecode(func).dis()).

Interviewers look for

  • "Python is interpreted" really means: compiled to bytecode once (cached in pycache/ *.pyc), then executed by the eval loop. 3.11+ adds a specializing adaptive interpreter (LOAD_ATTR_INSTANCE_VALUE, BINARY_OP_ADD_INT...), visible with dis(adaptive=True).
  • LOAD_FAST (array index into the frame) vs LOAD_GLOBAL (dict lookups in globals then builtins) - the basis of the "bind to a local" micro-optimisation.
  • Opcode names change between versions (3.13 LOAD_FAST_LOAD_FAST, 3.14 LOAD_FAST_BORROW...), so never hard-code exact bytecode in tests or tools.

import inspect
from collections.abc import Callable
from typing import Any

def opnames(func: Callable[..., Any]) -> set[str]:
    raise NotImplementedError

    raise NotImplementedError

import dis
import inspect
from collections.abc import Callable
from typing import Any


def opnames(func: Callable[..., Any]) -> set[str]:
    return {ins.opname for ins in dis.get_instructions(func)}


def global_names(func: Callable[..., Any]) -> set[str]:
    return {ins.argval for ins in dis.get_instructions(func) if ins.opname == "LOAD_GLOBAL"}


def code_info(func: Callable[..., Any]) -> dict[str, Any]:
    code = func.__code__
    return {
        "argcount": code.co_argcount,
        "locals": code.co_varnames,
        "is_generator": bool(code.co_flags & inspect.CO_GENERATOR),
        "is_coroutine": bool(code.co_flags & inspect.CO_COROUTINE),
    }


def folded_constants(source: str) -> tuple[Any, ...]:
    return compile(source, "<folded>", "exec").co_consts


def disassembly(func: Callable[..., Any]) -> str:
    return dis.Bytecode(func).dis()

Find the hot spot: cProfile, pstats and timeit★★☆ · ex02_profiling_timeit

Problem

"Measure, don't guess." Build a tiny profiling toolkit.

  1. profile_call(fn, *args, **kwargs) -> tuple[result, pstats.Stats] Run fn under cProfile.Profile and return fn's result plus a pstats.Stats object. The profiler must be disabled afterwards even if fn raises (exception propagates).

  2. hottest_functions(stats, n=3, key="tottime") -> list[str] Names (just the function name, e.g. "tokenize") of the n most expensive PYTHON functions, most expensive first. key="tottime" - time spent in the function's own body (excluding callees) key="cumtime" - time including everything it called any other key -> ValueError Skip built-in/C functions (in Stats.stats their filename is "~"). Hint: Stats.stats maps (filename, lineno, funcname) -> (primitive_calls, total_calls, tottime, cumtime, callers)

  3. call_counts(stats) -> dict[str, int] funcname -> TOTAL number of calls (recursive calls included) for Python functions.

  4. best_time(fn, number=1000, repeat=5) -> float Seconds per call of the zero-argument callable fn: run timeit repeat times with number calls each and take the MINIMUM run, divided by number.

  5. rank(candidates, number=1000, repeat=5) -> list[tuple[str, float]] candidates: {"label": zero-arg callable}. Return (label, best_time) pairs sorted fastest first.

Interviewers look for

  • Profile first (cProfile/py-spy) to find WHERE time goes; micro-benchmark (timeit) to compare alternatives for that one spot.
  • tottime vs cumtime: a function with huge cumtime but tiny tottime is just a caller - optimise where tottime is.
  • Why min() of repeats: noise only ever adds time. timeit disables GC during timing and uses time.perf_counter.
  • Deterministic profilers add per-call overhead (distorting tiny functions); sampling profilers (py-spy, scalene, PEP 799's profiling.sampling in 3.15) suit production.

    raise NotImplementedError

    raise NotImplementedError

def call_counts(stats: pstats.Stats) -> dict[str, int]:
    raise NotImplementedError

import cProfile
import pstats
import timeit
from collections.abc import Callable
from typing import Any


def profile_call(fn: Callable[..., Any], *args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> tuple[Any, pstats.Stats]:
    profiler = cProfile.Profile()
    profiler.enable()
    try:
        result = fn(*args, **kwargs)
    finally:
        profiler.disable()
    return result, pstats.Stats(profiler)


def hottest_functions(stats: pstats.Stats, n: int = 3, key: str = "tottime") -> list[str]:
    column = {"tottime": 2, "cumtime": 3}.get(key)
    if column is None:
        raise ValueError(f"key must be 'tottime' or 'cumtime', got {key!r}")
    rows = [
        (values[column], funcname)
        for (filename, _, funcname), values in stats.stats.items()  # type: ignore[attr-defined]
        if filename != "~"
    ]
    rows.sort(reverse=True)
    return [name for _, name in rows[:n]]


def call_counts(stats: pstats.Stats) -> dict[str, int]:
    counts: dict[str, int] = {}
    for (filename, _, funcname), values in stats.stats.items():  # type: ignore[attr-defined]
        if filename != "~":
            counts[funcname] = counts.get(funcname, 0) + values[1]
    return counts


def best_time(fn: Callable[[], Any], number: int = 1000, repeat: int = 5) -> float:
    return min(timeit.Timer(fn).repeat(repeat=repeat, number=number)) / number


def rank(
    candidates: dict[str, Callable[[], Any]], number: int = 1000, repeat: int = 5
) -> list[tuple[str, float]]:
    timings = [(label, best_time(fn, number, repeat)) for label, fn in candidates.items()]
    return sorted(timings, key=lambda pair: pair[1])

Threads for I/O: fan-out, partial failures, hedging★★☆ · ex03_threadpool_io

Problem

Blocking I/O (HTTP calls with a sync SDK, DB queries, file reads) releases the GIL, so a thread pool gives real concurrency for it. Implement with concurrent.futures:

  1. fetch_all(items, fetch, max_workers=8) -> list Call fetch(item) for every item concurrently (at most max_workers at a time) and return the results IN INPUT ORDER. If any call raises, the exception propagates. (Executor.map is made for this.)

  2. embed_settled(texts, embed, max_workers=8) -> tuple[list, dict[int, Exception]] Like fetch_all but failures don't abort the batch: return (results, errors) where results[i] is embed(texts[i]) or None if it failed, and errors maps index -> the exception raised. Use submit() + as_completed() (map can't do per-item errors).

  3. first_successful(endpoints, call, max_workers=4) -> result "Hedged request": call(endpoint) for all endpoints concurrently, return the FIRST successful result as soon as it arrives - do not wait for the slower calls to finish (hint: with ThreadPoolExecutor() waits for everything on exit; you need shutdown(wait=False, cancel_futures=True)). If every call fails raise ExceptionGroup("all endpoints failed", [the exceptions]).

  4. TokenMeter - thread-safe usage counter shared by worker threads: add(model, tokens) - accumulate; totals() -> dict copy {model: tokens} Many threads call add() concurrently; no update may be lost (use threading.Lock).

Interviewers look for

  • Threads help I/O-bound work (the GIL is released while blocked on sockets/files/sleep), not pure-Python CPU-bound work on the default (GIL) build.
  • map() preserves order and raises the first error when you reach it; as_completed() yields in completion order - keep a future->index mapping.
  • x += 1 / read-modify-write on shared state is not atomic: protect with a Lock.
  • Bounded concurrency = max_workers; for asyncio code the equivalent is a Semaphore.

Work in exercises/py/19_internals/ex03_threadpool_io.py (or copy the starter code into any scratch file).

import threading
from collections.abc import Callable, Iterable, Sequence
from concurrent.futures import Future, ThreadPoolExecutor, as_completed
from typing import TypeVar
T = TypeVar('T')
R = TypeVar('R')

def fetch_all(items: Iterable[T], fetch: Callable[[T], R], max_workers: int=8) -> list[R]:
    raise NotImplementedError

def embed_settled(texts: Sequence[str], embed: Callable[[str], R], max_workers: int=8) -> tuple[list[R | None], dict[int, Exception]]:
    raise NotImplementedError

def first_successful(endpoints: Sequence[T], call: Callable[[T], R], max_workers: int=4) -> R:
    raise NotImplementedError

class TokenMeter:

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        raise NotImplementedError

import threading
from collections.abc import Callable, Iterable, Sequence
from concurrent.futures import Future, ThreadPoolExecutor, as_completed
from typing import TypeVar

T = TypeVar("T")
R = TypeVar("R")


def fetch_all(items: Iterable[T], fetch: Callable[[T], R], max_workers: int = 8) -> list[R]:
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=max_workers) as pool:
        return list(pool.map(fetch, items))


def embed_settled(
    texts: Sequence[str], embed: Callable[[str], R], max_workers: int = 8
) -> tuple[list[R | None], dict[int, Exception]]:
    results: list[R | None] = [None] * len(texts)
    errors: dict[int, Exception] = {}
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=max_workers) as pool:
        futures = {pool.submit(embed, text): i for i, text in enumerate(texts)}
        for fut in as_completed(futures):
            i = futures[fut]
            exc = fut.exception()
            if exc is None:
                results[i] = fut.result()
            elif isinstance(exc, Exception):
                errors[i] = exc
            else:  # KeyboardInterrupt/SystemExit-style: don't swallow
                raise exc
    return results, errors


def first_successful(
    endpoints: Sequence[T], call: Callable[[T], R], max_workers: int = 4
) -> R:
    if not endpoints:
        raise ValueError("need at least one endpoint")
    pool = ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=max_workers)
    try:
        futures: list[Future[R]] = [pool.submit(call, ep) for ep in endpoints]
        errors: list[Exception] = []
        for fut in as_completed(futures):
            exc = fut.exception()
            if exc is None:
                return fut.result()
            if not isinstance(exc, Exception):
                raise exc
            errors.append(exc)
        raise ExceptionGroup("all endpoints failed", errors)
    finally:
        # don't block on the slow calls; drop the ones that haven't started
        pool.shutdown(wait=False, cancel_futures=True)


class TokenMeter:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._lock = threading.Lock()
        self._totals: dict[str, int] = {}

    def add(self, model: str, tokens: int) -> None:
        with self._lock:
            self._totals[model] = self._totals.get(model, 0) + tokens

    def totals(self) -> dict[str, int]:
        with self._lock:
            return dict(self._totals)

Processes for CPU: chunking, pickling, the GIL★★★ · ex04_processpool_cpu

internals.concurrency_models

Problem

Pure-Python CPU-bound work doesn't speed up with threads on the default CPython build (the GIL lets one thread execute bytecode at a time). Processes each have their own interpreter and GIL - but everything crossing the process boundary is PICKLED.

  1. gil_status() -> {"free_threaded_build": bool, "gil_enabled": bool} free_threaded_build - interpreter was built with --disable-gil (sysconfig config var "Py_GIL_DISABLED" == 1) gil_enabled - the GIL is active right now: sys._is_gil_enabled() where it exists (3.13+), else True. (A free-threaded build can re-enable the GIL, e.g. PYTHON_GIL=1 or an incompatible C extension.)

  2. split_ranges(n, parts) -> list[range] Split range(n) into at most parts contiguous, non-empty ranges whose lengths differ by at most 1 (longer ones first), covering 0..n-1 in order. split_ranges(10, 3) == [range(0, 4), range(4, 7), range(7, 10)] split_ranges(2, 5) == [range(0, 1), range(1, 2)] split_ranges(0, 3) == [] parts < 1 or n < 0 -> ValueError.

  3. parallel_sum_of_squares(n, workers=4) -> int sum(i*i for i in range(n)) computed with a ProcessPoolExecutor: one task per range from split_ranges(n, workers). The worker function must be picklable AND importable by a child process - use the builtin math.sumprod(r, r) (3.12+) on each range (ranges pickle cheaply: start/stop/step, not a list of numbers).

  4. run_cpu_bound(func, items, max_workers=4, chunksize=1) -> list Map func over items in a ProcessPoolExecutor, results in input order. BEFORE starting any process, verify func can be pickled (pickle.dumps); if not, raise TypeError("... not picklable ...") chained from the original error. Lambdas and functions defined inside other functions can't be pickled. Exceptions raised inside a worker propagate to the caller with their original type.

Note: child processes find a function by importing its module by name. With the "spawn" start method (macOS/Windows) and "forkserver" (Linux default since 3.14) a function from a module loaded by file path isn't importable in the child - stick to stdlib/builtin workers here. In real code, put worker functions at module top level and guard entry points with if __name__ == "__main__":.

Interviewers look for

  • CPU-bound -> processes (or C extensions / NumPy that release the GIL); I/O-bound -> threads or asyncio.
  • Process overhead: startup, pickling args/results both ways. Send small descriptions of work (a range, a file path), not big data; use chunksize for many tiny tasks.
  • Free-threaded CPython (PEP 703): experimental in 3.13 (python3.13t), officially supported but still optional in 3.14 (PEP 779) - the default build still has a GIL.

import math
import pickle
import sys
import sysconfig
from collections.abc import Callable, Iterable
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor
from typing import Any


def gil_status() -> dict[str, bool]:
    is_enabled = getattr(sys, "_is_gil_enabled", None)
    return {
        "free_threaded_build": sysconfig.get_config_var("Py_GIL_DISABLED") == 1,
        "gil_enabled": is_enabled() if is_enabled is not None else True,
    }


def split_ranges(n: int, parts: int) -> list[range]:
    if parts < 1 or n < 0:
        raise ValueError("need parts >= 1 and n >= 0")
    parts = min(parts, n)
    if parts == 0:
        return []
    base, extra = divmod(n, parts)
    ranges, start = [], 0
    for i in range(parts):
        stop = start + base + (1 if i < extra else 0)
        ranges.append(range(start, stop))
        start = stop
    return ranges


def parallel_sum_of_squares(n: int, workers: int = 4) -> int:
    chunks = split_ranges(n, workers)
    if not chunks:
        return 0
    with ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=len(chunks)) as pool:
        return sum(pool.map(math.sumprod, chunks, chunks))


def run_cpu_bound(
    func: Callable[[Any], Any], items: Iterable[Any], max_workers: int = 4, chunksize: int = 1
) -> list[Any]:
    try:
        pickle.dumps(func)
    except (pickle.PicklingError, AttributeError, TypeError) as exc:
        raise TypeError(f"{func!r} is not picklable; use a module-level function") from exc
    with ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=max_workers) as pool:
        return list(pool.map(func, items, chunksize=chunksize))

Make it O(n): rewriting slow eval-pipeline code★★★ · ex05_optimization

Problem

Three hot spots from a retrieval-eval script. Keep the exact behaviour, fix the complexity. (Tests count how often your code compares or reads objects, so an O(n^2) version fails even if it is "fast enough" on small inputs.)

  1. dedupe_preserve_order(items, key=None) -> list Original: out = [] for x in items: if x not in out: # list membership: O(len(out)) each time out.append(x) Keep the first occurrence of each item (or of each key(item) when key is given), preserving order, in O(n) using hashing. Items (or keys) are hashable.

  2. join_results(queries, docs) -> list[tuple[str, str]] Original (O(len(queries) * len(docs)) - 10k x 100k = a billion comparisons): out = [] for q in queries: for d in docs: if d["id"] == q["doc_id"]: out.append((q["qid"], d["title"])) return out Same output, same order (queries order, then docs order for duplicate doc ids; queries with no matching doc contribute nothing) in O(len(queries) + len(docs)): build an index once. Read each doc's fields only a constant number of times.

  3. top_k_frequent(tokens, k) -> list[tuple[str, int]] The k most common tokens with counts, most common first; ties broken by first appearance in tokens. k <= 0 -> []. Don't sort the full vocabulary by hand in a Python loop - collections.Counter (and heapq.nlargest inside most_common) exist.

Interviewers look for

  • Algorithmic wins (right data structure: set/dict O(1) average lookup) beat every micro-optimisation. Profile first, then fix the complexity.
  • Then, in a measured hot loop: bind attribute lookups to locals (append = out.append), prefer built-ins / comprehensions (C loops), "".join(parts) instead of += in a loop, avoid repeated work (cache with functools.lru_cache / cache), vectorise with NumPy.
  • Always preserve behaviour - ordering and duplicate semantics are where rewrites break.

from collections import Counter
from collections.abc import Callable, Hashable, Iterable, Mapping
from typing import Any, TypeVar

T = TypeVar("T")


def dedupe_preserve_order(
    items: Iterable[T], key: Callable[[T], Hashable] | None = None
) -> list[T]:
    seen: set[Hashable] = set()
    out: list[T] = []
    add, append = seen.add, out.append  # local binding in the hot loop
    for item in items:
        k = item if key is None else key(item)
        if k not in seen:
            add(k)
            append(item)
    return out


def join_results(
    queries: Iterable[Mapping[str, Any]], docs: Iterable[Mapping[str, Any]]
) -> list[tuple[str, str]]:
    titles_by_id: dict[Any, list[str]] = {}
    for d in docs:
        titles_by_id.setdefault(d["id"], []).append(d["title"])
    return [
        (q["qid"], title)
        for q in queries
        for title in titles_by_id.get(q["doc_id"], ())
    ]


def top_k_frequent(tokens: Iterable[str], k: int) -> list[tuple[str, int]]:
    if k <= 0:
        return []
    # Counter preserves first-insertion order and most_common() is stable for ties
    return Counter(tokens).most_common(k)

Embedding arrays: creation, dtype, shape, views★☆☆ · ex01_embedding_arrays

numpy.indexing, numpy.random, numpy.vs_lists

Problem

Embedding APIs give you Python lists of floats; everything downstream wants a (n_vectors, dim) float32 ndarray.

  1. to_matrix(rows) -> np.ndarray Convert a list of equal-length lists of numbers into a 2-D float32 array. ValueError if rows is empty, ragged (different lengths), or not 2-D (e.g. a flat list of numbers).

  2. describe(arr) -> dict with keys "shape" (tuple), "ndim", "dtype" (str, e.g. "float32"), "size" (number of elements), "nbytes", "itemsize".

  3. as_batches(flat, dim) -> np.ndarray A 1-D buffer of n*dim numbers (e.g. read from a binary file) reshaped to (n, dim) WITHOUT copying (the result must share memory with flat). ValueError if flat isn't 1-D or its length isn't a multiple of dim.

  4. random_embeddings(n, dim, seed) -> np.ndarray (n, dim) float32 standard-normal values from np.random.default_rng(seed). The same seed gives identical arrays; the legacy global state (np.random.seed / np.random.rand) must not be touched.

  5. every_other_dim(arr) -> np.ndarray Columns 0, 2, 4, ... of a 2-D array, as a VIEW (basic slicing, not fancy indexing).

  6. last_rows(arr, k) -> np.ndarray The last k rows of a 2-D array (k=0 -> shape (0, dim); k > n -> all rows).

Interviewers look for

  • An ndarray is one contiguous typed buffer + shape + strides; a list is an array of pointers to boxed Python objects (8-byte pointer + ~24-byte float each).
  • float32 halves memory vs float64 and is what vector DBs / GPUs use.
  • Basic slicing returns views (no copy); fancy/boolean indexing returns copies; reshape returns a view when strides allow.
  • np.random.default_rng(seed) (Generator API) instead of the legacy global np.random.seed.

import numpy as np
import numpy.typing as npt


def to_matrix(rows: list[list[float]]) -> np.ndarray:
    if not rows:
        raise ValueError("no rows")
    try:
        arr = np.asarray(rows, dtype=np.float32)
    except ValueError as exc:  # NumPy refuses ragged nested sequences
        raise ValueError("ragged rows: all embeddings must have the same dim") from exc
    if arr.ndim != 2:
        raise ValueError(f"expected a 2-D list of lists, got ndim={arr.ndim}")
    return arr


def describe(arr: np.ndarray) -> dict[str, object]:
    return {
        "shape": arr.shape,
        "ndim": arr.ndim,
        "dtype": str(arr.dtype),
        "size": arr.size,
        "nbytes": arr.nbytes,
        "itemsize": arr.itemsize,
    }


def as_batches(flat: npt.NDArray[np.floating], dim: int) -> np.ndarray:
    if flat.ndim != 1:
        raise ValueError("flat must be 1-D")
    if dim <= 0 or flat.size % dim:
        raise ValueError(f"length {flat.size} is not a multiple of dim={dim}")
    return flat.reshape(-1, dim)


def random_embeddings(n: int, dim: int, seed: int) -> np.ndarray:
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    return rng.standard_normal((n, dim), dtype=np.float32)


def every_other_dim(arr: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    return arr[:, ::2]


def last_rows(arr: np.ndarray, k: int) -> np.ndarray:
    if k <= 0:
        return arr[:0]
    return arr[-k:]

L2 normalisation and cosine similarity, vectorised★★☆ · ex02_cosine_similarity

numpy.axis

Problem

The core math of semantic search. NO Python loops over rows - whole-array operations only.

  1. l2_normalize(x, axis=-1) -> np.ndarray Scale vectors to unit L2 norm along axis (works for 1-D and 2-D input). Zero vectors must stay all-zero: no division-by-zero warnings, no NaN. Don't modify the input; keep the input's floating dtype (float32 in -> float32 out).

  2. cosine_similarity(a, b) -> np.ndarray a: (n, d), b: (m, d) -> (n, m) matrix with sim[i, j] = cos(a[i], b[j]). A 1-D a or b is treated as a single row (shape (d,) -> (1, d)). Similarity involving a zero vector is 0.0. Mismatched d -> ValueError.

  3. pairwise_l2(a, b) -> np.ndarray (n, m) Euclidean distances via the expansion ||a||^2 + ||b||^2 - 2 a.b (matrix product plus broadcasting), NOT by materialising an (n, m, d) difference array. Clip tiny negative values (floating-point error) to 0 before the square root.

Interviewers look for

  • keepdims=True (or [:, None]) so (n, 1) broadcasts against (n, d).
  • Normalise once, then cosine = dot product -> one matmul gives all n*m similarities.
  • Guarding zero norms with np.where / np.maximum(norm, eps) instead of letting NaN leak into your index.
  • The (n, m, d) broadcasting version is elegant but O(nmd) memory - a classic OOM. The expansion trick is memory-cheap but suffers cancellation error for near-identical vectors in float32 (distance ~1e-3 instead of 0) - fine for ranking.

import numpy as np

    raise NotImplementedError

def cosine_similarity(a: np.ndarray, b: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    raise NotImplementedError

    raise NotImplementedError

import numpy as np


def l2_normalize(x: np.ndarray, axis: int = -1) -> np.ndarray:
    x = np.asarray(x)
    if not np.issubdtype(x.dtype, np.floating):
        x = x.astype(np.float64)
    norms = np.linalg.norm(x, axis=axis, keepdims=True)
    # divide only where norm > 0; zero vectors stay zero (and no warning is raised)
    return np.divide(x, norms, out=np.zeros_like(x), where=norms > 0)


def cosine_similarity(a: np.ndarray, b: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    a, b = np.atleast_2d(a), np.atleast_2d(b)
    if a.shape[1] != b.shape[1]:
        raise ValueError(f"dimension mismatch: {a.shape[1]} vs {b.shape[1]}")
    return l2_normalize(a) @ l2_normalize(b).T


def pairwise_l2(a: np.ndarray, b: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    a, b = np.atleast_2d(a), np.atleast_2d(b)
    if a.shape[1] != b.shape[1]:
        raise ValueError(f"dimension mismatch: {a.shape[1]} vs {b.shape[1]}")
    sq = (a * a).sum(axis=1)[:, None] + (b * b).sum(axis=1)[None, :] - 2.0 * (a @ b.T)
    return np.sqrt(np.maximum(sq, 0.0))

Top-k retrieval and retrieval metrics★★☆ · ex03_topk_retrieval

numpy.vectorization

Problem

After computing similarity scores you need the best k documents per query, filtering, and offline metrics. No Python loops over queries or documents.

  1. top_k(scores, k) -> np.ndarray of int indices scores: 1-D. Indices of the k highest scores, highest first. Use np.argpartition (O(n)) to select, then sort only those k. k > len(scores) -> all indices; k <= 0 -> empty int array. (Inputs in tests have no ties.)

  2. top_k_rows(scores, k) -> (indices, values) scores: (n_queries, n_docs). Per row, the top-k indices and their scores, both of shape (n_queries, min(k, n_docs)), highest first in each row. Hint: argpartition along axis=1 and np.take_along_axis.

  3. filter_hits(ids, scores, min_score, exclude=None) -> (ids, scores) ids, scores: 1-D arrays of equal length. Keep hits with score >= min_score whose id is NOT in exclude (an iterable of ids already shown to the user, may be None), sorted by score descending. Use boolean masks (np.isin for exclusion).

  4. recall_at_k(retrieved, relevant) -> float retrieved: (n_queries, k) int doc indices; relevant: (n_queries,) the gold doc index per query. Fraction of queries whose gold doc appears anywhere in its row.

  5. mrr(retrieved, relevant) -> float Mean reciprocal rank: per query 1/(position+1) of the gold doc in its row (position 0 = first), or 0 if absent; averaged over queries.

Interviewers look for

  • argpartition vs argsort: O(n) selection + O(k log k) sort instead of O(n log n) for a million-doc corpus.
  • Broadcasting a comparison (retrieved == relevant[:, None]) to build a boolean matrix, then reducing along an axis with any()/argmax().
  • Boolean masks return copies; combining masks with & | ~ (not and/or).

    raise NotImplementedError

from collections.abc import Iterable

import numpy as np


def top_k(scores: np.ndarray, k: int) -> np.ndarray:
    n = scores.shape[0]
    if k <= 0 or n == 0:
        return np.empty(0, dtype=np.intp)
    k = min(k, n)
    idx = np.argpartition(-scores, k - 1)[:k] if k < n else np.arange(n)
    return idx[np.argsort(-scores[idx])]


def top_k_rows(scores: np.ndarray, k: int) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    n_docs = scores.shape[1]
    k = max(0, min(k, n_docs))
    if k == 0:
        empty = np.empty((scores.shape[0], 0), dtype=np.intp)
        return empty, np.empty((scores.shape[0], 0), dtype=scores.dtype)
    if k < n_docs:
        part = np.argpartition(-scores, k - 1, axis=1)[:, :k]  # unordered top-k per row
    else:
        part = np.broadcast_to(np.arange(n_docs), scores.shape)
    part_scores = np.take_along_axis(scores, part, axis=1)
    order = np.argsort(-part_scores, axis=1)
    indices = np.take_along_axis(part, order, axis=1)
    return indices, np.take_along_axis(scores, indices, axis=1)


def filter_hits(
    ids: np.ndarray, scores: np.ndarray, min_score: float, exclude: Iterable | None = None
) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    mask = scores >= min_score
    if exclude is not None:
        mask &= ~np.isin(ids, np.asarray(list(exclude)))
    kept_ids, kept_scores = ids[mask], scores[mask]
    order = np.argsort(-kept_scores, kind="stable")
    return kept_ids[order], kept_scores[order]


def recall_at_k(retrieved: np.ndarray, relevant: np.ndarray) -> float:
    hits = (retrieved == relevant[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    return float(hits.mean())


def mrr(retrieved: np.ndarray, relevant: np.ndarray) -> float:
    matches = retrieved == relevant[:, None]
    found = matches.any(axis=1)
    first_pos = matches.argmax(axis=1)  # argmax of a bool row = first True (0 if none)
    reciprocal = np.where(found, 1.0 / (first_pos + 1), 0.0)
    return float(reciprocal.mean())

Mean pooling, softmax and batched attention★★★ · ex04_pooling_attention

numpy.aggregation

Problem

What sentence-transformers and a transformer layer do, in NumPy. Shapes: B = batch, T = query tokens, S = key tokens, D = hidden size, H = heads. No Python loops over the batch, tokens or heads.

  1. mean_pool(token_embs, attention_mask) -> (B, D) token_embs (B, T, D); attention_mask (B, T) of 0/1 (or bools), 1 = real token, 0 = padding. Average only the real tokens of each sequence. A sequence with no real tokens pools to a zero vector (no NaN, no warnings).

  2. softmax(x, axis=-1) -> same shape Numerically stable (subtract the max along axis first): softmax([1000, 1000]) must be [0.5, 0.5], not NaN.

  3. attention(q, k, v, key_mask=None) -> (output (B, T, Dv), weights (B, T, S)) Scaled dot-product attention: weights = softmax(q @ k^T / sqrt(D)) over the S axis, output = weights @ v. q (B, T, D), k (B, S, D), v (B, S, Dv). key_mask (B, S): 1/True = attend, 0/False = padding key -> weight exactly 0. If ALL keys of a sequence are masked, its weights (and output) are all zeros.

  4. split_heads(x, n_heads) -> (B, H, T, D // H) Reshape the hidden dimension into heads and move the head axis before T. D not divisible by n_heads -> ValueError. merge_heads(x) -> (B, T, H * Dh) is the exact inverse.

Interviewers look for

  • Picking the right axis and keeping dims ((B, T, 1) mask broadcasting over D).
  • Why max-subtraction makes softmax stable (exp overflows above ~709 in float64, ~88 in float32) and doesn't change the result.
  • @ / np.matmul broadcasts over leading (batch) dims; transpose only the last two axes (k.swapaxes(-1, -2)), not k.T which reverses ALL axes.
  • reshape vs transpose: reshape reinterprets memory order, transpose permutes axes; you need both to split heads correctly.

import numpy as np

import numpy as np


def mean_pool(token_embs: np.ndarray, attention_mask: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    mask = attention_mask.astype(token_embs.dtype)[..., None]  # (B, T, 1)
    summed = (token_embs * mask).sum(axis=1)  # (B, D)
    counts = mask.sum(axis=1)  # (B, 1)
    return np.divide(summed, counts, out=np.zeros_like(summed), where=counts > 0)


def softmax(x: np.ndarray, axis: int = -1) -> np.ndarray:
    shifted = x - np.max(x, axis=axis, keepdims=True)
    e = np.exp(shifted)
    return e / e.sum(axis=axis, keepdims=True)


def attention(
    q: np.ndarray, k: np.ndarray, v: np.ndarray, key_mask: np.ndarray | None = None
) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    d = q.shape[-1]
    scores = q @ k.swapaxes(-1, -2) / np.sqrt(d)  # (B, T, S)
    if key_mask is not None:
        scores = np.where(key_mask.astype(bool)[:, None, :], scores, -np.inf)
    row_max = np.max(scores, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
    row_max = np.where(np.isfinite(row_max), row_max, 0.0)  # fully-masked rows
    e = np.exp(scores - row_max)  # exp(-inf) == 0 for masked keys
    total = e.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True)
    weights = np.divide(e, total, out=np.zeros_like(e), where=total > 0)
    return weights @ v, weights


def split_heads(x: np.ndarray, n_heads: int) -> np.ndarray:
    b, t, d = x.shape
    if n_heads <= 0 or d % n_heads:
        raise ValueError(f"hidden size {d} not divisible by n_heads={n_heads}")
    return x.reshape(b, t, n_heads, d // n_heads).transpose(0, 2, 1, 3)


def merge_heads(x: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    b, h, t, dh = x.shape
    return x.transpose(0, 2, 1, 3).reshape(b, t, h * dh)

A brute-force vector index★★★ · ex05_vector_index

numpy.vs_lists

Problem

Before reaching for FAISS/pgvector, build the exact (brute-force) version every ANN index is evaluated against.

VectorIndex(dim, metric="cosine") metric in {"cosine", "dot", "l2"}, else ValueError

add(ids, vectors) * ids: sequence of str; vectors: array-like of shape (len(ids), dim) * ValueError on wrong shape, on an id that already exists, or duplicate ids within the batch. Atomic: on error nothing is added. * stored as float32; for "cosine" store the L2-normalised vectors (normalise once at insert, not on every search). Zero vectors stay zero. * many small add() calls must not be O(n^2) overall: don't np.vstack the whole matrix on every call - keep a preallocated buffer and grow its capacity geometrically (like list does).

len() -> number of live (not removed) vectors

remove(id) -> None KeyError if the id isn't live. Removed vectors never appear in results.

search(query, k=5, allowed_ids=None) -> list[(id, score)] * query: shape (dim,); ValueError on wrong shape * "cosine": cosine similarity, "dot": raw dot product - highest first "l2": Euclidean distance - LOWEST first (score is the distance) * allowed_ids: optional collection of ids - only those may be returned (metadata pre-filtering). Unknown ids in it are ignored. * at most k results (fewer if fewer candidates); scores are Python floats * one matrix-vector product for the whole index, top-k via np.argpartition

search_batch(queries, k=5) -> list[list[(id, score)]] queries (q, dim); result i equals search(queries[i], k). One matrix-matrix product for all queries (no Python loop over the index rows).

Interviewers look for

  • Brute force is O(N*d) per query and exact; it's the ground truth for measuring ANN recall (HNSW/IVF trade recall for speed).
  • Normalise at write time so cosine == dot at read time.
  • Pre-filtering with a boolean mask vs post-filtering top-k (which can return < k hits).
  • Amortised growth: geometric capacity -> O(1) amortised append, the same trick as list.

Work in exercises/py/20_numpy/ex05_vector_index.py (or copy the starter code into any scratch file).

from collections.abc import Collection, Sequence
import numpy as np
import numpy.typing as npt

class VectorIndex:

    def __init__(self, dim: int, metric: str='cosine') -> None:
        raise NotImplementedError

    def __len__(self) -> int:
        raise NotImplementedError

    def add(self, ids: Sequence[str], vectors: npt.ArrayLike) -> None:
        raise NotImplementedError

    def remove(self, id_: str) -> None:
        raise NotImplementedError

    def search(self, query: npt.ArrayLike, k: int=5, allowed_ids: Collection[str] | None=None) -> list[tuple[str, float]]:
        raise NotImplementedError

    def search_batch(self, queries: npt.ArrayLike, k: int=5) -> list[list[tuple[str, float]]]:
        raise NotImplementedError

from collections.abc import Collection, Sequence

import numpy as np
import numpy.typing as npt

_METRICS = ("cosine", "dot", "l2")


def _normalize_rows(x: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    norms = np.linalg.norm(x, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    return np.divide(x, norms, out=np.zeros_like(x), where=norms > 0)


def _grow(vecs: np.ndarray, alive: np.ndarray, needed: int) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    capacity = vecs.shape[0]
    while capacity < needed:
        capacity *= 2  # geometric growth -> amortised O(1) per added row
    new_vecs = np.empty((capacity, vecs.shape[1]), dtype=vecs.dtype)
    new_vecs[: vecs.shape[0]] = vecs
    new_alive = np.zeros(capacity, dtype=bool)
    new_alive[: alive.shape[0]] = alive
    return new_vecs, new_alive


def _scores(mat: np.ndarray, qs: np.ndarray, metric: str) -> np.ndarray:
    """(q, n) scores where higher is better for every metric (l2 -> -squared distance)."""
    if metric == "cosine":
        qs = _normalize_rows(qs)
    dots = qs @ mat.T
    if metric != "l2":
        return dots
    sq = (qs * qs).sum(axis=1)[:, None] + (mat * mat).sum(axis=1)[None, :] - 2 * dots
    return -np.maximum(sq, 0.0)


def _rank(
    scores: np.ndarray, mask: np.ndarray, k: int, row_ids: list[str], metric: str
) -> list[tuple[str, float]]:
    candidates = np.flatnonzero(mask)
    k = min(k, candidates.size)
    if k <= 0:
        return []
    cand_scores = scores[candidates]
    top = np.argpartition(-cand_scores, k - 1)[:k]
    top = top[np.argsort(-cand_scores[top], kind="stable")]
    results = []
    for i in top:
        score = float(cand_scores[i])
        if metric == "l2":
            score = float(np.sqrt(-score))
        results.append((row_ids[candidates[i]], score))
    return results


class VectorIndex:
    def __init__(self, dim: int, metric: str = "cosine") -> None:
        if metric not in _METRICS:
            raise ValueError(f"metric must be one of {_METRICS}")
        if dim <= 0:
            raise ValueError("dim must be positive")
        self.dim = dim
        self.metric = metric
        self._vecs = np.empty((16, dim), dtype=np.float32)
        self._alive = np.zeros(16, dtype=bool)
        self._n = 0  # rows used (live + removed)
        self._row_ids: list[str] = []
        self._rows: dict[str, int] = {}  # live id -> row

    def __len__(self) -> int:
        return len(self._rows)

    def add(self, ids: Sequence[str], vectors: npt.ArrayLike) -> None:
        vecs = np.asarray(vectors, dtype=np.float32)
        ids = list(ids)
        if vecs.ndim != 2 or vecs.shape != (len(ids), self.dim):
            raise ValueError(f"expected shape ({len(ids)}, {self.dim}), got {vecs.shape}")
        if len(set(ids)) != len(ids) or any(i in self._rows for i in ids):
            raise ValueError("duplicate ids")
        if self.metric == "cosine":
            vecs = _normalize_rows(vecs)  # once at write time: cosine == dot at read time
        if self._n + len(ids) > self._vecs.shape[0]:
            self._vecs, self._alive = _grow(self._vecs, self._alive, self._n + len(ids))
        start, stop = self._n, self._n + len(ids)
        self._vecs[start:stop] = vecs
        self._alive[start:stop] = True
        self._row_ids.extend(ids)
        self._rows.update(zip(ids, range(start, stop), strict=True))
        self._n = stop

    def remove(self, id_: str) -> None:
        row = self._rows.pop(id_)  # KeyError if not live
        self._alive[row] = False

    def search(
        self, query: npt.ArrayLike, k: int = 5, allowed_ids: Collection[str] | None = None
    ) -> list[tuple[str, float]]:
        q = np.asarray(query, dtype=np.float32)
        if q.shape != (self.dim,):
            raise ValueError(f"query must have shape ({self.dim},), got {q.shape}")
        mask = self._alive[: self._n].copy()
        if allowed_ids is not None:
            allowed = np.zeros(self._n, dtype=bool)
            allowed[[self._rows[i] for i in allowed_ids if i in self._rows]] = True
            mask &= allowed
        scores = _scores(self._vecs[: self._n], q[None, :], self.metric)[0]
        return _rank(scores, mask, k, self._row_ids, self.metric)

    def search_batch(self, queries: npt.ArrayLike, k: int = 5) -> list[list[tuple[str, float]]]:
        qs = np.asarray(queries, dtype=np.float32)
        if qs.ndim != 2 or qs.shape[1] != self.dim:
            raise ValueError(f"queries must have shape (q, {self.dim}), got {qs.shape}")
        scores = _scores(self._vecs[: self._n], qs, self.metric)  # (q, n): one matmul
        mask = self._alive[: self._n]
        return [_rank(row, mask, k, self._row_ids, self.metric) for row in scores]

Data Processing with Pandas

LLM usage DataFrame: build, inspect, select★☆☆ · ex01_usage_frame

pandas.loc_iloc, pandas.sorting

Problem

You get per-request usage records from an LLM gateway: {"request_id": "r1", "model": "gpt-4o", "prompt_tokens": 1200, "completion_tokens": 300}

  1. usage_frame(records) -> DataFrame * index: request_id (named "request_id"); columns exactly, in order: ["model", "prompt_tokens", "completion_tokens", "total_tokens"] * total_tokens = prompt_tokens + completion_tokens (vectorised column arithmetic) * an empty list -> empty frame with those columns and index name

  2. summarize(df) -> dict {"rows": int, "columns": list of column names, "nulls": {column: number of missing values}, "numeric_columns": names of numeric columns, in column order}

  3. heavy_requests(df, min_total) -> DataFrame Rows with total_tokens >= min_total, only columns ["model", "total_tokens"], sorted by total_tokens descending; ties keep the original row order (stable sort).

  4. row_at(df, position) -> Series the row at integer POSITION (0 = first row) row_for(df, label) -> Series the row whose index LABEL is label (With an integer index like [10, 3, 7] these differ - that's the point.)

  5. flag_requests(df, labels, column="flagged") -> DataFrame Return a NEW frame with a boolean column that is True for the given index labels and False elsewhere. The input frame must not change. Use .loc[row_labels, column] = ... (chained assignment like df[column][labels] = True does nothing under pandas 3's Copy-on-Write).

Interviewers look for

  • A DataFrame is a dict of column Series sharing one index; a Series is values + index.
  • .loc is label-based (slices INCLUDE the end label), .iloc is position-based (slices exclude the end) - and plain df[...] means columns, or boolean row masks.
  • Boolean masks combine with & | ~ and parentheses.
  • Copy-on-Write (default in pandas 3): every indexing result behaves like a copy; modify with a single .loc call on the object you own.
